# Supersymmetry and supergravity {#sec-susy-sugra}

Every symmetry of the earlier chapters has a commuting parameter: a rotation angle, a boost rapidity, a gauge
function. Supersymmetry is the one extension of spacetime symmetry whose parameter is an anticommuting spinor. Its
generators turn bosons into fermions and back, and the anticommutator of two of them is a translation, so that a
supersymmetric theory always pairs particles of different spin with equal masses. When the spinor parameter is
allowed to depend on the spacetime point, the translations it generates become local, that is general coordinate
transformations, and gravity is forced into the theory: local supersymmetry is supergravity.

The chapter has two parts. The first, on global supersymmetry, introduces the anticommuting numbers and the
two-component spinors in which the subject is most economically written, the supersymmetry algebra and its
representations on particle states, the Wess-Zumino model of a scalar and a fermion with its auxiliary field, and
the superpotential, the gauge multiplets and the spontaneous breaking of supersymmetry. The second, on supergravity,
introduces Majorana spinors, the gravitino as the gauge field of local supersymmetry, the supergravity multiplets,
and eleven-dimensional supergravity, the largest theory of its kind, together with the Freund-Rubin solution in
which four dimensions of spacetime are curved into anti-de Sitter space and seven into a sphere.

Every statement is followed by three examples of increasing complexity and three exercises of increasing difficulty
with hidden solutions. The anticommuting computations, the matrix identities, the superpotential algebra, the
counting of states and the Freund-Rubin curvatures are derived in full, and the eleven-dimensional action is displayed
and cited rather than derived. The signature is
$(+, -, -, -)$ throughout, $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$, with the standard Weyl matrices
$\gamma^\mu = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma^\mu \\ \bar\sigma^\mu & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma^\mu = (1, \vec\sigma)$,
$\bar\sigma^\mu = (1, -\vec\sigma)$; the main sources, @martin1997 and @tanii1998, use the mostly-plus and our
signature respectively, and every formula taken from the former is converted, with the change of sign noted.

## Supersymmetry {#sec-supersymmetry}

Supersymmetry is a symmetry whose generators are spinors and whose anticommutator is a translation. This part
develops it in three sections. The superalgebra introduces the anticommuting numbers in which fermionic quantities
are written, the two-component Weyl spinors, the supercharges, the supersymmetry algebra and its irreducible
representations, the supermultiplets, whose massless states form ladders of helicities. The Wess-Zumino model
builds the simplest supersymmetric field theory, one complex scalar and one Weyl fermion, checks its invariance with
the anticommuting fields handled by the computer, and shows why an auxiliary field is needed for the algebra to
close without the equations of motion. The superpotential and gauge multiplets constructs all renormalisable
interactions from a single holomorphic function and the gauge couplings, derives the positive scalar potential,
and studies the spontaneous breaking of supersymmetry in the O'Raifeartaigh and Fayet-Iliopoulos models.

### The superalgebra {#sec-superalgebra}

Every symmetry met so far has had commuting parameters; supersymmetry is a symmetry whose parameter is an
anticommuting spinor, whose generators are fermionic, and whose algebra closes on the translations. This
section defines the anticommuting numbers, the two-component spinors in which supersymmetry is most economically
written, the supercharges and their algebra, and the supermultiplets, following @martin1997 [Secs. 1-2]. Martin
writes in the mostly-plus metric $(-, +, +, +)$; we use $(+, -, -, -)$ (@sec-conventions-indices), as @tanii1998
does, and every formula quoted from Martin that contains $\eta^{\mu\nu}$ or a contraction with it is converted
below, with the sign flip noted. The supersymmetric oscillator realises the whole structure on explicit matrices,
and the $\sigma$-matrix identities are established on the explicit Pauli matrices.

#### Anticommuting numbers

A classical fermion field cannot take values in the ordinary numbers: the Pauli principle requires that two
fermionic quantities anticommute, and in particular that each squares to zero. The algebra with this property is
the exterior algebra of differential forms, now read as an algebra of numbers rather than of forms, and its
generators are called Grassmann variables.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-grassmann-variable}
#### Grassmann variable

A **Grassmann variable** is a generator $\theta$ of an algebra in which generators anticommute, $\theta_i\theta_j = -
\theta_j\theta_i$, so that $\theta_i^2 = 0$; the algebra generated by $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_n$ is the exterior
algebra $\Lambda(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_n)$ of @sec-forms over the numbers, of dimension $2^n$. Products of an
even number of generators commute with everything (**bosonic**), products of an odd number anticommute among
themselves (**fermionic**). Classical fermion fields and supersymmetry parameters are Grassmann-valued.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest interesting case has two generators, and it already shows the two features that matter in practice.
Every function is a polynomial of bounded degree, and the product of the two generators behaves like an ordinary
commuting number that squares to zero.

::: {#exm-grassmann-two}
#### Two generators

$\Lambda(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ has the basis $1, \theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_1\theta_2$; a general element is $a + b\theta_1 +
c\theta_2 + d\theta_1\theta_2$, every function of the $\theta$ is a polynomial of degree at most two, and
$(\theta_1\theta_2)^2 = 0$ (@exr-grassmann).
:::

Spinors whose components are Grassmann variables are the objects of supersymmetry. Contracting two of them with the
antisymmetric symbol produces a product in which two minus signs meet, one from the anticommuting components and
one from the antisymmetric symbol, and the result is symmetric.

::: {#exm-grassmann-spinor-product}
#### The spinor product is symmetric

For two-component Grassmann spinors, $\xi\chi \equiv \xi^\alpha\chi_\alpha = \xi_2\chi_1 - \xi_1\chi_2 = \chi\xi$
(@def-weyl-spinor): the sign from reordering anticommuting components is cancelled by the antisymmetry of the
$\epsilon$ symbol [@martin1997, eq. 2.16], and $\xi\xi = 2\xi_2\xi_1 \neq 0$ although each component squares to zero
(@exr-grassmann).
:::

Keeping track of these signs by hand is the main source of error in supersymmetric computations. The third example
names the tool that removes the problem in this chapter: an exterior algebra whose coefficients may themselves be
polynomials in commuting fields.

::: {#exm-grassmann-sage}
#### Grassmann algebra in Sage

Sage's `ExteriorAlgebra` implements @def-grassmann-variable with coefficients in any ring, including a
polynomial ring in the commuting fields: this is how the Wess-Zumino invariance of @sec-wess-zumino is checked
with every sign handled by the computer (@exr-grassmann, @exr-wz-invariance).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is a direct check of the defining relations and of the two spinor products of the examples, run
in the exterior algebra on four generators. It also shows that a top-degree monomial annihilates every element of
positive degree.

::: {#exr-grassmann}
#### Grassmann variables in Sage

Build the exterior algebra on four generators, check $\theta^2 = 0$ and the anticommutation, and verify that the
spinor product $\xi\chi$ is symmetric while $\xi\xi = 2\xi_2\xi_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-grassmann >}}
:::

Functions of Grassmann variables are defined by their power series, which stop after finitely many terms. The second
exercise computes exponentials and inverses this way and finds which elements can be inverted at all.

::: {#exr-ssg-grassmann-functions}
#### Exponentials and inverses

In $\Lambda(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ compute $e^{a\theta_1\theta_2}$, $e^{\theta_1}e^{\theta_2}$ and the inverse of $1 + \theta_1\theta_2$.
Show that $z = a + b\theta_1 + c\theta_2 + d\theta_1\theta_2$ is invertible if and only if its number part $a$ is non-zero,
and give $z^{-1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $(\theta_1\theta_2)^2 = 0$, $e^{a\theta_1\theta_2} = 1 + a\theta_1\theta_2$. Each $\theta_i^2 = 0$, so $e^{\theta_i} = 1 + \theta_i$
and $e^{\theta_1}e^{\theta_2} = 1 + \theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_1\theta_2$; the exponents anticommute, and indeed
$e^{\theta_2}e^{\theta_1} = 1 + \theta_1 + \theta_2 - \theta_1\theta_2 \neq e^{\theta_1}e^{\theta_2}$. $(1 + \theta_1\theta_2)(1 - \theta_1\theta_2) =
1$. In general write $z = a(1 + n)$ with $n = (b\theta_1 + c\theta_2 + d\theta_1\theta_2)/a$, which is nilpotent: $n^2 =
(bc\theta_1\theta_2 + cb\theta_2\theta_1)/a^2 = 0$. So $z^{-1} = a^{-1}(1 - n) = a^{-1} - (b\theta_1 + c\theta_2 + d\theta_1\theta_2)/a^2$.
If $a = 0$, $z$ is nilpotent ($z^2 = 0$ by the same computation) and has no inverse. The number part, the **body**, decides invertibility,
and the nilpotent rest, the **soul**, never matters for it.
:::

Integration over Grassmann variables is defined algebraically, by $\int d\theta\,1 = 0$ and $\int d\theta\,\theta =
1$, so that the integral picks the coefficient of the top monomial. The third exercise computes the fermionic
Gaussian integral, which underlies the fermionic path integral, and finds a determinant where the bosonic integral
has an inverse determinant.

::: {#exr-ssg-berezin-gaussian}
#### The Grassmann Gaussian integral

With the Berezin rules, $\int d\bar\theta\,d\theta\,\theta\bar\theta = 1$, compute $\int d\bar\theta\,d\theta\,e^{-a\bar\theta\theta}$ and
$\int\prod_i d\bar\theta_i\,d\theta_i\,e^{-\bar\theta_iA_{ij}\theta_j}$ for a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$, in Sage's exterior algebra.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The exponential series stops, $e^{-a\bar\theta\theta} = 1 + a\theta\bar\theta$, and the integral is $a$. For two pairs the
quadratic term of the series gives $\tfrac12(\bar\theta A\theta)^2$, whose top coefficient is $A_{11}A_{22} - A_{12}A_{21} = \det A$,
where a bosonic Gaussian integral would give $\pi^2/\det A$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-berezin-gaussian >}}
:::
::::

#### Two-component spinors

The Lorentz group acts on spinors through $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, and the two inequivalent two-dimensional
representations, related by complex conjugation, are the left- and right-handed Weyl spinors. Supersymmetry is
written most economically with these two-component objects rather than with four-component Dirac spinors, and the
definition fixes the index conventions used everywhere below.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-weyl-spinor}
#### Two-component Weyl spinor

A **left-handed Weyl spinor** is a two-component Grassmann object $\xi_\alpha$, $\alpha = 1, 2$, transforming under
the Lorentz group by the $(\tfrac12, 0)$ representation; its Hermitian conjugate $\xi^\dagger_{\dot\alpha}$ is
**right-handed**. Indices are raised and lowered with $\epsilon^{12} = -\epsilon^{21} = \epsilon_{21} = -\epsilon_{12} = 1$,
$\xi^\alpha = \epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\xi_\beta$, and the invariant products are $\xi\chi = \xi^\alpha\chi_\alpha$,
$\xi^\dagger\chi^\dagger = \xi^\dagger_{\dot\alpha}\chi^{\dagger\dot\alpha}$ and $\xi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\chi =
\xi^\dagger_{\dot\alpha}(\bar\sigma^\mu)^{\dot\alpha\alpha}\chi_\alpha$, with $\sigma^\mu = (1, \vec\sigma)$ and
$\bar\sigma^\mu = (1, -\vec\sigma)$ [@martin1997, eqs. 2.7-2.18]. A Dirac spinor of @def-spinor-field is a pair
$\Psi_D = (\xi_\alpha, \chi^{\dagger\dot\alpha})$ of a left- and a right-handed Weyl spinor.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example connects the two-component language with the four-component one of the spinor chapter. In the
Weyl basis the Dirac matrices are off-diagonal blocks built from $\sigma^\mu$ and $\bar\sigma^\mu$, and the Dirac
Lagrangian splits into two Weyl kinetic terms joined by the mass.

::: {#exm-weyl-dirac}
#### The Dirac spinor in blocks

With the gamma matrices of @exm-gamma-weyl, $\gamma^\mu = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma^\mu \\ \bar\sigma^\mu & 0
\end{pmatrix}$ (@prp-sigma-identities), the left- and right-handed Weyl spinors of @exm-lorentz-chirality are the
upper and lower components, and the Dirac Lagrangian $\bar\Psi_D(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - M)\Psi_D$ becomes
$i\xi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\xi + i\chi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\chi - M(\xi\chi + \xi^\dagger\chi^\dagger)$
[@martin1997, eq. 2.28, whose form does not depend on the signature].
:::

The Clifford relations of the Dirac matrices become identities among the two-component matrices. These are used
in every supersymmetric computation, and their sign is the one place where the choice of signature enters the
two-component formalism.

::: {#exm-weyl-sigma-identities}
#### The $\sigma$-matrix identities

$\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu + \sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}$, $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu) =
2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ and $\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}\bar\sigma_\mu^{\dot\beta\beta} = 2\delta_\alpha^\beta\delta_{\dot\alpha}^{\dot\beta}$
in our metric $(+, -, -, -)$ are the two-component form of the Clifford relations @eq-clifford; @martin1997 [eqs.
2.21-2.25] writes them with $-2$ in place of $2$, the sign of $\eta$ in his signature. They hold on the explicit
matrices (@prp-sigma-identities, @exr-sigma-identities).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** the identities are proved on the explicit matrices in @prp-sigma-identities
(`KaluzaKlein.Supersymmetry.sigma_clifford`, `sigma_trace`, `sigma_fierz`).

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third example shows that nothing is lost by working with left-handed spinors only. A right-handed field is the
conjugate of a left-handed one, so every fermion of the Standard Model can be listed as a left-handed Weyl spinor,
which is how supersymmetric models are written.

::: {#exm-weyl-standard-model}
#### The Standard Model fermions

Every spin-$\tfrac12$ field can be written as a collection of left-handed Weyl spinors with $\mathcal{L} =
i\psi^{\dagger i}\bar\sigma^\mu\nabla_\mu\psi_i$; the quarks and leptons of a generation are the fifteen Weyl spinors $Q,
\bar u, \bar d, L, \bar e$ with their colours and weak isospin [@martin1997, eqs. 2.38-2.44], and the Weyl condition
of @exm-anomaly-chiral is what makes the theory chiral.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The index gymnastics of the definition is the first thing to master. The first exercise checks that raising and
lowering are inverse operations and finds the sign that appears when the position of a contracted index is swapped.

::: {#exr-ssg-epsilon-raise}
#### Raising and lowering

Show that $\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\epsilon^{\beta\gamma} = \delta_\alpha^\gamma$, so that $\xi_\alpha = \epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\xi^\beta$ undoes the raising,
and that $\xi^\alpha\chi_\alpha = -\xi_\alpha\chi^\alpha$ for commuting components. What happens for anticommuting ones?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
As matrices, $\epsilon^{\alpha\beta} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\epsilon_{\alpha\beta} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}$, whose product is the identity: $\epsilon_{12}\epsilon^{21} = (-1)(-1) = 1$ and $\epsilon_{21}\epsilon^{12} = 1$,
the off-diagonal entries vanishing. Then $\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\xi^\beta = \epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\epsilon^{\beta\gamma}\xi_\gamma = \xi_\alpha$. Next
$\xi^\alpha\chi_\alpha = \epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\xi_\beta\chi_\alpha$ and $\xi_\alpha\chi^\alpha = \xi_\alpha\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\chi_\beta = \epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\xi_\alpha\chi_\beta =
\epsilon^{\beta\alpha}\xi_\beta\chi_\alpha = -\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\xi_\beta\chi_\alpha$, so the two differ by a sign whatever the components;
the statistics enters only when the order of $\xi$ and $\chi$ is exchanged, and then $\xi^\alpha\chi_\alpha = -\chi_\alpha\xi^\alpha =
\chi^\alpha\xi_\alpha$ for anticommuting components, which is the symmetry of @exm-grassmann-spinor-product.
:::

The barred matrices are not an independent choice: they follow from the unbarred ones by raising both indices.
The second exercise checks this relation, and the Hermiticity of $\sigma^\mu$, on the explicit matrices.

::: {#exr-ssg-sigma-bar-epsilon}
#### $\bar\sigma$ from $\sigma$

Show that every $\sigma^\mu$ is Hermitian and that $(\bar\sigma^\mu)^{\dot\alpha\alpha} = \epsilon^{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}
\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\beta}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The identity and the Pauli matrices are Hermitian. In matrix form the relation reads $\bar\sigma^\mu = \epsilon(\sigma^\mu)^T
\epsilon^T$; for $\mu = 0$ this is $\epsilon\epsilon^T = 1$, and for the spatial matrices it is the familiar $\sigma_2\sigma_i^T\sigma_2
= -\sigma_i$, since $\epsilon = i\sigma_2$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-sigma-bar-epsilon >}}
:::

The name "Lorentz invariant product" has to be earned. The third exercise shows that $\xi\chi$ is invariant exactly
under matrices of unit determinant, and that a diagonal matrix of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ acts on vectors, written as
$2 \times 2$ Hermitian matrices, as a boost.

::: {#exr-ssg-sl2c-invariance}
#### Invariance under $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$

Show that $M^T\epsilon M = (\det M)\epsilon$ for every $2 \times 2$ matrix $M$, so that $\xi\chi$ is invariant under $\xi \to M\xi$,
$\chi \to M\chi$ when $\det M = 1$. For $M = e^{-r\sigma_3/2}$ and $X = x^\mu\sigma_\mu = x^0 - \vec x\cdot\vec\sigma$, compute
$MXM^\dagger$ and identify the Lorentz transformation of $x^\mu$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The product is $\xi\chi = -\xi^T\epsilon\chi$ with $\epsilon = \epsilon^{\alpha\beta}$, and it transforms into $-\xi^TM^T\epsilon M\chi$. A
direct computation gives $M^T\epsilon M = (\det M)\epsilon$; this is the statement that $\epsilon$ is the volume form of
$\mathbb{C}^2$. $\det X = x_\mu x^\mu$ is preserved by $X \to MXM^\dagger$ when $|\det M| = 1$, and for the diagonal
boost matrix the result is $t' = \cosh r\,t + \sinh r\,z$, $z' = \sinh r\,t + \cosh r\,z$: a boost of rapidity $r$
along $z$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-sl2c-invariance >}}
:::

Products of spinors with several indices decompose into pieces that do not mix under $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, and the
antisymmetric symbol is the tool that separates them. The fourth exercise decomposes the most important case, two
undotted and two dotted indices, which is how a two-index Lorentz tensor looks in spinor language.

::: {#exr-ssg-bispinor-decomposition}
#### A tensor with four spinor indices

A tensor $A_{\alpha\beta\dot\alpha\dot\beta}$ has $16$ components. Show that
$A_{\alpha\beta\dot\alpha\dot\beta} = \epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\epsilon_{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}A + \epsilon_{\alpha\beta}A_{(\dot\alpha\dot\beta)} +
\epsilon_{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}A_{(\alpha\beta)} + A_{(\alpha\beta)(\dot\alpha\dot\beta)}$ with tensors symmetric in the bracketed indices,
express the four pieces through $A_{\alpha\beta\dot\alpha\dot\beta}$, count their components, and say which Lorentz tensors they
describe [@nath2017supersymmetry, Problem 8.4].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For two indices, $X_{\alpha\beta} - X_{\beta\alpha}$ is antisymmetric and so a multiple $c\,\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}$ of the only antisymmetric
$2 \times 2$ symbol; contracting with $\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}$ and using $\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\epsilon_{\alpha\beta} = -2$ (@def-weyl-spinor) gives
$X_{\alpha\beta} = X_{(\alpha\beta)} - \tfrac12\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\epsilon^{\gamma\delta}X_{\gamma\delta}$ with $X_{(\alpha\beta)} = \tfrac12(X_{\alpha\beta} +
X_{\beta\alpha})$. Applying this to both index pairs,
$$
A = \tfrac14\epsilon^{\gamma\delta}\epsilon^{\dot\gamma\dot\delta}A_{\gamma\delta\dot\gamma\dot\delta}, \quad
A_{(\dot\alpha\dot\beta)} = -\tfrac12\epsilon^{\gamma\delta}A_{\gamma\delta(\dot\alpha\dot\beta)}, \quad
A_{(\alpha\beta)} = -\tfrac12\epsilon^{\dot\gamma\dot\delta}A_{(\alpha\beta)\dot\gamma\dot\delta},
$$
and $A_{(\alpha\beta)(\dot\alpha\dot\beta)}$ is the part symmetric in both pairs. A symmetric pair of two-valued indices takes $3$
values, so the count is $1 + 3 + 3 + 9 = 16$. Pairing $\alpha\dot\alpha$ and $\beta\dot\beta$ into vector indices with
$\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}$ (@exm-ssg-sigma-basis) turns $A$ into a two-index tensor $T^{\mu\nu}$: the singlet is its trace, the two
three-component pieces are the self-dual and anti-self-dual parts of its antisymmetric part (@exr-ssg-self-dual-sigma),
and the nine-component piece is its symmetric traceless part.
:::

The identities of @exm-weyl-sigma-identities are used so often that they are worth stating once on the explicit
matrices, together with the block form of the Dirac matrices. The proposition collects them; each of the four
statements is a finite check over all index values.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sigma-identities}
#### Two-component spinor identities

On the explicit matrices $\sigma^\mu = (1, \vec\sigma)$, $\bar\sigma^\mu = (1, -\vec\sigma)$, with $\eta =
\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$: $\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu + \sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}$,
$\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu) = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}$,
$\sum_\mu\eta_{\mu\mu}\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}\bar\sigma^{\mu\,\dot\beta\beta} = 2\delta_\alpha^\beta\delta_{\dot\alpha}^{\dot\beta}$,
and the Dirac matrices of @exm-gamma-weyl are $\gamma^\mu = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma^\mu \\ \bar\sigma^\mu & 0
\end{pmatrix}$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example evaluates the anticommutation identity on two pairs of indices, which is all there is to it.
The diagonal entries reproduce the signature, and distinct spatial indices anticommute as Pauli matrices do.

::: {#exm-ssg-sigma-components}
#### Evaluating the identities

For $\mu = \nu = 0$, $\sigma^0\bar\sigma^0 + \sigma^0\bar\sigma^0 = 2 = 2\eta^{00}$; for $\mu = \nu = 1$, $2\sigma_1(-\sigma_1) = -2 =
2\eta^{11}$; for $\mu = 1$, $\nu = 2$, $-\sigma_1\sigma_2 - \sigma_2\sigma_1 = 0$. The trace identity follows by taking half the
trace of the first one, since $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu) = \operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu)$.
:::

The second example uses the trace identity as an orthogonality relation. The four matrices $\sigma^\mu$ form a basis of
the $2 \times 2$ Hermitian matrices, and a four-vector can be stored as such a matrix and read back with a trace.

::: {#exm-ssg-sigma-basis}
#### Four-vectors as Hermitian matrices

Every Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrix is $X = p_\mu\sigma^\mu$ for a unique real $p_\mu$, recovered as $p^\nu =
\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(X\bar\sigma^\nu)$; for instance $p_\mu\sigma^\mu = \begin{pmatrix} p_0 + p_3 & p_1 - ip_2 \\ p_1 + ip_2 & p_0 - p_3
\end{pmatrix}$, and its determinant $p_0^2 - p_1^2 - p_2^2 - p_3^2 = p_\mu p^\mu$ is the Minkowski norm (@exr-ssg-pslash-det).
:::

The third example is the two-component form of $(\gamma^\mu p_\mu)^2 = p^2$, which is what makes a massive Weyl
spinor obey the Klein-Gordon equation. It is the identity behind the mass degeneracy of @exm-f-term-masses.

::: {#exm-ssg-sigma-mass-shell}
#### The mass shell

Contracting the first identity with $p_\mu p_\nu$ gives $(p\cdot\sigma)(p\cdot\bar\sigma) = p^2$: acting with
$i\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu$ and then $i\sigma^\nu\partial_\nu$ on a spinor gives $-\Box$, so the Weyl equations with a mass,
$i\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\xi = M\chi^\dagger$ and $i\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\chi^\dagger = M\xi$, imply $(\Box + M^2)\xi = 0$.
:::
::::

:::

The second exercise turns the examples into a computation with a general momentum. It also shows what is special
about a light-like momentum, which will decide the size of the massless supermultiplets.

::: {#exr-ssg-pslash-det}
#### $p\cdot\sigma$ and the Minkowski norm

For a general $p_\mu$ compute $\det(p\cdot\sigma)$, $(p\cdot\sigma)(p\cdot\bar\sigma)$ and $\operatorname{tr}((p\cdot\sigma)\bar\sigma^\nu)$. For
the null momentum $p^\mu = (E, 0, 0, E)$ show that $p\cdot\sigma$ has rank one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\det(p\cdot\sigma) = p_\mu p^\mu$, $(p\cdot\sigma)(p\cdot\bar\sigma) = p^2\cdot1$ and $\operatorname{tr}((p\cdot\sigma)\bar\sigma^\nu) = 2p^\nu$.
For $p^\mu = (E, 0, 0, E)$ the lower components are $p_\mu = (E, 0, 0, -E)$ and $p\cdot\sigma = \operatorname{diag}(0, 2E)$: a
null vector gives a singular matrix, because its determinant is its norm.

{{< sage exr-ssg-pslash-det >}}
:::

The Lorentz generators on Weyl spinors are commutators of the $\sigma$-matrices. The third exercise checks that they
satisfy the Lorentz algebra with our metric, and shows that the two chiralities differ only in the sign of the boosts.

::: {#exr-ssg-lorentz-generators}
#### The Lorentz generators on Weyl spinors

With $S^{\mu\nu}_L = \tfrac{i}{4}(\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu - \sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu)$ and $S^{\mu\nu}_R = \tfrac{i}{4}(\bar\sigma^\mu\sigma^\nu -
\bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\mu)$, verify $[S^{\mu\nu}, S^{\rho\sigma}] = i(\eta^{\nu\rho}S^{\mu\sigma} - \eta^{\mu\rho}S^{\nu\sigma} - \eta^{\nu\sigma}S^{\mu\rho} +
\eta^{\mu\sigma}S^{\nu\rho})$ for both, and compare their rotations and boosts.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both satisfy the algebra. The rotations agree, $S^{ij} = \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$, Hermitian, while the boosts are
$S^{0i}_L = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_i = -S^{0i}_R$, anti-Hermitian: the two chiralities are the two inequivalent
representations $(\tfrac12, 0)$ and $(0, \tfrac12)$, exchanged by parity, which flips the boosts:

{{< sage exr-ssg-lorentz-generators >}}
:::

The identities of the proposition concern products of two matrices. Products of three and four occur in every
superspace computation, and they contain the Levi-Civita symbol; the fourth exercise derives them in our signature,
where the signs differ from the mostly-plus forms in the literature.

::: {#exr-ssg-sigma-triple}
#### Products of three and four $\sigma$-matrices

Show that $\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\lambda = \eta^{\mu\nu}\sigma^\lambda - \eta^{\mu\lambda}\sigma^\nu + \eta^{\nu\lambda}\sigma^\mu +
c\,i\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho}\sigma_\rho$ with $\epsilon_{0123} = 1$, and find $c$. Deduce
$\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\lambda\bar\sigma^\rho)$ and the antisymmetric combination
$\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\lambda\bar\sigma^\rho - \sigma^\lambda\bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\rho)$ of
@nath2017supersymmetry [Problem 8.2], whose signs refer to the mostly-plus metric. Check all index values with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The four $\sigma^\mu$ span the $2 \times 2$ matrices, so the product is a combination of them. When two of the indices
coincide the anticommutator $\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu + \sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ of @prp-sigma-identities gives the
three $\eta$ terms; when all three differ only the $\epsilon$ term is left. For $(\mu, \nu, \lambda) = (1, 2, 3)$ the left side is
$\sigma_1(-\sigma_2)\sigma_3 = -i$, while $\epsilon^{1230} = -\epsilon^{0123} = 1$ makes the right side $c\,i\sigma_0 = c\,i$; hence $c = -1$:
$$
\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\lambda = \eta^{\mu\nu}\sigma^\lambda - \eta^{\mu\lambda}\sigma^\nu + \eta^{\nu\lambda}\sigma^\mu - i\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho}\sigma_\rho .
$$
Multiplying by $\bar\sigma^\rho$ and taking the trace with $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\lambda\bar\sigma^\rho) = 2\eta^{\lambda\rho}$ gives
$\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\lambda\bar\sigma^\rho) = 2(\eta^{\mu\nu}\eta^{\lambda\rho} - \eta^{\mu\lambda}\eta^{\nu\rho} +
\eta^{\mu\rho}\eta^{\nu\lambda}) - 2i\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho}$. Exchanging $\mu$ and $\lambda$ leaves the $\eta$ terms and reverses the
$\epsilon$ term, so the antisymmetric combination is $-4i\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho}$; in the mostly-plus metric with Nath's
orientation the same combination reads $+4i\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho}$. The barred product
$\bar\sigma^\mu\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\lambda$ obeys the same identity with $+i\epsilon$.

{{< sage exr-ssg-sigma-triple >}}
:::

![The supersymmetric oscillator $H = \omega(a^\dagger a + b^\dagger b)$ with one bosonic and one fermionic mode:
the supercharge $Q = \sqrt\omega\,a^\dagger b$ pairs every bosonic state $|n, 0\rangle$ with the fermionic state
$|n - 1, 1\rangle$ of the same energy, and only the ground state $|0, 0\rangle$, with $E = 0$, is unpaired. On the
truncated matrices $Q^2 = 0$ and $\{Q, Q^\dagger\} = H$. Generated by
`figures/susy_oscillator.sage`.](figures/susy_oscillator.svg){#fig-susy-oscillator width=55%}

#### Supercharges

A symmetry generator that changes the spin of a state by one half must itself carry a spinor index, and since it
changes the statistics it must be fermionic. The supercharges are such generators; the definition also introduces
the infinitesimal transformation they generate, with a Grassmann spinor as parameter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-supercharge}
#### Supercharge

A **supercharge** is a conserved fermionic generator $Q_\alpha$ carrying a spinor index, together with its
conjugate $Q^\dagger_{\dot\alpha}$, that maps bosons to fermions and fermions to bosons: $Q|\text{boson}\rangle = |
\text{fermion}\rangle$ and conversely [@martin1997, eq. 1.5]. An infinitesimal **supersymmetry transformation**
is $\delta = \epsilon Q + \epsilon^\dagger Q^\dagger$ with a Grassmann spinor parameter $\epsilon_\alpha$ of mass
dimension $-\tfrac12$; it is **global** when $\epsilon$ is constant and **local** when $\epsilon(x)$ depends on
position (@sec-gravitino).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest system with a supercharge has no space at all: one bosonic and one fermionic oscillator of the same
frequency. The supercharge trades a fermionic quantum for a bosonic one, as the figure shows.

::: {#exm-supercharge-oscillator}
#### The supersymmetric oscillator

For a bosonic mode $a$ and a fermionic mode $b$ with $\{b, b^\dagger\} = 1$, $Q = \sqrt\omega\,a^\dagger b$ turns a
fermionic quantum into a bosonic one; $Q^2 = 0$ because $b^2 = 0$, and $\{Q, Q^\dagger\} = \omega(a^\dagger a +
b^\dagger b) = H$ (@fig-susy-oscillator, @prp-susy-oscillator): the Hamiltonian is the anticommutator of the
supercharges.
:::

In field theory a conserved charge comes from a conserved current by Noether's theorem. The second example
anticipates the supercurrent of the Wess-Zumino model, a vector-spinor whose time component integrates to the
supercharge.

::: {#exm-supercharge-noether}
#### The supercurrent

In a supersymmetric field theory the Noether procedure of @sec-noether-currents gives a conserved **supercurrent**
$J^\mu_\alpha$, an anticommuting vector-spinor, and the supercharges are its integrals, $Q_\alpha = \sqrt2\int d^3x\,
J^0_\alpha$ [@martin1997, eqs. 3.1.17-3.1.20]; for the free chiral multiplet $J^\mu_\alpha = (\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu
\psi)_\alpha\partial_\nu\phi^*$ (@sec-wess-zumino).
:::

The third example connects the operator and the field pictures. The commutator of the supercharges with a field is
its variation, which turns a scalar into a fermion and a fermion into a derivative of the scalar.

::: {#exm-supercharge-action}
#### Action on fields

$\delta X = \tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}[\epsilon Q + \epsilon^\dagger Q^\dagger, X]$ [@martin1997, eq. 3.1.21] realises the
supercharge on the fields: for the chiral multiplet, $\delta\phi = \epsilon\psi$, a boson becoming a fermion, and
$\delta\psi_\alpha = -i(\sigma^\mu\epsilon^\dagger)_\alpha\partial_\mu\phi + \epsilon_\alpha F$, a fermion becoming the
derivative of a boson (@def-susy-transformation).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Dimensional analysis fixes much of supersymmetry before any computation. The first exercise finds the mass
dimensions of the supercharge and of its parameter from the algebra and the transformation of a scalar.

::: {#exr-ssg-supercharge-dimension}
#### Mass dimensions

From $\{Q, Q^\dagger\} = 2\sigma^\mu P_\mu$ find the mass dimension of $Q$. Show that $\delta = \epsilon Q + \epsilon^\dagger Q^\dagger$ is
dimensionless when $\epsilon$ has dimension $-\tfrac12$, and that $\delta\phi = \epsilon\psi$ is consistent with the dimensions $1$ of
$\phi$ and $\tfrac32$ of $\psi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$P_\mu$ has dimension $1$, so $Q^2$ has dimension $1$ and $Q$ has dimension $\tfrac12$. The product $\epsilon Q$ then has
dimension $-\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 0$, as a symmetry transformation must, and $\delta\phi$ has the dimension $1$ of $\phi$ since
$\epsilon\psi$ has $-\tfrac12 + \tfrac32 = 1$. The same count forces a derivative in $\delta\psi$: $\epsilon^\dagger\partial\phi$ has dimension
$-\tfrac12 + 2 = \tfrac32$, while $\epsilon^\dagger\phi$ would have dimension $\tfrac12$ (@exm-chiral-dimensions).
:::

On the oscillator every statement about the supercharge can be checked on explicit vectors. The second exercise
computes the action of $Q$ and $Q^\dagger$ on the basis states and the two products $Q^\dagger Q$ and $QQ^\dagger$, which
are the Hamiltonian on the fermionic and the bosonic states respectively.

::: {#exr-ssg-oscillator-pairing}
#### The pairing of states

On the basis $|n, f\rangle$ of the oscillator, compute $Q|n - 1, 1\rangle$, $Q|n, 0\rangle$ and $Q^\dagger|n, 1\rangle$, and show
that $Q^\dagger Q = H$ on the fermionic states and $QQ^\dagger = H$ on the bosonic ones.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$Q|n - 1, 1\rangle = \sqrt\omega\,a^\dagger|n - 1\rangle \otimes b|1\rangle = \sqrt{n\omega}\,|n, 0\rangle$, while $Q|n, 0\rangle = 0$ (no
fermion to remove) and $Q^\dagger|n, 1\rangle = 0$ (no second fermion can be created). Hence $\{Q, Q^\dagger\}$ reduces to
$Q^\dagger Q$ on fermionic states and to $QQ^\dagger$ on bosonic ones, and both give $n\omega$ on the level $n$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-oscillator-pairing >}}
:::

Since the supercharge pairs all states of positive energy, a weighted count with a sign for the fermions sees only
the unpaired states. The third exercise computes this count, the Witten index, for the oscillator, exactly and on a
truncation.

::: {#exr-ssg-witten-index}
#### The Witten index

Compute $\operatorname{Tr}(-1)^Fe^{-\beta H}$ and $\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H}$ for the supersymmetric oscillator, and explain why the first does not
depend on $\beta$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The bosonic states contribute $\sum_{n \geq 0}q^n = 1/(1 - q)$ with $q = e^{-\beta\omega}$, the fermionic ones $\sum_{n \geq
0}q^{n + 1} = q/(1 - q)$. The index is the difference, $1$, and the partition function the sum, $(1 + q)/(1 - q)$. Every
level $n \geq 1$ contains one boson and one fermion, which cancel in the index whatever their Boltzmann weight; only
the zero-energy ground state survives, so the index counts supersymmetric ground states. On a truncation the
unpaired top fermion leaves a correction $-e^{-\beta N\omega}$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-witten-index >}}
:::
::::

#### The algebra

The supercharges and the generators of the Poincaré group together form an algebra in which some brackets are
commutators and others anticommutators. The decisive relation is the anticommutator of a supercharge with its
conjugate, which is a translation; the definition states the algebra in our signature and records the conversion
from Martin's.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-superalgebra}
#### Supersymmetry algebra

The **$N = 1$ supersymmetry algebra** extends the Poincaré algebra by the anticommutators
$$
\{Q_\alpha, Q^\dagger_{\dot\alpha}\} = 2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}P_\mu, \qquad \{Q_\alpha, Q_\beta\} = \{Q^\dagger_{\dot\alpha},
Q^\dagger_{\dot\beta}\} = 0, \qquad [Q_\alpha, P^\mu] = [Q^\dagger_{\dot\alpha}, P^\mu] = 0,
$$ {#eq-superalgebra}
in our metric $(+, -, -, -)$, where $P_0 = P^0 = H$; @martin1997 [eqs. 3.1.30-3.1.32] writes $-2\sigma^\mu P_\mu$ in
the mostly-plus metric, where $P_0 = -H$, so both say that $\{Q_\alpha, Q^\dagger_{\dot\alpha}\}$ is $2H$ on a state at
rest. Two supersymmetry transformations compose to a
translation, $[\delta_{\epsilon_2}, \delta_{\epsilon_1}] X = i(-\epsilon_1\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2^\dagger +
\epsilon_2\sigma^\mu\epsilon_1^\dagger)\partial_\mu X$ (@def-off-shell-closure). It is a **Lie superalgebra**: a
$\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded algebra with commutators between even and anticommutators between odd generators, satisfying
a graded Jacobi identity. With $N$ supercharges $Q^i_\alpha$ it is the **$N$-extended** algebra.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The most striking consequence of the algebra is a statement about energy. Since the Hamiltonian is a sum of
anticommutators of operators with their adjoints, it is a sum of squares, and no state can have negative energy.

::: {#exm-superalgebra-energy}
#### Positivity of the energy

Taking the trace of @eq-superalgebra with $\operatorname{tr}\sigma^\mu = 2\delta^\mu_0$ and $P_0 = P^0$ gives $H = P^0 = \tfrac14(Q_1Q_1^\dagger +
Q_1^\dagger Q_1 + Q_2Q_2^\dagger + Q_2^\dagger Q_2)$ [@martin1997, eq. 7.1.1]: the Hamiltonian is a sum of squares,
$\langle\psi|H|\psi\rangle = \tfrac14\sum\|Q|\psi\rangle\|^2 \geq 0$, with zero energy exactly for states annihilated by
all supercharges (@exr-susy-positivity, @def-susy-breaking).
:::

The oscillator realises a version of the algebra in which time is the only dimension. The second example records
the correspondence, which is why the oscillator is a faithful model of everything that follows.

::: {#exm-superalgebra-oscillator}
#### The oscillator realisation

$\{Q, Q^\dagger\} = H$, $Q^2 = 0$, $[Q, H] = 0$ for the supersymmetric oscillator is the $0 + 1$-dimensional version
of @eq-superalgebra, with $H$ the only translation generator (@prp-susy-oscillator).
:::

The algebra can be enlarged in two ways, by more supercharges in four dimensions or by working in more dimensions.
The third example sketches both, since the second is what leads to the bound on the dimension of supergravity.

::: {#exm-superalgebra-extended}
#### Extended and higher-dimensional algebras

With $N$ supercharges in four dimensions the anticommutator may contain **central charges** $Z^{ij}$, and the
automorphism group $U(N)$ rotating the $Q^i$ is the **R-symmetry**; in $d$ dimensions $Q$ is a spinor of
$SO(1, d - 1)$ with $\{Q, Q^T\} = \gamma^aCP_a + \dots$ [@tanii1998, eq. 4.5], and the number of real components of
$Q$ grows like $2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$ (@sec-gravitino), which is what bounds the dimension by eleven (@sec-sugra11).
:::

The algebra just defined escapes a theorem that forbids every other way of mixing spacetime and internal symmetries.
The fourth example states that theorem and shows which of its two conclusions survives the fermionic generators.

::: {#exm-ssg-coleman-mandula}
#### The Coleman-Mandula theorem and its loophole

For bosonic symmetries of a relativistic scattering matrix the Coleman-Mandula theorem allows only the product of the
Poincaré group with an internal group whose generators $B_a$ commute with $P_\mu$ and $M_{\mu\nu}$
[@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 8.1]. Then $B_a$ commutes with the Casimir operators $P^2 = P_\mu P^\mu$ and $W^2 =
W_\mu W^\mu$, where $W^\mu = \tfrac12\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}P_\nu M_{\rho\sigma}$ is the Pauli-Lubanski vector; in the rest
frame of a particle of mass $m$ one finds $W^0 = 0$ and $W^2 = -m^2\vec J^2$, so all members of an internal multiplet
have the same mass and the same spin. A supercharge commutes with $P_\mu$, hence with $P^2$, but it is a spinor and does
not commute with $M_{\mu\nu}$, hence not with $W^2$: the states it connects have equal masses and spins differing by
$\tfrac12$, which is the structure of the supermultiplets defined below [@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 8.4-8.15].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the positivity of the energy from the algebra. The computation is short, and its
consequence, that a vacuum of positive energy cannot be supersymmetric, is the criterion for supersymmetry breaking.

::: {#exr-susy-positivity}
#### Positivity of the energy

Derive $H = \tfrac14\sum_\alpha(Q_\alpha Q_\alpha^\dagger + Q_\alpha^\dagger Q_\alpha)$ from @eq-superalgebra and conclude
that $\langle H\rangle \geq 0$ in every state, with equality exactly for supersymmetric states.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Setting $\dot\alpha = \alpha$ and summing, $\sum_\alpha\{Q_\alpha, Q^\dagger_\alpha\} = 2\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\mu)P_\mu =
4P_0 = 4P^0 = 4H$ in our metric ($\operatorname{tr}\sigma^\mu = 2\delta^\mu_0$, $P_0 = P^0$; in Martin's mostly-plus
metric the same follows from $-2\sigma^\mu P_\mu$ and $P_0 = -P^0$). Then
$\langle\psi|H|\psi\rangle = \tfrac14\sum_\alpha(\|Q_\alpha^\dagger|\psi\rangle\|^2 + \|Q_\alpha|\psi\rangle\|^2) \geq 0$, and it
vanishes if and only if $Q_\alpha|\psi\rangle = Q^\dagger_\alpha|\psi\rangle = 0$ for all $\alpha$ [@martin1997, eqs.
7.1.1-7.1.2]: a supersymmetric vacuum has zero energy, and a vacuum of positive energy breaks supersymmetry
(@def-susy-breaking).
:::

On a single-particle state the momentum operator has a definite value, and the algebra becomes a numerical matrix.
The second exercise evaluates it for a massive particle at rest and for a massless one, and finds that half of the
supercharges vanish in the massless case.

::: {#exr-ssg-algebra-rest-frame}
#### The algebra on one-particle states

Evaluate $2\sigma^\mu P_\mu$ for $P^\mu = (M, 0, 0, 0)$ and $P^\mu = (E, 0, 0, E)$, remembering $P_i = -P^i$. Show that in the
massless case $Q_1$ vanishes on every state of positive norm, and that for a general massive momentum the matrix
has positive eigenvalues.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At rest $\{Q_\alpha, Q^\dagger_{\dot\beta}\} = 2M\delta_{\alpha\dot\beta}$: two independent fermionic oscillators $Q_\alpha/\sqrt{2M}$. For the
massless momentum $P_\mu = (E, 0, 0, -E)$ and $2\sigma^\mu P_\mu = \operatorname{diag}(0, 4E)$, so $\{Q_1, Q_1^\dagger\} = 0$ and
$\|Q_1|\psi\rangle\|^2 + \|Q_1^\dagger|\psi\rangle\|^2 = 0$ for every state: $Q_1 = 0$ on the Hilbert space, and only $Q_2$ acts. In
general the matrix has determinant $4M^2$ and trace $4E$, hence eigenvalues $2(E \mp |\vec p|) > 0$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-algebra-rest-frame >}}
:::

A Lie superalgebra needs the graded Jacobi identity in place of the ordinary one. The third exercise checks it on
the smallest example, the $2 \times 2$ supermatrices $\mathfrak{gl}(1|1)$, whose odd part mimics a pair of
supercharges.

::: {#exr-ssg-gl11-jacobi}
#### The superalgebra $\mathfrak{gl}(1|1)$

Grade the $2 \times 2$ matrices by declaring diagonal ones even and off-diagonal ones odd, with bracket $[X, Y\} = XY -
(-1)^{|X||Y|}YX$. Show that $Q = E_{12}$ and $\bar Q = E_{21}$ satisfy $\{Q, \bar Q\} = 1$, $Q^2 = 0$, and that the graded
Jacobi identity holds on all basis triples.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\{Q, \bar Q\} = E_{12}E_{21} + E_{21}E_{12} = E_{11} + E_{22} = 1$, central, the analogue of $\{Q, Q^\dagger\} = H$; $Q^2 = 0$,
and $E_{11} - E_{22}$ acts on $Q$, $\bar Q$ with charges $\pm2$, the analogue of an R-symmetry. The graded Jacobi
identity holds on all 64 triples, while the commutator $[Q, \bar Q] = E_{11} - E_{22}$ would not be central:

{{< sage exr-ssg-gl11-jacobi >}}
:::
::::

The oscillator was introduced as an example, and it is worth recording as a proposition checked on the explicit
truncated matrices. It is the model to keep in mind for every statement about supermultiplets and about the
energy of supersymmetric states.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-susy-oscillator}
#### The supersymmetric oscillator

On the truncated tensor product of a bosonic and a fermionic mode, $\{b, b^\dagger\} = 1$, $b^2 = 0$, $Q^2 = 0$,
$\{Q, Q^\dagger\} = H$ away from the truncation level, and the spectrum is $n\omega$ with a unique ground state and
doubly degenerate excited levels.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Computed exactly with Sage's matrices (`figures/susy_oscillator.sage`).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A truncated matrix cannot represent the oscillator exactly, and the proposition says "away from the truncation
level". The first example locates the defect: it sits on the single state whose bosonic partner has been cut away.

::: {#exm-ssg-oscillator-truncation}
#### Where the truncation fails

With $N$ bosonic levels, $Q|N - 1, 1\rangle$ would be $\sqrt{N\omega}|N, 0\rangle$, which is not in the truncated space; there
$\{Q, Q^\dagger\} = Q^\dagger Q$ gives $0$ instead of $N\omega$, and this is the only discrepancy (@exr-ssg-oscillator-truncation). The
top fermionic state is unpaired, which is also why the truncated Witten index of @exr-ssg-witten-index deviates from $1$.
:::

The lowest levels make the pairing concrete. The second example lists them, so that the figure can be read state
by state.

::: {#exm-ssg-oscillator-levels}
#### The first levels

$E = 0$: $|0, 0\rangle$ alone, annihilated by $Q$ and $Q^\dagger$. $E = \omega$: $|1, 0\rangle$ and $|0, 1\rangle$, with $Q|0, 1\rangle =
\sqrt\omega|1, 0\rangle$ and $Q^\dagger|1, 0\rangle = \sqrt\omega|0, 1\rangle$. $E = 2\omega$: $|2, 0\rangle$ and $|1, 1\rangle$, with
$Q|1, 1\rangle = \sqrt{2\omega}|2, 0\rangle$. Each level $n \geq 1$ is a two-state supermultiplet (@fig-susy-oscillator).
:::

The oscillator is the special case of supersymmetric quantum mechanics with a quadratic superpotential. The third
example states the general construction, which produces partner Hamiltonians with identical spectra except
possibly for a zero mode.

::: {#exm-ssg-susy-qm}
#### Supersymmetric quantum mechanics

For a superpotential $W(x)$ let $A = \tfrac{d}{dx} + W'$; the supercharge $Q = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}A^\dagger b$ has $Q^2 = 0$, and $H = \{Q,
Q^\dagger\}$ is $H_- = \tfrac12A^\dagger A$ on the bosonic and $H_+ = \tfrac12AA^\dagger$ on the fermionic states, $H_\mp =
\tfrac12(-\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2} + W'^2 \mp W'')$ (with $\hbar = 1$ and unit mass). For $W = \tfrac12\omega x^2$
these are the oscillator shifted by $\mp\tfrac12\omega$, whose spectra $n\omega$ and $(n + 1)\omega$ reproduce the proposition, and
$Q = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}A^\dagger b = \sqrt\omega\,a^\dagger b$
(@exr-ssg-susy-qm).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise makes the truncation defect explicit for several truncation levels. It is a check on the
statement of the proposition rather than a new fact, and it takes a few lines of matrix algebra.

::: {#exr-ssg-oscillator-truncation}
#### The truncation defect

For $N = 4, 6, 8$ bosonic levels compute $\{Q, Q^\dagger\} - H$ (with $\omega = 1$) and locate its non-zero entries.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The difference is diagonal with a single non-zero entry $-N$, on the top fermionic state $|N - 1, 1\rangle$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-oscillator-truncation >}}
:::

Supersymmetry requires equal frequencies for the two oscillators. The second exercise shows what goes wrong
otherwise, using only the commutation relations.

::: {#exr-ssg-oscillator-frequencies}
#### Unequal frequencies

For $H = \omega_Ba^\dagger a + \omega_Fb^\dagger b$ and $Q = a^\dagger b$, compute $[H, Q]$ and $\{Q, Q^\dagger\}$. When is $Q$
conserved, and what is the spectrum otherwise?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[a^\dagger a, a^\dagger] = a^\dagger$ and $[b^\dagger b, b] = -b$, so $[H, Q] = (\omega_B - \omega_F)Q$: $Q$ is conserved only for $\omega_B = \omega_F$.
$\{Q, Q^\dagger\} = a^\dagger a\,bb^\dagger + aa^\dagger\,b^\dagger b = a^\dagger a + b^\dagger b$, using $bb^\dagger = 1 - b^\dagger b$ and
$(b^\dagger b)^2 = b^\dagger b$; it equals $H/\omega$ only for equal frequencies. Otherwise the states $|n, 0\rangle$ and $|n - 1, 1\rangle$
have energies $n\omega_B$ and $(n - 1)\omega_B + \omega_F$, split by $\omega_B - \omega_F$: the pairing survives as a map between states
but no longer as a degeneracy, the situation of broken supersymmetry.
:::

The third exercise works out the general supersymmetric quantum mechanics of the third example. It shows when the
zero mode of $A$ is normalisable, which decides whether supersymmetry is unbroken.

::: {#exr-ssg-susy-qm}
#### Partner Hamiltonians

With $A = \tfrac{d}{dx} + W'$ and $A^\dagger = -\tfrac{d}{dx} + W'$, show that $\tfrac12A^\dagger A$ and $\tfrac12AA^\dagger$ are
$\tfrac12(-\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2} + W'^2 \mp W'')$. For $W = \tfrac12\omega x^2$ identify them with the oscillator, and find the zero modes
of $A$ and $A^\dagger$ for $W = \tfrac12\omega x^2$ and $W = \tfrac13gx^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Acting on a test function, $A^\dagger Af = -f'' + W'^2f - W''f$ and $AA^\dagger f = -f'' + W'^2f + W''f$. For the quadratic $W$ these
are $-\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2} + \omega^2x^2 \mp \omega$, twice the oscillator Hamiltonian shifted by $\mp\tfrac12\omega$. The zero mode of $A$ is
$e^{-W}$ and that of $A^\dagger$ is $e^{W}$; for $W = \tfrac12\omega x^2$ the first is the normalisable Gaussian, a supersymmetric
ground state, while for $W = \tfrac13gx^3$ both grow on one side, there is no zero-energy state, and supersymmetry is
broken:

{{< sage exr-ssg-susy-qm >}}
:::
::::

#### Supermultiplets

The particles of a supersymmetric theory are organised by representations of the whole superalgebra, not of the
Poincaré group alone. Two consequences follow at once from the algebra: the members of such a representation have
equal masses, and they contain as many bosonic as fermionic states.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-supermultiplet}
#### Supermultiplet

A **supermultiplet** is an irreducible representation of the supersymmetry algebra on fields or states: a set of
bosons and fermions mapped into each other by the supercharges. Since $P^2$ commutes with $Q$, all members have
the same mass, and since $(-1)^{2s}$ anticommutes with $Q$ while $P^\mu$ commutes, a massive or
non-zero-momentum multiplet contains equally many bosonic and fermionic states, $n_B = n_F$ [@martin1997,
eqs. 1.8-1.12].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest multiplet pairs a spin-zero particle with a spin-one-half one. It is the multiplet of matter, and its
off-shell completion with an auxiliary field is the subject of the next section.

::: {#exm-multiplet-chiral}
#### The chiral multiplet

A complex scalar $\phi$ and a left-handed Weyl spinor $\psi$: $2 + 2$ on-shell degrees of freedom, and with the
auxiliary field $F$ of @def-auxiliary-field, $4 + 4$ off-shell [@martin1997, Table 3.1]. The quarks, leptons and
Higgs bosons of the minimal supersymmetric Standard Model live in chiral multiplets with their squarks, sleptons
and higgsinos.
:::

Gauge fields need partners too, and these must sit in the same representation of the gauge group, the adjoint. The
second example is the multiplet of a gauge boson and its gaugino.

::: {#exm-multiplet-vector}
#### The gauge multiplet

A massless vector $A_\mu$ and a Weyl spinor $\lambda$, the gaugino, both in the adjoint representation: $2 + 2$
on-shell, $4 + 4$ off-shell with the auxiliary field $D$ (@def-gauge-multiplet); the gluons, $W$, $Z$ and photon with
their gauginos.
:::

The graviton's partner has spin three halves. The third example is the multiplet of pure supergravity, which
reappears in the second part of the chapter.

::: {#exm-multiplet-gravity}
#### The gravity multiplet

The graviton, helicities $\pm2$, and the gravitino, helicities $\pm\tfrac32$ (@def-gravitino): $2 + 2$ on-shell
degrees of freedom, the multiplet of pure supergravity [@tanii1998, p. 3]; the oscillator pairing of
@fig-susy-oscillator is the same structure in zero space dimensions.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The equality $n_B = n_F$ deserves a proof. The first exercise derives it with the operator $(-1)^F$ and the cyclicity
of the trace, the same argument that underlies the Witten index.

::: {#exr-ssg-fermion-number}
#### Why $n_B = n_F$

Let $(-1)^F$ be $+1$ on bosonic and $-1$ on fermionic states, so that $(-1)^FQ = -Q(-1)^F$. On a finite-dimensional
multiplet of fixed momentum $p \neq 0$, show that $\operatorname{Tr}[(-1)^F\{Q_\alpha, Q^\dagger_{\dot\beta}\}] = 0$ and deduce $n_B = n_F$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{Tr}[(-1)^FQ_\alpha Q^\dagger_{\dot\beta}] = \operatorname{Tr}[Q^\dagger_{\dot\beta}(-1)^FQ_\alpha] = -\operatorname{Tr}[(-1)^FQ^\dagger_{\dot\beta}Q_\alpha]$ by
cyclicity and anticommutation, so the trace of $(-1)^F$ times the anticommutator vanishes. The anticommutator is
$2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}p_\mu$ times the identity on the multiplet, so $2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}p_\mu\operatorname{Tr}(-1)^F = 0$; for $p \neq 0$
some entry of $p\cdot\sigma$ is non-zero, hence $\operatorname{Tr}(-1)^F = n_B - n_F = 0$ [@martin1997, eq. 1.12]. For $p = 0$ the
argument fails, which is why a supersymmetric vacuum may be a single bosonic state.
:::

A massive particle at rest sees two pairs of fermionic oscillators (@exr-ssg-algebra-rest-frame). The second exercise
builds the massive multiplets of $N = 1$ from this and counts their states.

::: {#exr-ssg-massive-multiplet}
#### Massive multiplets

Using $a_\alpha = Q_\alpha/\sqrt{2M}$ as two fermionic annihilation operators forming a spin-$\tfrac12$ doublet, build the
multiplet from a Clifford vacuum of spin $j$, annihilated by both. List the spins for $j = 0$ and $j = \tfrac12$ and
count the states.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Clifford vacuum $|\Omega\rangle$ is annihilated by both $a_\alpha$; the states $|\Omega\rangle$, $a^\dagger_1|\Omega\rangle$,
$a^\dagger_2|\Omega\rangle$, $a^\dagger_1a^\dagger_2|\Omega\rangle$ carry spins $j \otimes (0 \oplus \tfrac12 \oplus 0)$, the creation operators
forming a doublet and their product a singlet. For $j = 0$: two spin-$0$ states and one spin-$\tfrac12$ doublet, $2 + 2$,
the massive chiral multiplet. For $j = \tfrac12$: spins $\tfrac12 \otimes (0 \oplus \tfrac12 \oplus 0) = \tfrac12 \oplus (0 \oplus 1) \oplus
\tfrac12$, so one spin $1$ ($3$ states), one spin $0$, two spin-$\tfrac12$ doublets: $4 + 4$, the massive vector multiplet that
results when a gauge multiplet eats a chiral one in the Higgs mechanism.
:::

For a massless particle only one supercharge acts (@exr-ssg-algebra-rest-frame), and it raises the helicity by one
half. The third exercise builds the massless multiplets of $N = 1$ from this, and shows why the CPT conjugate must
be added.

::: {#exr-ssg-massless-n1}
#### Massless $N = 1$ multiplets

The normalised $Q_2/\sqrt{4E}$ and its adjoint form one fermionic oscillator, and one of them, call it $a^\dagger$, raises the
helicity by $\tfrac12$. Build the massless multiplet from a Clifford vacuum of helicity $\lambda$, annihilated by $a$. Which values of $\lambda$ give the chiral, the gauge and the gravity multiplets, and why does each need its CPT
conjugate?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The multiplet is $\{|\lambda\rangle, a^\dagger|\lambda\rangle\}$ with helicities $\lambda$ and $\lambda + \tfrac12$, one boson and one fermion.
$\lambda = 0$ gives $(0, \tfrac12)$, $\lambda = \tfrac12$ gives $(\tfrac12, 1)$, $\lambda = \tfrac32$ gives $(\tfrac32, 2)$. CPT reverses helicities,
so a local quantum field theory containing helicity $\lambda$ also contains $-\lambda$: each multiplet is accompanied by
$(-\lambda - \tfrac12, -\lambda)$, giving the chiral multiplet $(0, \pm\tfrac12, 0)$ with a complex scalar, the gauge multiplet
$(\pm\tfrac12, \pm1)$ and the gravity multiplet $(\pm\tfrac32, \pm2)$, $2 + 2$ states each, as in the three examples.
:::
::::

![Massless supermultiplets as helicity ladders: the number of states of each helicity in the gravity multiplets
(top helicity $2$) of $N = 1, \dots, 8$ extended supersymmetry, completed by their CPT conjugates, with bosons in
blue and fermions in red. Each ladder is a row of Pascal's triangle; $N = 7$ and $N = 8$ give the same
self-conjugate multiplet $1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1$, and $N = 9$ would need helicity $\tfrac52$. Generated by
`figures/supermultiplets.sage`.](figures/supermultiplets.svg){#fig-supermultiplets width=95%}

{{< interactive supermultiplets 460 >}}

The construction of the last exercise extends to $N$ supercharges, and the result is the counting that bounds the
number of supersymmetries. The proposition records it; the ladders are built one creation operator at a time, as in
the figure.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-ssg-massless-multiplets}
#### Massless supermultiplets

For a massless momentum the $N$-extended algebra acts through $N$ fermionic creation operators, each raising the
helicity by $\tfrac12$, so the multiplet built on a Clifford vacuum of helicity $\lambda_0$ has $\binom{N}{k}$ states of helicity
$\lambda_0 + \tfrac{k}{2}$, $2^N$ states in all, half of them bosonic. The gravity multiplet of $N = 8$, from $\lambda_0 = -2$, has
multiplicities $1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1$ and is its own CPT conjugate; since a ladder spans $\tfrac{N}{2}$ units of
helicity, $|\lambda| \leq 2$ requires $N \leq 8$ and $|\lambda| \leq 1$ requires $N \leq 4$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation of the ladders in Sage (`figures/supermultiplets.sage`).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example reads the proposition for $N = 1$, where each ladder has two rungs. It recovers the multiplets of
the definition and of @exr-ssg-massless-n1.

::: {#exm-ssg-ladders-n1}
#### The $N = 1$ ladders

$N = 1$, $2^1 = 2$ states: $(\lambda_0, \lambda_0 + \tfrac12)$, which for $\lambda_0 = 0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32$ are the chiral, gauge,
gravitino and gravity multiplets, each with its CPT conjugate (@fig-supermultiplets, first panel).
:::

The second example is the largest multiplet without gravity. With top helicity one, the ladder can be at most four
rungs of one half long, and the resulting $N = 4$ multiplet is its own conjugate.

::: {#exm-ssg-ladders-n4}
#### $N = 4$ super-Yang-Mills

From $\lambda_0 = -1$ with $N = 4$: one vector of helicity $-1$, four helicity $-\tfrac12$ states, six scalars, four helicity
$+\tfrac12$ states, one of helicity $+1$: $1, 4, 6, 4, 1$, self-conjugate, $8 + 8$ states. It is the field content of $N = 4$
super-Yang-Mills theory, a gauge field, four Weyl gauginos and six real scalars in the adjoint.
:::

The third example is the maximal multiplet with gravity. Its field content is that of $N = 8$ supergravity, which
appears again as the reduction of the eleven-dimensional theory.

::: {#exm-ssg-ladders-n8}
#### $N = 8$ supergravity

From $\lambda_0 = -2$: $1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1$ at helicities $-2, \dots, 2$, that is one graviton, eight gravitini, $28$
vectors, $56$ spin-$\tfrac12$ fields and $70$ scalars, $128 + 128$ states (@exm-sugra-multiplet-extended, @fig-supermultiplets).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise applies the proposition to $N = 2$. It finds the two multiplets used in $N = 2$ theories, the
vector multiplet and the hypermultiplet.

::: {#exr-ssg-n2-multiplets}
#### $N = 2$ multiplets

List the helicities of the $N = 2$ multiplets with $\lambda_0 = 0$ and $\lambda_0 = -\tfrac12$, add CPT conjugates where needed, and
count the states.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\lambda_0 = 0$: helicities $0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, 1$, not self-conjugate; with the conjugate $-1, -\tfrac12, -\tfrac12, 0$ this is the $N = 2$
vector multiplet, a vector, two Weyl fermions and a complex scalar, $4 + 4$. $\lambda_0 = -\tfrac12$: $-\tfrac12, 0, 0, \tfrac12$, which
looks self-conjugate, but the two scalars form a doublet of the $SU(2)$ R-symmetry and CPT requires a second copy;
the result is the hypermultiplet, two complex scalars and two Weyl fermions, $4 + 4$ [@tanii1998, Sec. 3].
:::

The gravity multiplets for every $N$ are a short computation. The second exercise lists them in Sage and checks the
coincidence of $N = 7$ and $N = 8$ visible in the figure.

::: {#exr-ssg-ladders}
#### The gravity ladders

For $N = 1, \dots, 8$ list the CPT-completed gravity multiplets, count bosons and fermions, and check that $N = 7$ gives
the same states as $N = 8$. Show that $N = 9$ forces a helicity above $2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each ladder has $2^N$ states, doubled by CPT except for $N = 8$; bosons and fermions are equal in number. For $N = 7$
the ladder from $-\tfrac32$ to $2$ plus its conjugate gives exactly the $N = 8$ multiplet, so $N = 7$ supergravity has an
eighth supersymmetry automatically. A ladder of $N = 9$ spans $\tfrac92 > 4$ units, so its ends cannot both lie in
$[-2, 2]$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-ladders >}}
:::

The multiplicities $\binom{N}{k}$ have a group-theoretic meaning: the level-$k$ states are antisymmetric in $k$ indices of the
R-symmetry $SU(N)$. The third exercise identifies them with the fundamental representations of $SU(8)$ and $SU(4)$
using Sage's Weyl character rings.

::: {#exr-ssg-r-symmetry}
#### The R-symmetry representations

Show that the level-$k$ states of the $N = 8$ ladder form $\Lambda^k\mathbf{8}$ of $SU(8)$, check their dimensions with the Weyl
character ring, decompose $\mathbf{8} \otimes \mathbf{8}$, and show that the $70$ scalars form a self-conjugate
representation. Do the same for the scalars of $N = 4$ super-Yang-Mills.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The state $a^\dagger_{i_1}\cdots a^\dagger_{i_k}|\lambda_0\rangle$ is antisymmetric in $i_1, \dots, i_k$ because the $a^\dagger_i$ anticommute, so
level $k$ carries $\Lambda^k\mathbf{8}$, the $k$-th fundamental representation of $SU(8)$ (@sec-lie-algebras). Its dimension is
$\binom8k$; $\mathbf 8 \otimes \mathbf 8 = \mathbf{28} \oplus \mathbf{36}$, the $28$ vectors being the antisymmetric part; $\Lambda^k$ and
$\Lambda^{8 - k}$ are conjugate, so $\Lambda^4 = \mathbf{70}$ is self-conjugate, as $70$ real scalars must be. For $N = 4$ the six
scalars are $\Lambda^2\mathbf 4 = \mathbf 6$ of $SU(4) \cong SO(6)$, the real vector:

{{< sage exr-ssg-r-symmetry >}}
:::
::::

### The Wess-Zumino model {#sec-wess-zumino}

The simplest supersymmetric field theory contains one complex scalar and one Weyl fermion. This section builds it
step by step as in @martin1997 [Sec. 3.1]: the transformation rules are guessed from dimensional analysis, the
variation of the action is shown to be a total derivative, the algebra is found to close only on-shell, and the
auxiliary field is introduced to close it off-shell. Every one of these computations, which involve anticommuting
fields, is carried out exactly in an exterior algebra, where every Grassmann sign is automatic, and the algebraic step
of eliminating the auxiliary field is a completion of the square.

#### The chiral multiplet

The chiral multiplet of @exm-multiplet-chiral is now realised by fields. Besides the scalar and the Weyl fermion it
contains a third field without derivatives, the auxiliary field, whose role will become clear when the algebra is
computed; the definition gives the free Lagrangian of all three in our signature.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-chiral-multiplet}
#### Chiral multiplet

A **chiral multiplet** consists of a complex scalar field $\phi$, a left-handed Weyl spinor $\psi_\alpha$
(@def-weyl-spinor) and a complex **auxiliary field** $F$ (@def-auxiliary-field), with the free Lagrangian
$$
\mathcal{L} = \partial^\mu\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi + i\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi + F^*F
$$ {#eq-wz-free}
[@martin1997, eqs. 3.1.2 and 3.1.12, where the scalar term reads $-\partial^\mu\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi$ in the
mostly-plus metric; the fermion and auxiliary terms contain no $\eta$ and are the same in both signatures]. Without
$F$ it is the **massless free Wess-Zumino model**, the Klein-Gordon
Lagrangian of @def-klein-gordon for a complex scalar plus the massless Weyl Lagrangian of @exm-weyl-dirac.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Dimensional analysis is the first tool for guessing supersymmetry transformations. The first example records the
mass dimensions of the three fields and of the parameter, which follow from the kinetic terms.

::: {#exm-chiral-dimensions}
#### Mass dimensions

$\phi$ has dimension $1$, $\psi$ dimension $\tfrac32$ (@exm-dimension-counting) and $F$ dimension $2$, so the
parameter $\epsilon$ relating $\delta\phi = \epsilon\psi$ has dimension $-\tfrac12$ [@martin1997, p. 18]; this fixes
the form of all the transformation rules up to constants.
:::

A supermultiplet must contain equal numbers of bosonic and fermionic degrees of freedom. The second example counts
them for the chiral multiplet, on-shell and off-shell, and shows where the auxiliary field is needed.

::: {#exm-chiral-dof}
#### Counting degrees of freedom

On-shell: $\phi$ has $2$ real degrees of freedom and $\psi$, a complex two-component field with a first-order
equation, has $2$; off-shell: $\phi$ still $2$, $\psi$ has $4$, and $F$ supplies the missing $2$ bosonic ones
[@martin1997, Table 3.1]: $n_B = n_F$ both on- and off-shell, as @def-supermultiplet requires (@exr-wz-dof).
:::

Realistic models contain many chiral multiplets, labelled by gauge and flavour indices. The third example writes
the free Lagrangian for several of them, the form in which interactions will be added.

::: {#exm-chiral-many}
#### Many chiral multiplets

With an index $i$ over gauge and flavour, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{free}} = \partial^\mu\phi^{*i}\partial_\mu\phi_i +
i\psi^{\dagger i}\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi_i + F^{*i}F_i$ [@martin1997, eq. 3.2.1, converted], the starting point for the
interactions of @sec-superpotential.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The field equations of the free model are the starting point of every on-shell statement below. The first exercise
derives them from the Lagrangian, with attention to the sign of the scalar term in our signature.

::: {#exr-ssg-wz-free-eom}
#### The free field equations

Derive the Euler-Lagrange equations of @eq-wz-free for $\phi^*$, $\psi^\dagger$ and $F^*$, and check that the scalar term has
positive kinetic energy in our signature.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Varying $\phi^*$: $\partial_\mu\partial^\mu\phi = \Box\phi = 0$, the massless Klein-Gordon equation with $\Box = \partial_t^2 - \nabla^2$.
Varying $\psi^\dagger$: $i\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi = 0$, the Weyl equation. Varying $F^*$: $F = 0$. The scalar term is
$\partial^\mu\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi = |\dot\phi|^2 - |\nabla\phi|^2$, with positive time-derivative part; in Martin's mostly-plus metric
the same expression needs the minus sign that @eq-wz-free removes.
:::

The degrees of freedom were counted in the second example; the exercise asks for the reason behind the count. It
is the first-order nature of the fermion equation that halves the fermionic components on-shell.

::: {#exr-wz-dof}
#### Degrees of freedom

Count the real degrees of freedom of $\phi$, $\psi$ and $F$ on-shell and off-shell and explain why a Weyl spinor has
only two on-shell.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Off-shell, $\phi$ has $2$, $\psi$ has $2$ complex $= 4$ real and $F$ has $2$. The Weyl Lagrangian is first order in
time derivatives, so the canonical momenta are not independent of the coordinates and half of the components are
eliminated on-shell: $\psi$ has $2$, matching the $2$ of $\phi$, while $F = 0$ on-shell contributes nothing
[@martin1997, Table 3.1]. The totals are $4 + 4$ off-shell and $2 + 2$ on-shell.
:::

The halving can also be seen directly in the plane-wave solutions of the Weyl equation. The third exercise finds
them for a momentum along the third axis and identifies the single helicity they carry.

::: {#exr-ssg-weyl-plane-wave}
#### Plane waves of the Weyl equation

Insert $\psi = u\,e^{-ip\cdot x}$ into $i\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi = 0$. Show that a non-zero $u$ requires $p^2 = 0$, find all
solutions for $p^\mu = (E, 0, 0, E)$, and compute their helicity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The equation becomes $(p_\mu\bar\sigma^\mu)u = 0$, with a non-zero solution only if $\det(p\cdot\bar\sigma) = p^2 = 0$. For the given
momentum $p\cdot\bar\sigma = \operatorname{diag}(2E, 0)$ and the solutions are $u = c\,(0, 1)$ with a complex constant $c$: two real
on-shell degrees of freedom, against four off-shell. The rotation generator about the momentum is $\tfrac12\sigma_3$
(@exr-ssg-lorentz-generators), with eigenvalue $-\tfrac12$ on $u$: a left-handed particle.

{{< sage exr-ssg-weyl-plane-wave >}}
:::
::::

A field whose equation is algebraic carries no propagating degree of freedom, and can be removed by solving its
equation. Such fields are the device by which supersymmetry is realised without equations of motion, and the
definition states what is meant.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-auxiliary-field}
#### Auxiliary field

An **auxiliary field** is a field without kinetic term whose equation of motion is algebraic, so that it can be
eliminated without changing the dynamics; it is introduced to make the number of bosonic and fermionic components
match off-shell and the supersymmetry algebra close without equations of motion.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In the free theory the auxiliary field vanishes on-shell, but its transformation is not empty. The first example
shows what it does despite having no dynamics.

::: {#exm-auxiliary-free}
#### $F$ in the free theory

$\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = F^*F$ gives the equation of motion $F = 0$: the field does nothing on-shell, but its
transformation $\delta F = -i\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi$, proportional to the fermion equation of
motion, is exactly what closes the algebra on $\psi$ (@def-off-shell-closure).
:::

With interactions the auxiliary field is no longer zero on-shell. The second example eliminates it in the presence
of a superpotential and finds the scalar potential.

::: {#exm-auxiliary-interacting}
#### $F$ with a superpotential

With the terms $W^iF_i + \text{c.c.}$ of @sec-superpotential, $F^*F + W'F + \bar W'F^* = |F + \bar W'|^2 - |W'|^2$, so
the equation of motion is $F = -\bar W'$ and eliminating $F$ leaves the potential $|W'|^2$
(@prp-auxiliary-elimination, @exr-wz-potential).
:::

The gauge multiplet has its own auxiliary field, which is real because the gauge field is. The third example
anticipates it and the bosonic component it supplies.

::: {#exm-auxiliary-d}
#### $D$ in the gauge multiplet

The gauge multiplet has the real auxiliary field $D$ with $\mathcal{L} \ni \tfrac12D^2$, supplying the one bosonic
component that $A_\mu$ lacks off-shell (@def-gauge-multiplet).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise explains, by power counting, why the auxiliary field has no kinetic term. A term with derivatives
of $F$ would have too high a dimension for a renormalisable theory.

::: {#exr-ssg-aux-dimension}
#### Why $F$ has no kinetic term

Show from $\mathcal{L} \ni F^*F$ that $F$ has mass dimension $2$, and that $\partial^\mu F^*\partial_\mu F$ would have dimension $6$.
What would such a term mean for the counting of degrees of freedom?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Lagrangian density has dimension $4$, so $F^*F$ requires $[F] = 2$, consistent with $\delta\psi \ni \epsilon F$:
$-\tfrac12 + 2 = \tfrac32$. A kinetic term $\partial F^*\partial F$ has dimension $2 + 2 + 2 = 6 > 4$, a non-renormalisable operator
with a dimensionful coupling. It would also make $F$ propagate, adding two on-shell bosonic degrees of freedom with
no fermionic partners, and destroying the on-shell matching $2 + 2$ of @exm-chiral-dof.
:::

Auxiliary fields appear in classical mechanics too, and there the elimination can be checked against the equations
of motion. The second exercise does this for a particle with a superpotential.

::: {#exr-ssg-aux-classical}
#### An auxiliary variable in mechanics

For $L = \tfrac12\dot x^2 + \tfrac12F^2 + FW'(x)$, solve the equation of $F$, substitute, and show that the equation of motion of $x$
obtained before and after the elimination is the same. Where does the reduced potential vanish?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial L/\partial F = F + W' = 0$ gives $F = -W'(x)$, and the reduced Lagrangian is $\tfrac12\dot x^2 - \tfrac12W'^2$. The full
Euler-Lagrange equation $\ddot x = FW''$ with $F = -W'$ equals the reduced one, $\ddot x = -W'W''$. The potential $\tfrac12W'^2$
vanishes at the critical points of $W$, for instance at $x = \pm1$ for $W = \tfrac13x^3 - x$: the bosonic part of the
supersymmetric quantum mechanics of @exm-ssg-susy-qm.

{{< sage exr-ssg-aux-classical >}}
:::

Quantum mechanically an auxiliary field is integrated out rather than eliminated. The third exercise shows that,
because the integral is Gaussian, the two procedures agree exactly.

::: {#exr-ssg-aux-gaussian}
#### Integrating out an auxiliary field

In a path integral with weight $e^{iS}$, show that integrating over an auxiliary field with $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} =
\tfrac12D^2 + JD$, where $J$ depends on the other fields, gives the same result, up to a field-independent constant, as
substituting the solution of its equation of motion.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Complete the square: $\tfrac12D^2 + JD = \tfrac12(D + J)^2 - \tfrac12J^2$. Shifting the integration variable $D \to D - J$ at each
point leaves the measure invariant, so $\int\mathcal{D}D\,e^{i\int(\frac12D^2 + JD)} = e^{-i\int\frac12J^2}\int\mathcal{D}D\,
e^{i\int\frac12D^2}$; the last factor is a constant independent of the other fields. The exponent $-\tfrac12J^2$ is the
value of $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$ at $D = -J$, the classical solution: for Gaussian integrals the stationary-phase
approximation is exact. The same argument with $F^*F + wF + \bar w\bar F$ gives the potential $|w|^2$.
:::
::::

The elimination of the auxiliary field is a completion of the square. Its algebraic content is stated as a
proposition, because it is the step that turns the superpotential into the scalar potential.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-auxiliary-elimination}
#### Eliminating the auxiliary field

$F^*F + wF + \bar w\bar F = |F + \bar w|^2 - |w|^2$ for complex $w$ and $F$, so the auxiliary Lagrangian is extremised
at $F = -\bar w$ with value $-|w|^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Supersymmetry.auxiliary_complete_square`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Supersymmetry.auxiliary_complete_square >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example applies the proposition to a mass term. The auxiliary field then tracks the scalar itself, and
the potential is the mass term of a complex scalar.

::: {#exm-ssg-aux-mass}
#### A mass term

For $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2$, $w = W' = m\phi$, so $F = -m^*\phi^*$ and the Lagrangian acquires $-|m|^2|\phi|^2$: the scalar mass
term of a complex field of mass $|m|$. On a constant background $\phi = 1$, $m = 2i$: $F = 2i$ and $V = 4$.
:::

With several chiral multiplets the square is completed field by field. The second example records the result, the
F-term potential of @def-f-term-potential.

::: {#exm-ssg-aux-several}
#### Several fields

With $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \sum_i(F^{*i}F_i + W^iF_i + W^*_iF^{*i})$ the proposition applies to each $i$ separately:
$F_i = -W^*_i$, and the eliminated Lagrangian contains $-\sum_i|W^i|^2$, the F-term potential with the opposite sign
(@eq-f-term).
:::

The real auxiliary field of a gauge multiplet is eliminated in the same way. The third example completes the
square for it, anticipating the D-term potential.

::: {#exm-ssg-aux-d}
#### The real case

For a real $D$ with $\tfrac12D^2 + jD$, $j$ real, $\tfrac12D^2 + jD = \tfrac12(D + j)^2 - \tfrac12j^2$: $D = -j$ and the value is
$-\tfrac12j^2$. With $j = g\phi^*T^a\phi$ this is the D-term potential $\tfrac12g^2(\phi^*T^a\phi)^2$ of @def-d-term-potential.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the proposition in real components and determines the nature of the stationary point.
The auxiliary Lagrangian has a minimum there, and its value enters the potential with a minus sign.

::: {#exr-ssg-complete-square}
#### Completing the square in components

With $F = a + ib$ and $w = u + iv$, verify the identity of the proposition, find the stationary point in $(a, b)$, and
compute the Hessian of $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$ there.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The stationary point is $a = -u$, $b = v$, that is $F = -\bar w$; the Hessian is $2\cdot1$, a minimum of $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$
with value $-(u^2 + v^2) = -|w|^2$. Since $V = -\mathcal{L}$ for the non-derivative terms, the potential is $+|w|^2$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-complete-square >}}
:::

The relative normalisation of the auxiliary terms matters for the factor in the potential. The second exercise
compares the complex and the real case and finds the factor $\tfrac12$ of the D-terms.

::: {#exr-ssg-aux-normalisation}
#### Normalisations
