Eliminate $F$ from $cF^*F + wF + \bar w\bar F$ with $c > 0$, and $D$ from $\tfrac{c}{2}D^2 + jD$. Why is the normalisation $c = 1$ fixed
by supersymmetry rather than by convention?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F = -\bar w/c$ with value $-|w|^2/c$, and $D = -j/c$ with value $-j^2/(2c)$. The normalisation of $F^*F$ is tied to that of
the kinetic terms by the transformations @eq-wz-transformation: $\delta(F^*F)$ must cancel the terms produced by $\epsilon F$
in $\delta\psi$ (@exm-transformation-auxiliary), which fixes $c = 1$ once $\delta\psi \ni \epsilon F$; rescaling $F$ changes $c$ and the
transformation together, and the potential $|W'|^2$ is unchanged.
:::

When the kinetic terms of the chiral multiplets are not canonical, the auxiliary terms involve a Hermitian matrix,
the Kähler metric of supersymmetric sigma models. The third exercise eliminates the auxiliary fields in that case
and finds a positive potential with the inverse metric.

::: {#exr-ssg-aux-matrix}
#### A matrix of auxiliary fields

For $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = F^{*i}K_{ij}F_j + w^jF_j + \bar w^j F^*_j$ with a positive Hermitian matrix $K$, find the stationary
point and the potential, and check the result for $K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 + i \\ 1 - i & 3 \end{pmatrix}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Varying $F^*$: $KF + \bar w = 0$, so $F = -K^{-1}\bar w$, and the value is $-wK^{-1}w^\dagger$; the potential $V = wK^{-1}w^\dagger$ is
positive because $K^{-1}$ is. For $K = 1$ it is $\sum_i|w_i|^2$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-aux-matrix >}}
:::
::::

![The scalar potential of the interacting Wess-Zumino model with $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2 + \tfrac16y\phi^3$, $V = |m\phi +
\tfrac12y\phi^2|^2$. Left: contours over the complex $\phi$-plane with the two supersymmetric vacua $\phi = 0$ and
$\phi = -2m/y$, where $V = 0$. Right: $V$ along the real axis and the quadratic $|m|^2|\phi|^2$ whose coefficient,
the scalar mass squared, equals the fermion mass squared. Generated by
`figures/wz_potential.sage`.](figures/wz_potential.svg){#fig-wz-potential width=90%}

{{< interactive wz_potential 460 >}}

#### The transformation rules

The transformation rules are fixed, up to normalisation, by linearity in $\epsilon$, by the dimensions of
@exm-chiral-dimensions and by the requirement that the action be invariant. The definition states them with their
conjugates, which contain no metric and are therefore the same as Martin's.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-susy-transformation}
#### Supersymmetry transformation of the chiral multiplet

With a constant Grassmann spinor $\epsilon_\alpha$,
$$
\delta\phi = \epsilon\psi, \qquad
\delta\psi_\alpha = -i(\sigma^\mu\epsilon^\dagger)_\alpha\partial_\mu\phi + \epsilon_\alpha F, \qquad
\delta F = -i\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi,
$$ {#eq-wz-transformation}
and the conjugates $\delta\phi^* = \epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger$, $\delta\psi^\dagger_{\dot\alpha} = i(\epsilon\sigma^\mu)_{\dot\alpha}
\partial_\mu\phi^* + \epsilon^\dagger_{\dot\alpha}F^*$, $\delta F^* = i\partial_\mu\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\epsilon$ [@martin1997,
eqs. 3.1.3, 3.1.13, 3.1.15]; the rules contain no $\eta$ and are the same in both signatures. The action
@eq-wz-free is invariant: $\delta\mathcal{L} = \partial_\mu K^\mu$ for an explicit $K^\mu$ (@prp-wz-invariance).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The invariance is checked term by term. The first example varies the scalar kinetic term, which produces terms
linear in $\epsilon$ and in the derivative of the fermion; these are the terms the fermion variation must cancel.

::: {#exm-transformation-scalar}
#### The variation of the scalar term

$\delta\mathcal{L}_{\text{scalar}} = \epsilon\partial^\mu\psi\,\partial_\mu\phi^* + \epsilon^\dagger\partial^\mu\psi^\dagger
\partial_\mu\phi$ [@martin1997, eq. 3.1.4, with the opposite sign in his metric]: linear in $\epsilon$ and in $\partial\psi$, which is what the variation of
the fermion term must cancel, and which forces $\delta\psi$ to contain $\sigma^\mu\epsilon^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi$.
:::

The fermion term is where the $\sigma$-matrix identity enters. The second example shows how the symmetric part of
$\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu$ produces exactly the terms needed, while the rest is a total derivative.

::: {#exm-transformation-fermion}
#### The variation of the fermion term

$\delta\mathcal{L}_{\text{fermion}} = -\epsilon\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu\partial_\nu\psi\,\partial_\mu\phi^* + \psi^\dagger
\bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\mu\epsilon^\dagger\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi$; using $\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu + \sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu =
2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ (@prp-sigma-identities) and the symmetry of $\partial_\mu\partial_\nu$ it becomes
$-\epsilon\partial^\mu\psi\,\partial_\mu\phi^* - \epsilon^\dagger\partial^\mu\psi^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi - \partial_\mu(\epsilon
\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu\psi\,\partial_\nu\phi^* - \epsilon\psi\,\partial^\mu\phi^* - \epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger\partial^\mu\phi)$
[@martin1997, eqs. 3.1.6-3.1.7, in which the terms with a raised index have the opposite sign]: the first two
terms cancel @exm-transformation-scalar and the rest is a total derivative (@exr-wz-invariance).
:::

Off-shell, the auxiliary term contributes as well. The third example shows that its variation is cancelled by the
$\epsilon F$ term of $\delta\psi$, which is why that term is there.

::: {#exm-transformation-auxiliary}
#### The auxiliary terms

$\delta(F^*F) = -i\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi\,F^* + i\partial_\mu\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\epsilon\,F$ vanishes
on-shell but not off-shell; it is cancelled, up to the total derivative $i\partial_\mu(\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\epsilon
F)$, by the $\epsilon F$ term added to $\delta\psi$ [@martin1997, eq. 3.1.14]. The complete $K^\mu$ is the sum of the
two total derivatives (@prp-wz-invariance).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The conjugate rules are not independent of @eq-wz-transformation. The first exercise derives them, using the rules
for the Hermitian conjugate of products of anticommuting spinors.

::: {#exr-ssg-transformation-conjugate}
#### The conjugate rules

Using $(\xi\chi)^\dagger = \chi^\dagger\xi^\dagger = \xi^\dagger\chi^\dagger$ and $(\xi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\chi)^\dagger = \chi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\xi$, derive
$\delta\phi^*$, $\delta\psi^\dagger$ and $\delta F^*$ from $\delta\phi$, $\delta\psi$ and $\delta F$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\delta\phi^* = (\epsilon\psi)^\dagger = \epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger$. $\delta F^* = (-i\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi)^\dagger =
i\partial_\mu\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\epsilon$, using the Hermiticity of the $\bar\sigma^\mu$. For the fermion, $(\sigma^\mu\epsilon^\dagger)_\alpha$
conjugates to $(\epsilon\sigma^\mu)_{\dot\alpha}$, since $\sigma^\mu$ is Hermitian (@exr-ssg-sigma-bar-epsilon), so $\delta\psi^\dagger_{\dot\alpha} = +
i(\epsilon\sigma^\mu)_{\dot\alpha}\partial_\mu\phi^* + \epsilon^\dagger_{\dot\alpha}F^*$, the sign of the $i$ flipping under conjugation.
:::

The second exercise reproduces the first example. It is a one-line computation once the rule $\delta(\partial_\mu X) =
\partial_\mu\delta X$ for a constant parameter is used.

::: {#exr-ssg-transformation-scalar}
#### Varying the scalar term

Compute $\delta(\partial^\mu\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi)$ from @eq-wz-transformation and show that, up to a total derivative, it equals
$-\epsilon\psi\,\Box\phi^* - \epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger\Box\phi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\delta(\partial^\mu\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi) = \partial^\mu(\epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger)\partial_\mu\phi + \partial^\mu\phi^*\partial_\mu(\epsilon\psi) =
\epsilon^\dagger\partial^\mu\psi^\dagger\,\partial_\mu\phi + \epsilon\partial^\mu\psi\,\partial_\mu\phi^*$, the expression of @exm-transformation-scalar
(products of an even number of Grassmann factors commute with the bosonic $\partial\phi$). Integrating by parts,
$\epsilon\partial^\mu\psi\,\partial_\mu\phi^* = \partial^\mu(\epsilon\psi\,\partial_\mu\phi^*) - \epsilon\psi\,\Box\phi^*$, and likewise for the
conjugate: the variation vanishes on the scalar field equation up to a total derivative, but not off-shell.
:::

The heart of the invariance is the step in the second example. The third exercise carries it out, isolating the
role of the $\sigma$-matrix identity.

::: {#exr-ssg-transformation-fermion}
#### The key step

Show that $\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\mu\epsilon^\dagger\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi = \psi^\dagger\epsilon^\dagger\,\Box\phi$, and explain how this term
combines with $\epsilon^\dagger\partial^\mu\psi^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi$ of the scalar variation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $\partial_\mu\partial_\nu$ is symmetric, only the symmetric part $\tfrac12(\bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\mu + \bar\sigma^\mu\sigma^\nu) = \eta^{\mu\nu}$
(@prp-sigma-identities, in the barred form of @exr-sigma-identities) survives, giving $\psi^\dagger\epsilon^\dagger\,\Box\phi =
\epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger\,\Box\phi$. Adding the scalar variation, $\epsilon^\dagger\partial^\mu\psi^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi + \epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger\Box\phi =
\partial^\mu(\epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi)$, a total derivative: this is how the $2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ of the Clifford relation, with
the sign of our signature, makes the boson and fermion kinetic terms compatible.
:::
::::

The term-by-term computation of the examples is summarised in a single exact identity. It holds in the exterior
algebra generated by the fields and their derivatives, which handles every Grassmann sign.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-wz-invariance}
#### Invariance of the Wess-Zumino action

With the fields, their derivatives and $\epsilon$ as generators of an exterior algebra over the ring of commuting
jets, $\delta\mathcal{L} = \partial_\mu K^\mu$ holds as an exact identity for @eq-wz-free and @eq-wz-transformation, with
$K^\mu = -\epsilon\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu\psi\,\partial_\nu\phi^* + \epsilon\psi\,\partial^\mu\phi^* + \epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger
\partial^\mu\phi + i\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\epsilon F$, and likewise for the model without $F$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Computed exactly with Sage's exterior algebra (`sage/oracles/wz_invariance.sage`, @exr-wz-invariance).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The current $K^\mu$ has a recognisable structure. The first example sorts its four terms by origin, which is useful
when the supercurrent is computed from it.

::: {#exm-ssg-k-structure}
#### The pieces of $K^\mu$

The first three terms of $K^\mu$ come from the fermion kinetic term (@exm-transformation-fermion), the term with
$\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu$ from the antisymmetric part of $\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu$ and the two with $\partial^\mu$ from the symmetric
part; the last, $i\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\epsilon F$, comes from the auxiliary terms (@exm-transformation-auxiliary). The
middle two are the total derivatives found in @exr-ssg-transformation-scalar and @exr-ssg-transformation-fermion.
:::

The second example records the statement for the model without auxiliary field. There the transformation of the
fermion has no $F$ term, and the invariance still holds off-shell.

::: {#exm-ssg-invariance-massless}
#### Without the auxiliary field

With $\delta_0\psi = -i\sigma^\mu\epsilon^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi$ and $\mathcal{L}_0 = \partial^\mu\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi + i\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi$,
$\delta_0\mathcal{L}_0 = \partial_\mu K_0^\mu$ with $K_0^\mu$ the first three terms of $K^\mu$ [@martin1997, eq. 3.1.8]: the action is
invariant without $F$; what fails without $F$ is the closure of the algebra (@exm-closure-fermion).
:::

Interactions keep the invariance if they come from a holomorphic superpotential. The third example states the
total derivative for the interaction terms, which @exr-ssg-wz-superpotential-invariance checks exactly.

::: {#exm-ssg-invariance-superpotential}
#### With a superpotential

For $\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}} = W'F - \tfrac12W''\psi\psi + \text{c.c.}$ with $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2 + \tfrac16y\phi^3$, the terms with $F$ cancel
between $\delta(W'F)$ and $\delta(-\tfrac12W''\psi\psi)$, and the rest is $\partial_\mu K^\mu_{\text{int}}$ with $K^\mu_{\text{int}} = -
iW'\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\psi + iW'^*\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\epsilon$ [@martin1997, eqs. 3.2.9-3.2.12]: no metric is involved,
and the result holds in both signatures.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is the computation behind the proposition. It sets up the exterior algebra over the jet ring
and checks the identity with and without the auxiliary field.

::: {#exr-wz-invariance}
#### The variation of the action in Sage

Set up the Wess-Zumino fields as an exterior algebra over the jet ring, implement $\delta$ and $\partial_\mu$ as
derivations, and check $\delta\mathcal{L} = \partial_\mu K^\mu$ with and without the auxiliary field.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-wz-invariance >}}
:::

The superpotential must be holomorphic, and the reason can be seen in the variation. The second exercise examines
what goes wrong with a term containing $\phi^*$.

::: {#exr-ssg-holomorphy}
#### Why the superpotential is holomorphic

Vary the term $\phi^*\psi\psi$ and show that it produces a term $(\epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger)(\psi\psi)$ with three fermions. Which other
terms of a renormalisable Lagrangian could cancel it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\delta(\phi^*\psi\psi) = \epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger\,\psi\psi + 2\phi^*\psi\delta\psi$; the first term is cubic in fermions and
contains no derivative and no $F$. Every other term of a renormalisable Lagrangian varies into terms with at most
two fermion fields, or with a derivative, or with $F$; a total derivative of such terms cannot produce
$\epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger\psi\psi$ either. So the coefficient must vanish: the Yukawa and mass terms depend on $\phi$ only through the
holomorphic $W''(\phi)$ [@martin1997, p. 22]. The exact computation is part of @exr-ssg-wz-superpotential-invariance.
:::

The third exercise extends the computer check to the interacting model. The couplings enter as additional
commuting variables, and the result confirms the total derivative of the third example.

::: {#exr-ssg-wz-superpotential-invariance}
#### Invariance of the interactions in Sage

Add $m, m^*, y, y^*$ to the jet ring of @exr-wz-invariance, form $\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}}$ for $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2 + \tfrac16y\phi^3$, and
check $\delta\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}} = \partial_\mu K^\mu_{\text{int}}$. Vary also $\phi^*\psi\psi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The variation of the interaction terms has 24 monomials and equals the divergence of $K^\mu_{\text{int}}$ exactly; the
non-holomorphic term produces three-fermion terms:

{{< sage exr-ssg-wz-superpotential-invariance >}}
:::
::::

#### Closure of the algebra

Invariance of the action is not the whole story: the transformations must also represent the algebra
@eq-superalgebra, that is, two of them must compose to a translation. The definition makes this precise and
distinguishes closure that needs the equations of motion from closure that does not.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-off-shell-closure}
#### Off-shell closure

The supersymmetry algebra **closes** on a field $X$ if the commutator of two transformations is a translation,
$$
(\delta_{\epsilon_2}\delta_{\epsilon_1} - \delta_{\epsilon_1}\delta_{\epsilon_2})X = i(-\epsilon_1\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2^\dagger +
\epsilon_2\sigma^\mu\epsilon_1^\dagger)\,\partial_\mu X,
$$ {#eq-wz-closure}
the field-theory form of @eq-superalgebra; it closes **on-shell** if this holds only modulo the equations of
motion and **off-shell** if it holds identically [@martin1997, eqs. 3.1.9-3.1.16].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The scalar is the easiest field on which to check closure. The first example does it in two lines, and finds that the
auxiliary field drops out of the commutator.

::: {#exm-closure-scalar}
#### Closure on the scalar

$\delta_2\delta_1\phi = \epsilon_1\delta_2\psi = -i\epsilon_1\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi + \epsilon_1\epsilon_2F$;
antisymmetrising, the $F$ terms cancel because $\epsilon_1\epsilon_2 = \epsilon_2\epsilon_1$ (@exm-grassmann-spinor-product)
and @eq-wz-closure follows with no equation of motion [@martin1997, eq. 3.1.9] (@exr-wz-closure).
:::

The fermion is where the auxiliary field earns its place. The second example shows the extra terms that appear
without it and how they are cancelled when it is present.

::: {#exm-closure-fermion}
#### Closure on the fermion

Without $F$, $(\delta_2\delta_1 - \delta_1\delta_2)\psi_\alpha$ contains, after the Fierz identity, the extra terms
$i\epsilon_{1\alpha}\epsilon_2^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi - i\epsilon_{2\alpha}\epsilon_1^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi$,
proportional to the equation of motion $\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi = 0$ [@martin1997, eq. 3.1.11]: the algebra
closes only on-shell. With $\delta\psi \ni \epsilon F$ and $\delta F = -i\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi$ the
extra terms cancel identically (@prp-wz-closure).
:::

Counting components explains the need for the auxiliary field without any computation. The third example gives the
argument, and notes where it leads in supergravity.

::: {#exm-closure-counting}
#### Why the auxiliary field is needed

Off-shell $\psi$ has four real components and $\phi$ two; a representation of the algebra on the off-shell fields
needs $n_B = n_F$ (@def-supermultiplet), and $F$ supplies the missing two bosonic components [@martin1997, p.
20]. The same reasoning gives $D$ for the gauge multiplet; for supergravities beyond $N = 1$ in four dimensions no
off-shell formulation is known [@tanii1998, p. 6].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise repeats the closure on the scalar with all steps shown. It is short, but it shows clearly where the
symmetry of the spinor product is used.

::: {#exr-ssg-closure-scalar}
#### Closure on $\phi$ by hand

Compute $\delta_{\epsilon_2}\delta_{\epsilon_1}\phi$ and antisymmetrise to obtain @eq-wz-closure on $\phi$. Where is the Grassmann nature of
$\epsilon$ used?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\delta_{\epsilon_1}\phi = \epsilon_1\psi$, and $\delta_{\epsilon_2}$ acts only on $\psi$: $\delta_{\epsilon_2}\delta_{\epsilon_1}\phi = \epsilon_1^\alpha(-i(\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2^\dagger)_\alpha
\partial_\mu\phi + \epsilon_{2\alpha}F) = -i\epsilon_1\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi + \epsilon_1\epsilon_2F$. Exchanging $1 \leftrightarrow 2$ and
subtracting, the $F$ terms cancel since $\epsilon_1\epsilon_2 = \epsilon_2\epsilon_1$, which holds precisely because the components
anticommute (@exm-grassmann-spinor-product); the remaining terms are @eq-wz-closure.
:::

A translation parameter should be a real vector. The second exercise checks that the combination of spinor
parameters in @eq-wz-closure is real, up to the factor $i$ that makes $i\xi^\mu\partial_\mu$ Hermitian.

::: {#exr-ssg-closure-parameter}
#### The translation vector is real

Let $v^\mu = -\epsilon_1\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2^\dagger + \epsilon_2\sigma^\mu\epsilon_1^\dagger$. Using $(\chi\sigma^\mu\xi^\dagger)^\dagger = \xi\sigma^\mu\chi^\dagger$, show
that $v^{\mu\dagger} = -v^\mu$, so that $iv^\mu$ is real (Hermitian) and @eq-wz-closure is a translation by a real vector.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$v^{\mu\dagger} = -(\epsilon_1\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2^\dagger)^\dagger + (\epsilon_2\sigma^\mu\epsilon_1^\dagger)^\dagger = -\epsilon_2\sigma^\mu\epsilon_1^\dagger +
\epsilon_1\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2^\dagger = -v^\mu$. Hence $(iv^\mu)^\dagger = -i(-v^\mu) = iv^\mu$: the coefficient $a^\mu = iv^\mu$ is a real
(bosonic, Hermitian) vector, and $(\delta_2\delta_1 - \delta_1\delta_2)X = a^\mu\partial_\mu X$ is the infinitesimal translation by $a^\mu$.
:::

The counting argument of the third example applies to every multiplet. The third exercise applies it to the
gauge multiplet and to the model without auxiliary field.

::: {#exr-ssg-closure-count}
#### Counting for closure

Count the off-shell components of $(A_\mu, \lambda)$, modulo gauge transformations, and show that one bosonic component is
missing. For the chiral multiplet without $F$, how many components would the algebra have to identify on-shell?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A_\mu$ has four components minus one gauge function, $3$; the Weyl spinor $\lambda$ has $4$: one bosonic component is
missing, supplied by the real $D$ (@def-gauge-multiplet). Without $F$ the chiral multiplet has $2$ bosonic and $4$
fermionic components off-shell; the fermion equation removes $2$, and the algebra can only close where this equation
holds, which is the statement of @exm-closure-fermion.
:::
::::

The closure on all three fields, with no equation of motion, is the content of the next proposition. Like the
invariance, it is an identity in the exterior algebra.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-wz-closure}
#### Off-shell closure

@eq-wz-closure holds identically on $\phi$, on $F$ and on $\psi_\alpha$ for @eq-wz-transformation, with no equation of
motion used.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Computed exactly with Sage's exterior algebra (`sage/oracles/wz_closure.sage`, @exr-wz-closure).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The auxiliary field itself is the second field on which closure is checked. The first example records the
computation, in which the $\sigma$-matrix identity removes a term symmetric in the two parameters.

::: {#exm-ssg-closure-f}
#### Closure on $F$

$\delta_2\delta_1F = -i\epsilon_1^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\delta_2\psi = -\epsilon_1^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\sigma^\nu\epsilon_2^\dagger\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi -
i\epsilon_1^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2\partial_\mu F$. The first term is $-\epsilon_1^\dagger\epsilon_2^\dagger\Box\phi$, symmetric in $1 \leftrightarrow
2$; the second is $i\epsilon_2\sigma^\mu\epsilon_1^\dagger\partial_\mu F$, and antisymmetrising gives @eq-wz-closure on $F$ [@martin1997, eq. 3.
1.16] (@exr-ssg-closure-f).
:::

When the two parameters are equal, the commutator must vanish. The second example checks that the translation
vector does, which is a quick consistency test of signs.

::: {#exm-ssg-closure-equal}
#### Equal parameters

For $\epsilon_1 = \epsilon_2 = \epsilon$, $v^\mu = -\epsilon\sigma^\mu\epsilon^\dagger + \epsilon\sigma^\mu\epsilon^\dagger = 0$: two identical transformations
commute, as they must. For $\epsilon_2 = c\,\epsilon_1$ with a complex number $c$, $v^\mu = (c - \bar c)\,\epsilon_1\sigma^\mu\epsilon_1^\dagger$, which
vanishes for real $c$ and is a translation along $\epsilon_1\sigma^\mu\epsilon_1^\dagger$ for imaginary $c$: the two
transformations then differ by a phase, which is a genuinely different direction in the space of parameters.
:::

The oscillator of @prp-susy-oscillator realises the same structure in one dimension. The third example translates
@eq-wz-closure into the anticommutator of the supercharges.

::: {#exm-ssg-closure-oscillator}
#### Closure as $\{Q, Q^\dagger\} = H$

On the oscillator, with Grassmann parameters $\epsilon_i$, $\bar\epsilon_i$ and $G_i = \epsilon_iQ + \bar\epsilon_iQ^\dagger$ acting by commutators,
$[G_2, [G_1, X]] - [G_1, [G_2, X]] = [[G_2, G_1], X]$, and $Q^2 = 0$ with the anticommutation of the parameters past
$Q$ gives $[G_2, G_1] = (\bar\epsilon_1\epsilon_2 - \bar\epsilon_2\epsilon_1)\{Q, Q^\dagger\} = (\bar\epsilon_1\epsilon_2 - \bar\epsilon_2\epsilon_1)H$: the commutator of two
supersymmetries is a time translation, the $0 + 1$-dimensional @eq-wz-closure.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is the computation behind the proposition. It checks closure on the scalar and on $F$ in the
exterior algebra with two independent spinor parameters.

::: {#exr-wz-closure}
#### Closure of the algebra in Sage

Compute $(\delta_2\delta_1 - \delta_1\delta_2)X$ for $X = \phi, F, \psi_\alpha$ and compare with @eq-wz-closure.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-wz-closure >}}
:::

The second exercise fills in the steps of the first example. The only identity needed is the symmetric part of
$\bar\sigma^\mu\sigma^\nu$, as in @exr-ssg-transformation-fermion.

::: {#exr-ssg-closure-f}
#### Closure on $F$ by hand

Derive the two terms of @exm-ssg-closure-f, show that the first is symmetric under $1 \leftrightarrow 2$, and rewrite the
second using $\chi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\xi = -\xi\sigma^\mu\chi^\dagger$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\delta_2\psi = -i\sigma^\nu\epsilon_2^\dagger\partial_\nu\phi + \epsilon_2F$, so $-i\epsilon_1^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\delta_2\psi$ gives the two terms. In
the first, $\partial_\mu\partial_\nu$ symmetric selects $\tfrac12(\bar\sigma^\mu\sigma^\nu + \bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\mu) = \eta^{\mu\nu}$, giving $-\epsilon_1^\dagger
\epsilon_2^\dagger\Box\phi$, symmetric since $\epsilon_1^\dagger\epsilon_2^\dagger = \epsilon_2^\dagger\epsilon_1^\dagger$; it drops out of the commutator. In the
second, $-i\epsilon_1^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2 = i\epsilon_2\sigma^\mu\epsilon_1^\dagger$; antisymmetrising gives $i(\epsilon_2\sigma^\mu\epsilon_1^\dagger -
\epsilon_1\sigma^\mu\epsilon_2^\dagger)\partial_\mu F$, which is @eq-wz-closure.
:::

Eliminating the auxiliary field in an interacting theory brings the equations of motion back into the algebra. The
third exercise identifies what is lost.

::: {#exr-ssg-closure-eliminated}
#### Closure after eliminating $F$

In the interacting model, substitute $F = -W'^*$ into $\delta\psi$. Explain why the algebra on $\psi$ now closes only up to
terms proportional to the fermion equation of motion $i\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi - W''^*\psi^\dagger = 0$, while before the
elimination it closed identically.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Before elimination the transformations @eq-wz-transformation do not depend on $W$, so @prp-wz-closure applies unchanged
to the interacting theory. After substituting $F = -W'^*$, $\delta F$ is no longer an independent rule: $\delta(-W'^*) = -
W''^*\epsilon^\dagger\psi^\dagger$, while the closure required $\delta F = -i\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi$. The two agree only when
$i\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi = W''^*\psi^\dagger$, the fermion equation of motion of the interacting model, so the algebra closes
on-shell, with the defect proportional to the equation of motion, as in @exm-closure-fermion.
:::
::::

#### The supercurrent

A continuous symmetry of the action has a conserved Noether current, and supersymmetry is no exception. Its current
carries a spinor index and integrates to the supercharges of @def-supercharge, which closes the circle between the
field theory and the algebra.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-supercurrent}
#### Supercurrent

The **supercurrent** of a supersymmetric Lagrangian is the Noether current (@def-noether-current) of the
transformation @eq-wz-transformation, $\epsilon J^\mu + \epsilon^\dagger J^{\dagger\mu} = \sum_X\delta X\,\partial\mathcal{L}/
\partial(\partial_\mu X) - K^\mu$, an anticommuting vector-spinor; it is conserved on-shell, $\partial_\mu J^\mu_\alpha = 0$, and
its charges $Q_\alpha = \sqrt2\int d^3x\,J^0_\alpha$ are the supercharges [@martin1997, eqs. 3.1.17-3.1.20].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the free model the current is a single bilinear in the scalar and the fermion. The first example gives it,
together with its conjugate.

::: {#exm-supercurrent-free}
#### The free supercurrent

For @eq-wz-free, $J^\mu_\alpha = (\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu\psi)_\alpha\partial_\nu\phi^*$ and $J^{\dagger\mu}_{\dot\alpha} =
(\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\sigma^\nu)_{\dot\alpha}\partial_\nu\phi$ [@martin1997, eq. 3.1.18], bilinear in the boson and the
fermion as a current that exchanges them must be.
:::

Interactions add terms to the current, one for each new term in the transformations. The second example lists them
and notes their role in supersymmetry breaking.

::: {#exm-supercurrent-interacting}
#### With interactions

With a superpotential and gauge fields the supercurrent acquires the terms $i(\sigma^\mu\psi^{\dagger i})_\alpha W_i^*$ and
the gaugino terms [@martin1997, eq. 4.3.13]; its conservation is what relates the goldstino to the auxiliary
fields when supersymmetry breaks (@def-susy-breaking).
:::

In supergravity the supercurrent has a gauge field of its own. The third example anticipates the second part of the
chapter.

::: {#exm-supercurrent-gravitino}
#### The source of the gravitino

In supergravity the supercurrent couples to the gravitino as the electromagnetic current couples to the photon,
$\mathcal{L} \ni \bar\psi_\mu J^\mu$ (@sec-gravitino): local supersymmetry gauges the supercurrent.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the dimensions of the supercurrent and of the supercharge built from it. It confirms the
dimension $\tfrac12$ of $Q$ found from the algebra.

::: {#exr-ssg-supercurrent-dimension}
#### Dimensions

Find the mass dimension of $J^\mu_\alpha$ from @exm-supercurrent-free, and that of $Q_\alpha = \sqrt2\int d^3x\,J^0_\alpha$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\psi] + [\partial\phi] = \tfrac32 + 2 = \tfrac72$, so $J^\mu$ has dimension $\tfrac72$ and $\epsilon J^\mu$ dimension $3$, that of a current
($\partial_\mu J^\mu$ has dimension $4$). Integrating over three-space subtracts $3$: $[Q] = \tfrac12$, in agreement with
@exr-ssg-supercharge-dimension.
:::

Conservation on-shell is a short computation with the identities of @prp-sigma-identities. The second exercise
carries it out for the free current.

::: {#exr-ssg-supercurrent-conservation}
#### Conservation of the free supercurrent

Show that $\partial_\mu J^\mu_\alpha = 0$ for $J^\mu = \sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu\psi\,\partial_\nu\phi^*$ when $\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi = 0$ and $\Box\phi^* = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_\mu J^\mu = \sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi\,\partial_\nu\phi^* + \sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu\psi\,\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi^*$. The first term vanishes by the
Weyl equation. In the second only the symmetric part $\tfrac12(\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu + \sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu) = \eta^{\mu\nu}$ survives,
giving $\psi\,\Box\phi^* = 0$ by the Klein-Gordon equation. Both field equations are needed: the current is conserved
on-shell only, as Noether currents are.
:::

The supercharge is the integral of the time component, and in terms of canonical variables it has a simple form. The
third exercise derives it.

::: {#exr-ssg-supercurrent-charge}
#### The supercharge in canonical variables

With $\pi = \partial_0\phi^*$ the momentum conjugate to $\phi$, write $J^0_\alpha$ for the free current in terms of $\pi$ and the
spatial derivatives, and give $Q_\alpha$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$J^0 = \sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^0\psi\,\partial_\nu\phi^* = \sigma^\nu\psi\,\partial_\nu\phi^*$ since $\bar\sigma^0 = 1$. The $\nu = 0$ term is $\psi\,\pi$ and the spatial
ones $\sigma_i\psi\,\partial_i\phi^*$. So $Q_\alpha = \sqrt2\int d^3x\,(\psi_\alpha\pi + (\sigma_i\psi)_\alpha\partial_i\phi^*)$: it removes a
fermion and creates a boson, with the spatial term making the result Lorentz covariant. With the canonical
(anti)commutators it generates @eq-wz-transformation through @exm-supercharge-action [@martin1997, eqs. 3.1.21-3.1.23].
:::
::::

#### Superspace

The transformation rules of the chiral multiplet were found by trial, and the auxiliary field had to be added by
hand to close the algebra. Both become automatic when the three fields are packaged as one function on an enlarged
space whose extra coordinates are anticommuting spinors, the superspace of Salam and Strathdee, and this
subsection introduces that packaging for the chiral multiplet [@nath2017supersymmetry, Secs. 8.4-8.8].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-ssg-chiral-superfield}
#### Chiral superfield

**Superspace** has the coordinates $(x^\mu, \theta^\alpha, \theta^{\dagger\dot\alpha})$, where $\theta^\alpha$ and $\theta^{\dagger\dot\alpha}$ are
two-component spinors whose components are Grassmann variables (@def-grassmann-variable, @def-weyl-spinor), and a
**superfield** is a function on superspace, a polynomial in $\theta$ and $\theta^\dagger$ with fields as coefficients. A
**chiral superfield** is a superfield that depends on $\theta^\dagger$ only through the combination $y^\mu = x^\mu +
i\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger$:
$$
\Phi = \phi(y) + \sqrt2\,\theta\psi(y) + \theta\theta\,F(y) ,
$$ {#eq-ssg-chiral-superfield}
whose three coefficients are the fields of a chiral multiplet (@def-chiral-multiplet) [@martin1997, Sec. 4.4;
@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 8.75]. Equivalently, $\Phi$ is annihilated by the first-order operator $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}$, built
from $\partial/\partial\theta^{\dagger\dot\alpha}$ and $\partial_\mu$, that annihilates $y^\mu$ and $\theta^\alpha$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs.
8.59-8.74].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The variable $y^\mu$ hides the dependence on $\theta^\dagger$. The first example expands it out, using the
Grassmann identities of @exr-ssg-theta-fierz, and finds that the superfield is determined by the three component
fields and their derivatives.

::: {#exm-ssg-superfield-x-expansion}
#### The superfield in terms of $x$

Taylor expansion in $i\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger$ stops at second order, and with $(\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger)(\theta\sigma^\nu\theta^\dagger) =
\tfrac12\eta^{\mu\nu}\theta\theta\,\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger$ and $(\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger)(\theta\chi) = -\tfrac12\theta\theta\,\chi\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger$,
$$
\Phi = \phi + i\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi - \tfrac14\theta\theta\,\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger\,\Box\phi + \sqrt2\,\theta\psi
- \tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}\theta\theta\,\partial_\mu\psi\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger + \theta\theta F ,
$$
all fields at $x$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 8.82, where the $\Box$ term has the opposite sign because of the
mostly-plus metric]. No new field appears: the higher components are derivatives of $\phi$ and $\psi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A general superfield has many more components than a chiral one. The second example counts them, and finds that
the chiral condition cuts the count down to exactly the off-shell content of the Wess-Zumino multiplet.

::: {#exm-ssg-superfield-count}
#### Counting components

The monomials in the four Grassmann coordinates $\theta^1, \theta^2, \theta^{\dagger1}, \theta^{\dagger2}$ number $2^4 = 16$, so a general
complex superfield has $16$ complex component fields, $8$ of them bosonic (even degree) and $8$ fermionic. A chiral
superfield keeps one complex scalar $\phi$, one Weyl spinor $\psi$ and one complex $F$: $4$ real bosonic and $4$ real
fermionic components off-shell, the balance of @exr-wz-dof that the auxiliary field was introduced to achieve.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The complex conjugate of a chiral superfield is not chiral: it depends on $\theta^\dagger$ freely and on $\theta$ only through
the conjugate variable. The third example records this antichiral superfield, which supplies the conjugate fields.

::: {#exm-ssg-antichiral}
#### The antichiral superfield

$\Phi^\dagger = \phi^*(y^*) + \sqrt2\,\theta^\dagger\psi^\dagger(y^*) + \theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger F^*(y^*)$ with $y^{*\mu} = x^\mu -
i\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger$ is annihilated by the conjugate operator $D_\alpha$; it is a function of $\theta^\dagger$ and $y^*$ alone
[@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 8.5, eq. 8.102]. A product $\Phi^\dagger\Phi$ depends on both sets of coordinates and is
neither chiral nor antichiral; its top component is the kinetic Lagrangian (@exm-ssg-kahler-term).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Grassmann identities used in the expansion are statements about four anticommuting generators, so they can be
checked by direct computation in the exterior algebra. The first exercise does this in our conventions.

::: {#exr-ssg-theta-fierz}
#### The $\theta$ identities

With $\epsilon^{12} = 1$, $\theta\theta = \theta^\alpha\theta_\alpha$ and $\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger = \theta^\dagger_{\dot\alpha}\theta^{\dagger\dot\alpha}$, show that $\theta^\alpha\theta^\beta =
-\tfrac12\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\theta\theta$, $\theta^{\dagger\dot\alpha}\theta^{\dagger\dot\beta} = \tfrac12\epsilon^{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger$ and
$(\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger)(\theta\sigma^\nu\theta^\dagger) = \tfrac12\eta^{\mu\nu}\theta\theta\,\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger$, and deduce the
$\Box\phi$ term of @exm-ssg-superfield-x-expansion. Check everything with Sage's exterior algebra.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\theta_1 = \epsilon_{12}\theta^2 = -\theta^2$ and $\theta_2 = \theta^1$, $\theta\theta = -\theta^1\theta^2 + \theta^2\theta^1 = -2\theta^1\theta^2$, so
$\theta^1\theta^2 = -\tfrac12\theta\theta = -\tfrac12\epsilon^{12}\theta\theta$, and the other components follow by antisymmetry; the dotted
case differs by the order of the contraction, $\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger = 2\theta^{\dagger1}\theta^{\dagger2}$. Then
$(\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger)(\theta\sigma^\nu\theta^\dagger) = -\theta^\alpha\theta^\beta\theta^{\dagger\dot\alpha}\theta^{\dagger\dot\beta}
\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}\sigma^\nu_{\beta\dot\beta} = \tfrac14\theta\theta\,\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger\,\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\epsilon^{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}
\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}\sigma^\nu_{\beta\dot\beta}$, and the last contraction is $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu) = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ by the
relation between $\bar\sigma$ and $\sigma$ of @exr-ssg-sigma-bar-epsilon. The second-order Taylor term is
$\tfrac12(i\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger)(i\theta\sigma^\nu\theta^\dagger)\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi = -\tfrac14\theta\theta\,\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger\,\Box\phi$.

{{< sage exr-ssg-theta-fierz >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The expansion of the example is the content of @nath2017supersymmetry [eqs. 8.76-8.82]. The second exercise asks for
the analogous expansion of the antichiral superfield, where the sign of the imaginary unit changes.

::: {#exr-ssg-antichiral-expansion}
#### Expanding the antichiral superfield

Expand $\Phi^\dagger$ of @exm-ssg-antichiral in powers of $\theta$ and $\theta^\dagger$ at the point $x$, and check that the result is
the complex conjugate of the expansion in @exm-ssg-superfield-x-expansion.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Replacing $i \to -i$ in the Taylor expansion, $\phi^*(y^*) = \phi^* - i\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi^* -
\tfrac14\theta\theta\,\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger\,\Box\phi^*$, since the second-order term contains $(-i)^2 = i^2$. For the fermion,
$\sqrt2\,\theta^\dagger\psi^\dagger(y^*) = \sqrt2\,\theta^\dagger\psi^\dagger - \sqrt2\,i(\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger)(\theta^\dagger\partial_\mu\psi^\dagger)$, and the
dotted analogue of the identity of @exr-ssg-theta-fierz turns the last term into $\tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger\,
\theta\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi^\dagger$. So
$\Phi^\dagger = \phi^* - i\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger\partial_\mu\phi^* - \tfrac14\theta\theta\,\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger\,\Box\phi^* + \sqrt2\,\theta^\dagger\psi^\dagger +
\tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger\,\theta\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi^\dagger + \theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger F^*$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 8.106,
up to the sign of the $\Box$ term]. Conjugation reverses the order of Grassmann factors, $(\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger)^\dagger =
\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger$ (the $\sigma^\mu$ are Hermitian) and $(\theta\psi)^\dagger = \theta^\dagger\psi^\dagger$, so term by term this is the conjugate
of @exm-ssg-superfield-x-expansion.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A vector, or real, superfield satisfies $V = V^\dagger$ instead of the chiral condition, and it carries the gauge
multiplet. The third exercise counts its components and finds the gauge freedom that removes most of them.

::: {#exr-ssg-vector-superfield}
#### The components of a real superfield

A real superfield $V = V^\dagger$ has the components $C, \chi, p, v_\mu, \lambda, D$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 8.147]: $C$ and
$D$ real, $p$ complex, $v_\mu$ a real vector, $\chi$ and $\lambda$ Weyl spinors. Count its real bosonic and fermionic
components, and show that the shift $V \to V + \Lambda + \Lambda^\dagger$ by a chiral superfield $\Lambda$ removes $C$, $\chi$ and $p$
and shifts $v_\mu$ by a gradient, leaving the gauge multiplet of @def-gauge-multiplet.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Bosonic: $1 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 8$ ($C$, $p$, $v_\mu$, $D$); fermionic: $4 + 4 = 8$ ($\chi$, $\lambda$). Writing $\Lambda = \phi_\Lambda +
\sqrt2\,\theta\psi_\Lambda + \theta\theta F_\Lambda$, the combination $\Lambda + \Lambda^\dagger$ has lowest component $\phi_\Lambda + \phi_\Lambda^*$, $\theta$
component $\sqrt2\,\psi_\Lambda$, $\theta\theta$ component $F_\Lambda$, and $\theta\sigma^\mu\theta^\dagger$ component $i\partial_\mu(\phi_\Lambda - \phi^*_\Lambda)$
(@exm-ssg-superfield-x-expansion), while its $\lambda$ and $D$ components are total derivatives that drop out once $\lambda$ and $D$
are defined as in @nath2017supersymmetry [eqs. 8.149-8.157]. Choosing $\operatorname{Re}\phi_\Lambda$, $\psi_\Lambda$ and $F_\Lambda$ to
cancel $C$, $\chi$ and $p$ is the **Wess-Zumino gauge**; the remaining $\operatorname{Im}\phi_\Lambda$ shifts $v_\mu$ by a gradient, the
ordinary gauge transformation. What is left is $v_\mu$, $\lambda$, $D$, with $3 + 1 = 4$ bosonic components off-shell modulo
gauge and $4$ fermionic ones, the content of @def-gauge-multiplet.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Superfields earn their keep through multiplication: products of chiral superfields are chiral, and the top
component of any superfield transforms into a total derivative, so it is a candidate Lagrangian. The proposition
gives the components of a product and identifies the superpotential couplings of the next section as a top
component.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-ssg-chiral-products}
#### Products of chiral superfields

The product of chiral superfields $\Phi_1 = \phi_1 + \sqrt2\,\theta\psi_1 + \theta\theta F_1$ and $\Phi_2$ is chiral, with the components
$$
\Phi_1\Phi_2 = \phi_1\phi_2 + \sqrt2\,\theta(\phi_1\psi_2 + \psi_1\phi_2) + \theta\theta\,(\phi_1F_2 + F_1\phi_2 - \psi_1\psi_2) ,
$$
all at the point $y$. Consequently, for a polynomial $W(\Phi_i)$, the $\theta\theta$ component of $W(\Phi)$ is
$W^iF_i - \tfrac12W^{ij}\psi_i\psi_j$ with $W^i = \partial W/\partial\phi_i$ and $W^{ij} = \partial^2W/\partial\phi_i\partial\phi_j$
[@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 8.108-8.111 and 8.135].
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest products already reproduce couplings met earlier. The first example takes the square of one chiral
superfield and recovers the mass terms of the quadratic superpotential.

::: {#exm-ssg-product-mass}
#### The square of a chiral superfield

For $\Phi_1 = \Phi_2 = \Phi$ the proposition gives $\Phi^2 = \phi^2 + 2\sqrt2\,\phi\,\theta\psi + \theta\theta(2\phi F - \psi\psi)$, so the
$\theta\theta$ component of $\tfrac12m\Phi^2$ is $m\phi F - \tfrac12m\psi\psi$: the fermion mass and the $F$ coupling of
@exm-superpotential-mass, now produced by a single superspace expression.
:::

A cubic product brings in the Yukawa coupling. The second example applies the proposition twice and recovers the
coupling of @exm-superpotential-yukawa with its normalisation.

::: {#exm-ssg-product-cubic}
#### The cube of a chiral superfield

Multiplying $\Phi^2$ by $\Phi$ once more, the $\theta\theta$ component of $\Phi^3$ is $3\phi^2F - 3\phi\,\psi\psi$, so
$\tfrac16y\Phi^3$ contributes $\tfrac12y\phi^2F - \tfrac12y\phi\,\psi\psi$, which is $W^\phi F - \tfrac12W^{\phi\phi}\psi\psi$ for $W =
\tfrac16y\phi^3$: the Yukawa coupling of @exm-superpotential-yukawa and the $F$ term whose elimination gives the quartic
potential.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The kinetic terms come from a different component of a different product. The third example quotes the top
component of $\Phi^\dagger\Phi$ and relates it to the free Wess-Zumino Lagrangian.

::: {#exm-ssg-kahler-term}
#### The kinetic term as a top component

The $\theta\theta\,\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger$ component of $\Phi^\dagger\Phi$ is, up to a total derivative, $\partial^\mu\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi +
i\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi + F^*F$, the free Lagrangian @eq-wz-free [@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 8.127-8.128,
with $-\partial\phi^*\partial\phi$ there because of the mostly-plus metric]. The full Wess-Zumino model is the top component of
$\Phi^\dagger\Phi$ plus the $\theta\theta$ component of $W(\Phi)$ and its conjugate, which is how @eq-superpotential arises; its
invariance needs no computation, since a supersymmetry transformation changes a top component by a total derivative.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The product rule follows from the identity $\theta^\alpha\theta^\beta = -\tfrac12\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\theta\theta$ with the fermion components
anticommuting. The first exercise verifies the proposition by machine, with every Grassmann sign handled by the
exterior algebra.

::: {#exr-ssg-chiral-products}
#### The product rule in Sage

Represent $\theta^1, \theta^2$ and the components $\psi_{i\alpha}$ of two chiral superfields as generators of an exterior algebra over
a polynomial ring in $\phi_i, F_i$, and check the components of $\Phi_1\Phi_2$, the $\theta\theta$ component of $W(\Phi) = L\Phi +
\tfrac12M\Phi^2 + \tfrac16y\Phi^3$, and that of a cubic superpotential in two fields.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By hand, the only non-obvious term is $(\sqrt2\,\theta\psi_1)(\sqrt2\,\theta\psi_2) = -2\theta^\alpha\theta^\beta\psi_{1\alpha}\psi_{2\beta} =
\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\psi_{1\alpha}\psi_{2\beta}\,\theta\theta = -\psi_1\psi_2\,\theta\theta$, using $\psi^\beta = \epsilon^{\beta\alpha}\psi_\alpha$ and the
anticommutation of the components. The machine confirms this and the superpotential components:

{{< sage exr-ssg-chiral-products >}}
:::

The single-field Wess-Zumino model with all three superpotential terms is worked out in @nath2017supersymmetry
[eqs. 8.142-8.145 and 8.250-8.253]. The second exercise follows it in our normalisation and asks when its vacuum is
supersymmetric.

::: {#exr-ssg-single-field}
#### One chiral superfield with a linear term

For $W = c\Phi + \tfrac12m\Phi^2 + \tfrac13\lambda\Phi^3$ with real $c, m, \lambda$, write the scalar potential, expand it in powers of $\phi$
and $\phi^*$, and find its supersymmetric minima. Show that supersymmetry is broken when $m = \lambda = 0$, $c \neq 0$, but
that the vacuum energy is then a constant with no physical effect in the absence of gravity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$V = |W'|^2 = |c + m\phi + \lambda\phi^2|^2 = c^2 + mc(\phi + \phi^*) + m^2|\phi|^2 + c\lambda(\phi^2 + \phi^{*2}) + m\lambda|\phi|^2(\phi + \phi^*) +
\lambda^2|\phi|^4$, as in @nath2017supersymmetry [eq. 8.144]. Since $V \geq 0$ the minima with $V = 0$ are the roots $\phi =
(-m \pm \sqrt{m^2 - 4\lambda c})/2\lambda$ of $W' = 0$, which exist for every $\lambda \neq 0$ (complex roots are allowed); for $\lambda = 0$,
$m \neq 0$ the root is $\phi = -c/m$. For $m = \lambda = 0$, $W' = c$ never vanishes, $F = -c$ in every state and $V = c^2 > 0$:
supersymmetry is broken by @def-susy-breaking. The potential is then flat, every field is free and massless, and the
constant $c^2$ is invisible without gravity; the goldstino is the free fermion $\psi$ itself. A linear term breaks supersymmetry
only when nothing else in $W$ can cancel it, which is why the O'Raifeartaigh model needs three fields.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The covariant derivatives of superspace satisfy their own algebra, whose anticommutator is a translation. The third
exercise uses that algebra to show that the field strength of a real superfield, the superspace form of $F_{\mu\nu}$, is
gauge invariant.

::: {#exr-ssg-field-strength-superfield}
#### The gauge invariance of $W_\alpha$

Let $D_\alpha$ and $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}$ be the superspace derivatives, with $\{D_\alpha, D_\beta\} = \{\bar D_{\dot\alpha}, \bar D_{\dot\beta}\} = 0$
and $\{D_\alpha, \bar D_{\dot\beta}\}$ proportional to $\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$, and let $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\Lambda = 0 = D_\alpha\Lambda^\dagger$ for a chiral
$\Lambda$. Show that $W_\alpha = -\tfrac14\bar D\bar D D_\alpha V$ is unchanged by $V \to V + \Lambda + \Lambda^\dagger$, and that $\bar D_{\dot\beta}W_\alpha = 0$
[@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 8.10 and Problem 8.9].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$D_\alpha\Lambda^\dagger = 0$ removes the $\Lambda^\dagger$ term. For $\Lambda$, $\bar D\bar D D_\alpha\Lambda = \bar D^{\dot\beta}\bar D_{\dot\beta}D_\alpha\Lambda$, and
$\bar D_{\dot\beta}D_\alpha\Lambda = \{\bar D_{\dot\beta}, D_\alpha\}\Lambda - D_\alpha\bar D_{\dot\beta}\Lambda = c\,\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu\Lambda$; applying
$\bar D^{\dot\beta}$, which commutes with $\partial_\mu$, gives $c\,\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu\bar D^{\dot\beta}\Lambda = 0$. So $\delta W_\alpha = 0$
[@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 8.165-8.170]. Finally $\bar D_{\dot\beta}\bar D\bar D = 0$, because $\bar D\bar D$ already contains both
anticommuting components of $\bar D$ and any third one squares to zero; hence $W_\alpha$ is chiral. Its components are the
gaugino, $D$ and $F_{\mu\nu}$, and the $\theta\theta$ component of $\tfrac14W^\alpha W_\alpha$ plus its conjugate is the gauge Lagrangian
@eq-gauge-multiplet in the abelian case [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 8.185].
:::

### The superpotential and gauge multiplets {#sec-superpotential}

Supersymmetry restricts interactions severely: all non-gauge couplings of chiral multiplets descend from a single
holomorphic function, the superpotential, the scalar potential is a sum of squares, and the gauge couplings fix the
remaining quartic terms. This section defines the superpotential and the resulting potential, the gauge
multiplet and its $D$-term, and spontaneous supersymmetry breaking, following @martin1997 [Secs. 3.2-3.4 and
7.1-7.3]; the algebraic facts are proved and the spectra computed exactly. Dimensional reduction of
supersymmetric theories in Part V produces potentials of exactly this form.

#### The superpotential

The interactions of chiral multiplets that are compatible with supersymmetry and renormalisability are few. They are
all generated by one holomorphic function of the scalars, from whose first derivatives come the F-terms and from
whose second derivatives come the fermion masses and Yukawa couplings.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-superpotential}
#### Superpotential

The **superpotential** $W(\phi_i)$ is a holomorphic function of the complex scalars of the chiral multiplets, in a
renormalisable theory
$$
W = L^i\phi_i + \tfrac12M^{ij}\phi_i\phi_j + \tfrac16y^{ijk}\phi_i\phi_j\phi_k ,
$$ {#eq-superpotential}
with $M^{ij}$ symmetric and $y^{ijk}$ totally symmetric; the interactions it generates are $\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}} = -
\tfrac12W^{ij}\psi_i\psi_j + W^iF_i + \text{c.c.}$ with $W^i = \partial W/\partial\phi_i$ and $W^{ij} = \partial^2W/\partial\phi_i
\partial\phi_j$ [@martin1997, eqs. 3.2.6-3.2.15]. Holomorphy, the absence of $\phi^*$, is forced by supersymmetry:
a dependence on $\phi^*_k$ would produce a term $(\epsilon^\dagger\psi^{\dagger k})(\psi_i\psi_j)$ in $\delta\mathcal{L}$ that
nothing can cancel.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The quadratic superpotential is the simplest case. The first example shows that it gives the boson and the fermion
the same mass, the first instance of the mass degeneracy within a supermultiplet.

::: {#exm-superpotential-mass}
#### A mass term

$W = \tfrac12m\phi^2$ gives $-\tfrac12m\psi\psi + m\phi F + \text{c.c.}$: a Majorana-type mass for the fermion and,
after eliminating $F$, the potential $|m\phi|^2$ for the scalar, so that boson and fermion have the same mass $|m|$
(@fig-wz-potential, @exr-wz-potential).
:::

A cubic term in the superpotential produces two couplings at once. The second example shows that the Yukawa coupling
and the quartic scalar coupling are governed by the same constant.

::: {#exm-superpotential-yukawa}
#### A Yukawa coupling

$W = \tfrac16y\phi^3$ gives the Yukawa coupling $-\tfrac12y\phi\psi\psi$ and the quartic $\tfrac14|y|^2|\phi|^4$: the
same constant $y$ controls the fermion-scalar and the scalar self-coupling, the hallmark of supersymmetry
(@exr-wz-potential).
:::

The superpotential of the supersymmetric Standard Model is short. The third example displays it and notes the
consequence of holomorphy for the Higgs sector.

::: {#exm-superpotential-mssm}
#### The superpotential of the Standard Model

$W_{\text{MSSM}} = \bar u\,y_uQH_u - \bar d\,y_dQH_d - \bar e\,y_eLH_d + \mu H_uH_d$ [@martin1997, eq. 6.1.1] contains the
quark and lepton Yukawa couplings and the Higgs mass $\mu$; every term is holomorphic, which is why two Higgs
doublets are needed.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise expands the interaction Lagrangian for the cubic superpotential used throughout the section. It
is a direct application of the definition and produces all couplings of the interacting Wess-Zumino model.

::: {#exr-ssg-superpotential-terms}
#### The interacting Wess-Zumino Lagrangian

For $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2 + \tfrac16y\phi^3$ write out $\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}}$, eliminate $F$, and list every interaction term with its
coupling.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W' = m\phi + \tfrac12y\phi^2$ and $W'' = m + y\phi$, so $\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}} = (m\phi + \tfrac12y\phi^2)F - \tfrac12(m + y\phi)\psi\psi +
\text{c.c.}$ Eliminating $F = -W'^*$ gives $-|m\phi + \tfrac12y\phi^2|^2 = -|m|^2|\phi|^2 - \tfrac12(m^*y\phi^{*}\phi^2 + \text{c.c.}) -
\tfrac14|y|^2|\phi|^4$. The interactions are the fermion mass $-\tfrac12m\psi\psi$, the Yukawa coupling $-\tfrac12y\phi\psi\psi$, the
cubic scalar coupling with strength $\tfrac12m^*y$ and the quartic with $\tfrac14|y|^2$, all from two parameters
[@martin1997, eq. 3.2.18].
:::

Renormalisability limits the degree of the superpotential. The second exercise finds the bound from the dimension of
the terms it generates.

::: {#exr-ssg-superpotential-degree}
#### Why at most cubic

Show that $W$ has mass dimension $3$, and that a quartic term $\tfrac{1}{24}\lambda\phi^4$ would produce couplings of negative mass
dimension. Which terms would it generate?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W^iF_i$ must have dimension $4$ and $F$ has dimension $2$, so $W^i$ has dimension $2$ and $W$ dimension $3$. A quartic term
needs $[\lambda] = -1$; it would generate $-\tfrac14\lambda\phi^2\psi\psi$, of dimension $5$, and the sextic scalar term $|\lambda\phi^3/6|^2$,
of dimension $6$, both non-renormalisable. So a renormalisable $W$ is at most cubic, as in @eq-superpotential.
:::

With two chiral multiplets a mass term can couple them. The third exercise computes the spectrum of the resulting
model and finds a Dirac fermion degenerate with two complex scalars.

::: {#exr-ssg-dirac-superpotential}
#### A Dirac mass

For $W = m\Phi_1\Phi_2$ compute the F-terms, the potential, the fermion mass matrix $W^{ij}$ and its squared singular values, and
compare with the scalar mass matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F_1 = -m^*\phi_2^*$, $F_2 = -m^*\phi_1^*$, $V = |m|^2(|\phi_1|^2 + |\phi_2|^2)$; $W^{ij} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & m \\ m & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ with
$M^\dagger M = |m|^2\cdot1$: the term $-m\psi_1\psi_2$ is a Dirac mass for the pair, and the scalar mass matrix is the same
$|m|^2\cdot1$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-dirac-superpotential >}}
:::

Holomorphy is one reason for the second Higgs doublet of @exm-superpotential-mssm. The other is the consistency of the
quantum theory, since the superpartner of a Higgs doublet is a chiral fermion that contributes to the gauge anomalies
of @def-anomaly; the fourth exercise counts its contribution [@nath2017supersymmetry, Ch. 10].

::: {#exr-ssg-higgsino-anomaly}
#### Why higgsinos come in pairs

The fermions of one generation have no hypercharge anomaly: $\sum Y = 0$, $\sum Y^3 = 0$ and $\sum_{\text{doublets}}Y = 0$ over
left-handed Weyl fermions (@exm-anomaly-standard-model). The superpartner of the Higgs doublet $H_u$ is a left-handed
Weyl doublet $\tilde H_u$ of hypercharge $\tfrac12$. Compute the three sums after adding $\tilde H_u$, and show that a second
higgsino doublet $\tilde H_d$ of hypercharge $-\tfrac12$ restores all three.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The doublet $\tilde H_u$ adds two Weyl fermions of $Y = \tfrac12$: $\sum Y$ becomes $1$, $\sum Y^3$ becomes $2 \cdot \tfrac18 = \tfrac14$, and
the mixed $SU(2)^2U(1)$ sum over doublets becomes $\tfrac12$. All three are non-zero, so the theory with one higgsino is
inconsistent. A doublet of $Y = -\tfrac12$ contributes exactly the negatives, since every sum is odd in $Y$, and the pair
$\tilde H_u, \tilde H_d$ is anomaly-free; it is vector-like with respect to the hypercharge. Both requirements, anomaly
cancellation and the holomorphy of $W$, lead to the two doublets $H_u, H_d$ of @exm-superpotential-mssm
[@nath2017supersymmetry, Ch. 10, Table 10.1].
:::

Once the auxiliary fields are eliminated, the superpotential determines a scalar potential. The definition gives it
and names the points where it vanishes, which are the vacua that preserve supersymmetry.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-f-term-potential}
#### F-term potential

Eliminating the auxiliary fields with $F_i = -W^*_i$ (@prp-auxiliary-elimination) gives the **F-term potential**
$$
V_F(\phi, \phi^*) = \sum_iW^iW^*_i = \sum_i|F_i|^2 \geq 0,
$$ {#eq-f-term}
non-negative as a sum of squares [@martin1997, eqs. 3.2.16-3.2.18] (@prp-f-term); a **supersymmetric vacuum** is a
point where all $F_i$ vanish, so that $V_F = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The cubic superpotential has two supersymmetric vacua. The first example locates them, and the figure shows the
potential over the complex plane of the field.

::: {#exm-f-term-cubic}
#### The cubic superpotential

For $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2 + \tfrac16y\phi^3$, $V_F = |m\phi + \tfrac12y\phi^2|^2$ vanishes exactly at $\phi = 0$ and $\phi = -
2m/y$ (@fig-wz-potential): two supersymmetric vacua (@prp-f-term).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Supersymmetry.wz_vacua` (see @prp-f-term).

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Expanding around a supersymmetric vacuum gives the masses. The second example shows that the scalars and the
fermions see the same mass matrix, as a supermultiplet requires.

::: {#exm-f-term-masses}
#### Mass degeneracy

Linearising the equations of motion, the scalars satisfy $\partial^2\phi_i = -M^*_{ik}M^{kj}\phi_j$ and the fermions
$\partial^2\psi_i = -M^*_{ik}M^{kj}\psi_j$ with $\partial^2 = \Box = \partial_t^2 - \nabla^2$ [@martin1997, eqs. 3.2.20-3.2.22,
with the opposite sign in his metric]: the same squared-mass matrix, so each
chiral multiplet contains a mass-degenerate complex scalar and Weyl fermion, as @def-supermultiplet demands.
:::

A sum of squares can vanish on more than a point. The third example introduces flat directions, which are a recurring
feature of supersymmetric potentials.

::: {#exm-f-term-flat}
#### Flat directions

$V_F$ can vanish along whole lines or surfaces in field space, **flat directions** or **moduli**, as $\phi_1$ in the
O'Raifeartaigh model (@fig-oraifeartaigh) or the many flat directions of the supersymmetric Standard Model
[@martin1997, p. 76]; the moduli of a compactification in Part VI are flat directions of this kind.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is a variant of the cubic model with symmetric vacua. It is the model of the first integrative
exercise, and here only its vacua are needed.

::: {#exr-ssg-fterm-vacua}
#### Vacua of a symmetric model

For $W = \lambda(\tfrac13\Phi^3 - \mu^2\Phi)$ with $\lambda, \mu > 0$, find $V_F$, its zeros, and its value at $\phi = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W' = \lambda(\phi^2 - \mu^2)$, so $V_F = \lambda^2|\phi^2 - \mu^2|^2$, which vanishes at $\phi = \pm\mu$, two supersymmetric vacua related by
$\phi \to -\phi$. At $\phi = 0$, $V_F = \lambda^2\mu^4 > 0$: a saddle point of the potential between the two vacua (a maximum
along the real axis, a minimum along the imaginary one, where $V_F = \lambda^2(t^2 + \mu^2)^2$ for $\phi = it$).
:::

The second vacuum of the cubic model also has degenerate masses, which the general argument of the second example
predicts. The second exercise checks this directly and computes the height of the barrier between the vacua.

::: {#exr-ssg-wz-second-vacuum}
#### The second vacuum

For $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2 + \tfrac16y\phi^3$ with real $m, y > 0$, compute $W''$ at both vacua and the value of $V_F$ at $\phi = -m/y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W''(0) = m$ and $W''(-2m/y) = m - 2m = -m$: the same mass $|m|$ in both vacua, for the fermion directly and for the scalar
because the scalar mass matrix is $|W''|^2$ at a supersymmetric vacuum. At the midpoint $\phi = -m/y$, $W' = -m^2/y + m^2/(2y) = -
m^2/(2y)$ and $V_F = m^4/(4y^2)$, the height of the barrier along the real axis (@fig-wz-potential).
:::

Several fields allow a continuous family of supersymmetric vacua. The third exercise finds one, and identifies the
massless multiplet that moves along it.

::: {#exr-ssg-fterm-moduli}
#### A moduli space

For $W = \Phi_0(\Phi_1\Phi_2 - \mu^2)$ find all supersymmetric vacua, the fermion mass matrix at $(0, \mu, \mu)$, and the massless
direction.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W^0 = \phi_1\phi_2 - \mu^2$, $W^1 = \phi_0\phi_2$, $W^2 = \phi_0\phi_1$ vanish together exactly for $\phi_0 = 0$, $\phi_1\phi_2 = \mu^2$, a complex
curve of vacua. At $(0, \mu, \mu)$ the mass matrix has rank $2$, with squared masses $2\mu^2, 2\mu^2, 0$; the null vector
$(0, 1, -1)$ is tangent to the curve, so the massless multiplet is the modulus, the flat direction of
@exm-f-term-flat:

{{< sage exr-ssg-fterm-moduli >}}
:::
::::

The positivity of the F-term potential and the two vacua of the cubic model are stated as a proposition. Together
they say that supersymmetric vacua are global minima, and that the cubic model has exactly two of them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-f-term}
#### The F-term potential and its vacua

$\sum_i|W_i|^2 \geq 0$; for $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2 + \tfrac16y\phi^3$ with $y \neq 0$, $|m\phi + \tfrac12y\phi^2|^2 = 0$ if and only
if $\phi = 0$ or $\phi = -2m/y$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Positivity has an immediate consequence. The first example states it: a zero of the potential is automatically a
global minimum, so supersymmetric vacua are stable.

::: {#exm-ssg-fterm-global}
#### Zeros are global minima

Since $V_F \geq 0$, any point with $V_F = 0$ is a global minimum; no fine tuning or stability analysis is needed for
the two vacua of the cubic model. The converse fails: a minimum with $V_F > 0$ is possible, and it breaks
supersymmetry (@def-susy-breaking).
:::

The two vacua of the cubic model are related by a field redefinition. The second example finds it, and explains why
the masses agree.

::: {#exm-ssg-fterm-symmetry}
#### Two equivalent vacua

The shift $\phi = -2m/y + \chi$ gives $dW/d\chi = -m\chi + \tfrac12y\chi^2$: the theory around $\phi = -2m/y$ is the original
model around $\chi = 0$ with $m \to -m$, and since only $|m|$ enters the masses (the sign of $m$ can be absorbed in a
phase of $\psi$), the two vacua are physically equivalent (@exr-ssg-wz-second-vacuum).
:::

Between two supersymmetric vacua there can be a field configuration that interpolates. The third example states the
energy bound for such domain walls, which is fixed by the superpotential alone.

::: {#exm-ssg-fterm-bps}
#### Domain walls

For a static field depending on one coordinate, the energy per area is $\int(|\phi'|^2 + |W'|^2)\,dx \geq 2|W(\phi_+) - W(\phi_-)|$,
with equality for $\phi' = e^{i\alpha}\overline{W'(\phi)}$: the **BPS** walls, whose tension is fixed by the superpotential at the
two vacua (@exr-ssg-wz-domain-wall).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is the computation behind the proposition, including the solution of the auxiliary equations
and the zeros of the potential. It is short, and it fixes the sign conventions.

::: {#exr-wz-potential}
#### Eliminating $F$

For $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2 + \tfrac16y\phi^3$, solve the auxiliary equations, find $V$, its zeros and the masses at
$\phi = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-wz-potential >}}
:::

Positivity of a sum of squares is elementary, but the step from $F$ to $W$ uses the complex conjugate. The second
exercise asks for the proof with care about which quantities are complex.

::: {#exr-ssg-fterm-nonneg}
#### Positivity in components

Write $W^i = a_i + ib_i$ and show $V_F = \sum_i(a_i^2 + b_i^2)$. Conclude that $V_F = 0$ if and only if every $W^i = 0$, and that
this does not require $W$ itself to vanish.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W^iW^*_i = (a_i + ib_i)(a_i - ib_i) = a_i^2 + b_i^2 \geq 0$ for each $i$, so the sum is non-negative and vanishes only if all
$a_i = b_i = 0$. $W$ enters only through its derivatives: adding a constant to $W$ changes nothing in the potential
(though it matters in supergravity), and the vacua of @exr-ssg-fterm-vacua have $W(\pm\mu) = \mp\tfrac23\lambda\mu^3 \neq 0$.
:::

The bound of the third example can be saturated explicitly for the cubic model. The third exercise finds the wall
between the two vacua and computes its energy.

::: {#exr-ssg-wz-domain-wall}
#### The BPS wall

For real $W = \tfrac12\phi^2 + \tfrac16\phi^3$ and real static $\phi(x)$, show that $E = \int(\phi'^2 + W'^2)dx \geq 2|W(\phi(\infty)) -
W(\phi(-\infty))|$, check that $\phi(x) = -2/(1 + e^{-x})$ solves $\phi' = W'(\phi)$, and compute its energy.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\phi'^2 + W'^2 = (\phi' - W')^2 + 2\phi'W'$ and $\int2\phi'W'(\phi)\,dx = 2[W]_{-\infty}^{\infty}$, so $E \geq 2|\Delta W|$ (choosing the sign of
the first-order equation according to the sign of $\Delta W$), with equality when $\phi' = \pm W'$. The kink runs from $0$ to
$-2$ and has $E = 4/3 = 2|W(-2) - W(0)|$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-wz-domain-wall >}}
:::
::::

![The O'Raifeartaigh model $W = -k\Phi_1 + m\Phi_2\Phi_3 + \tfrac12y\Phi_1\Phi_3^2$. Left: $V$ along the real
$\phi_3$ direction at $\phi_1 = \phi_2 = 0$, with its minimum $V = k^2 > 0$ at the origin when $m^2 > yk$ and a
saddle there when $m^2 < yk$; in both cases $V$ never reaches zero. Right: $V$ is flat along $\phi_1$ at tree
level. Generated by `figures/oraifeartaigh.sage`.](figures/oraifeartaigh.svg){#fig-oraifeartaigh width=90%}

{{< interactive oraifeartaigh 460 >}}

#### Gauge multiplets

Gauge fields enter supersymmetric theories through multiplets of their own, with a fermionic partner in the adjoint
representation and a real auxiliary field. The definition gives the Lagrangian and the transformations, with the one
sign that changes between Martin's metric and ours.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gauge-multiplet}
#### Gauge multiplet

A **gauge multiplet** consists of a gauge field $A^a_\mu$, a Weyl spinor $\lambda^a$ (the **gaugino**) and a real
auxiliary field $D^a$, all in the adjoint representation, with the Lagrangian
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{gauge}} = -\tfrac14F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu a} + i\lambda^{\dagger a}\bar\sigma^\mu\nabla_\mu\lambda^a + \tfrac12D^aD^a
$$ {#eq-gauge-multiplet}
and the transformations $\delta A^a_\mu = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma_\mu\lambda^a + \lambda^{\dagger a}
\bar\sigma_\mu\epsilon)$, $\delta\lambda^a_\alpha = \tfrac{i}{2\sqrt2}(\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu\epsilon)_\alpha F^a_{\mu\nu} +
\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\epsilon_\alpha D^a$, $\delta D^a = \tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}(-\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\nabla_\mu\lambda^a +
\nabla_\mu\lambda^{\dagger a}\bar\sigma^\mu\epsilon)$ [@martin1997, eqs. 3.3.3-3.3.8; his $\delta A^a_\mu$ carries the opposite
sign, since $\bar\sigma_\mu = \eta_{\mu\nu}\bar\sigma^\nu$ changes sign with the metric]; $A_\mu$ has $3$ off-shell
components, $\lambda$ has $4$, and $D$ supplies the fourth bosonic one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The abelian case is simpler and admits one extra term. The first example notes it, since it is the origin of one of
the two mechanisms of supersymmetry breaking.

::: {#exm-gauge-multiplet-abelian}
#### The abelian gauge multiplet

For $U(1)$ the structure constants vanish, the gaugino is neutral, and $\delta D$ is a total derivative, so a term
linear in $D$ is allowed: the Fayet-Iliopoulos term of @exm-breaking-fi.
:::

Charged chiral multiplets couple to the gauge multiplet through more than the covariant derivative. The second
example lists the extra terms, whose strength is fixed by the gauge coupling.

::: {#exm-gauge-multiplet-coupling}
#### Coupling to chiral multiplets

Supersymmetry requires, beyond the covariant derivatives, the terms $-\sqrt2g(\phi^*T^a\psi)\lambda^a + \text{c.c.} +
g(\phi^*T^a\phi)D^a$ [@martin1997, eq. 3.4.9], with the gauge coupling fixing their strength: the gaugino couples
to matter as the gauge boson does, and the superpotential must be gauge invariant, $W^i(T^a\phi)_i = 0$.
:::

Gauge multiplets in four dimensions also arise from higher-dimensional ones. The third example describes the
reduction of a ten-dimensional gauge multiplet, which produces chiral multiplets from internal components.

::: {#exm-gauge-multiplet-reduction}
#### Gauge multiplets from reduction

A ten-dimensional gauge multiplet $(A_M, \lambda)$ with a Majorana-Weyl gaugino reduces on a six-dimensional
internal space to four-dimensional gauge multiplets plus chiral multiplets whose scalars are the internal
components $A_m$: the supersymmetric version of the CSDR Higgs sector of Part V.
:::

In the supersymmetric Standard Model the gauginos mix with the higgsinos once the Higgs fields acquire expectation
values, through the coupling of the gaugino to a scalar and a fermion of the same chiral multiplet. The fourth example
writes the resulting mass matrix of the neutral fermions.

::: {#exm-ssg-neutralino}
#### The neutralino mass matrix

The neutral gauginos $\tilde B$, $\tilde W^3$ and higgsinos $\tilde H_d^0$, $\tilde H_u^0$ have the symmetric mass matrix
$$
M_N = \begin{pmatrix} M_1 & 0 & -c_\beta s_W m_Z & s_\beta s_W m_Z \\ 0 & M_2 & c_\beta c_W m_Z & -s_\beta c_W m_Z \\
-c_\beta s_W m_Z & c_\beta c_W m_Z & 0 & -\mu \\ s_\beta s_W m_Z & -s_\beta c_W m_Z & -\mu & 0 \end{pmatrix},
$$
with $c_\beta = \cos\beta$, $s_\beta = \sin\beta$, $\tan\beta = v_u/v_d$, $s_W = \sin\theta_W$ and $c_W = \cos\theta_W$
[@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 10.51-10.53]. The off-diagonal entries come from the gaugino couplings of the gauge
multiplet evaluated on the Higgs vacuum, the $\mu$ entries from the superpotential of @exm-superpotential-mssm and
$M_1, M_2$ from soft gaugino masses; its four eigenvectors are the **neutralinos**, Majorana fermions
(@def-majorana-spinor).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
