**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The counting of components behind the auxiliary field $D$ is the subject of the first exercise. It also asks for the
on-shell count, which matches the massless gauge multiplet of the first part of this section.

::: {#exr-ssg-gauge-dof}
#### Counting the gauge multiplet

Count the real components of $A_\mu$ (modulo gauge transformations), $\lambda$ and $D$ off-shell, and the physical states
on-shell.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Off-shell: $A_\mu$ has $4 - 1 = 3$, $\lambda$ has $4$, $D$ has $1$: $4 + 4$. On-shell: the massless vector has $2$ helicities,
the Weyl gaugino $2$, $D = 0$: $2 + 2$, the helicities $(\pm\tfrac12, \pm1)$ of @exr-ssg-massless-n1 [@martin1997, Table 3.2].
:::

The sign of $\delta A_\mu$ is the one place in the gauge multiplet where the signature enters. The second exercise
traces it, and checks that the field strength and the rest of the multiplet are unaffected.

::: {#exr-ssg-gauge-sign}
#### The sign of $\delta A_\mu$

Martin writes $\delta A_\mu = -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma_\mu\lambda + \lambda^\dagger\bar\sigma_\mu\epsilon)$ with $\bar\sigma_\mu = \eta^{\text{M}}_{\mu\nu}\bar\sigma^\nu$
in the metric $\eta^{\text{M}} = -\eta$. Show that this is the same transformation of the same field $A_\mu$ as the one in the
definition, and that $\delta\lambda$ and $\delta D$ need no change.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The matrices $\bar\sigma^\nu$ with upper index are the same in both conventions, so $\bar\sigma^{\text{M}}_\mu = \eta^{\text{M}}_{\mu\nu}\bar\sigma^\nu = -
\eta_{\mu\nu}\bar\sigma^\nu = -\bar\sigma_\mu$, and Martin's formula equals $+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\epsilon^\dagger\bar\sigma_\mu\lambda + \dots)$ in our notation,
with the components $A_\mu$ (lower index, $A = A_\mu dx^\mu$) identical. Then $F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$ is identical,
$\delta\lambda$ contracts upper-index matrices with the lower-index $F_{\mu\nu}$ and needs no metric, and $\delta D$ contracts
$\bar\sigma^\mu$ with $\nabla_\mu$; neither changes. The Lagrangian terms $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ (two metrics) and $\tfrac12D^2$ are
unchanged too.
:::

The gaugino variation contains $\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu F_{\mu\nu}$, which sees only half of the field strength. The third
exercise shows why: the six matrices $\sigma^{\mu\nu}$ span only three dimensions, those of one duality component.

::: {#exr-ssg-self-dual-sigma}
#### Self-duality of $\sigma^{\mu\nu}$

With $\sigma^{\mu\nu} = \tfrac14(\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu - \sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu)$ and $\bar\sigma^{\mu\nu} = \tfrac14(\bar\sigma^\mu\sigma^\nu - \bar\sigma^\nu\sigma^\mu)$,
compute $\tfrac12\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\sigma_{\rho\sigma}$ with $\epsilon_{0123} = 1$ in our metric, and the dimension of the span of the
$\sigma^{\mu\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac12\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\sigma_{\rho\sigma} = -i\sigma^{\mu\nu}$ and $\tfrac12\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\bar\sigma_{\rho\sigma} = +i\bar\sigma^{\mu\nu}$: each set is an
eigenspace of the Hodge dual, and the six $\sigma^{\mu\nu}$ span the three traceless $2 \times 2$ matrices. Hence $\sigma^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}$
depends only on the component $F - i{\star}F$ (up to normalisation): the left-handed gaugino is paired with one
duality component of the field strength, the right-handed one with the other.

{{< sage exr-ssg-self-dual-sigma >}}
:::

The charged gauginos and higgsinos mix in the same way, but their mass matrix is not symmetric, so its eigenvalues are
replaced by singular values. The fourth exercise computes them in closed form and for a numerical case.

::: {#exr-ssg-chargino-masses}
#### Chargino masses

The charged gaugino-higgsino mass matrix is $M_C = \begin{pmatrix} M_2 & \sqrt2\,m_W\sin\beta \\ \sqrt2\,m_W\cos\beta & \mu
\end{pmatrix}$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 10.43]. Show that the squared chargino masses, the eigenvalues of
$M_CM_C^T$, are $m^2_\pm = \tfrac12\bigl[(M_2^2 + \mu^2 + 2m_W^2) \pm \sqrt{(M_2^2 + \mu^2 + 2m_W^2)^2 - 4(M_2\mu -
m_W^2\sin2\beta)^2}\,\bigr]$, and evaluate them with Sage for $M_2 = 200$ GeV, $\mu = 300$ GeV, $\tan\beta = 10$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A real matrix is diagonalised by two orthogonal matrices, $U M_C V^T = \operatorname{diag}(m_1, m_2)$, and the $m_i^2$ are the
eigenvalues of $M_CM_C^T$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 10.44]. Its trace is $M_2^2 + \mu^2 + 2m_W^2(\sin^2\beta + \cos^2\beta) = M_2^2 +
\mu^2 + 2m_W^2$ and its determinant $(\det M_C)^2 = (M_2\mu - 2m_W^2\sin\beta\cos\beta)^2 = (M_2\mu - m_W^2\sin2\beta)^2$, so the
quadratic formula gives the stated roots [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 10.49]. Numerically the masses are $175.3$ GeV
and $335.0$ GeV: close to $M_2$ and $\mu$, pushed apart by the mixing.

{{< sage exr-ssg-chargino-masses >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

When the auxiliary fields $D^a$ are eliminated, the gauge couplings produce a second positive contribution to the
scalar potential. The definition gives it, and with it the complete potential of a renormalisable supersymmetric
theory.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-d-term-potential}
#### D-term potential

Eliminating $D^a = -g(\phi^*T^a\phi)$ gives the **D-term potential**, and the complete scalar potential of a
renormalisable supersymmetric theory is
$$
V = \sum_i|W^i|^2 + \tfrac12\sum_ag_a^2(\phi^*T^a\phi)^2 ,
$$ {#eq-susy-potential}
F-terms fixed by the superpotential and D-terms by the gauge couplings, with no free quartic couplings
[@martin1997, eqs. 3.4.11-3.4.12].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example evaluates the D-term potential for a doublet of $SU(2)$. The result is a quartic potential whose
coupling is the gauge coupling.

::: {#exm-d-term-doublet}
#### The $SU(2)$ doublet

For a doublet with $T^a = \tfrac12\sigma^a$, $\tfrac12g^2\sum_a(\phi^\dagger\tfrac12\sigma^a\phi)^2 = \tfrac18g^2(\phi^\dagger\phi)^2$
(@exr-d-term-doublet): a quartic potential with coupling fixed by $g$, which is why the Higgs quartic coupling
of the supersymmetric Standard Model is predicted.
:::

For an abelian group the D-term is a single square. The second example shows that it vanishes along directions that
need fields of both signs of charge.

::: {#exm-d-term-u1}
#### A $U(1)$ with charges $q_i$

$V_D = \tfrac12g^2(\sum_iq_i|\phi_i|^2)^2$, vanishing on the **D-flat** directions $\sum q_i|\phi_i|^2 = 0$, which require
fields of opposite charges.
:::

For fields in the adjoint representation the D-term is a commutator. The third example identifies it with the quartic
potential of the reduced Yang-Mills theory.

::: {#exm-d-term-csdr}
#### D-terms as commutators

For adjoint scalars, $(\phi^*T^a\phi)$ is $\operatorname{Tr}(T^a[\phi, \phi^\dagger])$ and $V_D \propto \operatorname{Tr}[\phi,
\phi^\dagger]^2$: the quartic commutator potential that the reduction of a Yang-Mills field produces (@exm-ym-reduction),
now recognised as a D-term.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves the doublet formula with the Fierz identity of the Pauli matrices. The computation is a
standard one and gives the Higgs quartic of the supersymmetric Standard Model.

::: {#exr-d-term-doublet}
#### The D-term of a doublet

Show that for an $SU(2)$ doublet $\tfrac12g^2\sum_a(\phi^\dagger T^a\phi)^2 = \tfrac18g^2(\phi^\dagger\phi)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $T^a = \tfrac12\sigma^a$ and the Fierz identity $\sum_a\sigma^a_{ij}\sigma^a_{kl} = 2\delta_{il}\delta_{jk} - \delta_{ij}
\delta_{kl}$ (@exm-gamma-euclidean), $\sum_a(\phi^\dagger\sigma^a\phi)^2 = 2(\phi^\dagger\phi)^2 - (\phi^\dagger\phi)^2 = (\phi^\dagger
\phi)^2$, so $V_D = \tfrac12g^2\cdot\tfrac14(\phi^\dagger\phi)^2 = \tfrac18g^2(\phi^\dagger\phi)^2$. With two doublets $H_u, H_d$
this gives the quartic terms of the supersymmetric Higgs potential [@martin1997, eq. 8.1.1], whose coupling is a
gauge coupling rather than a free parameter.
:::

D-flat directions are where gauge symmetry can be broken without cost in energy. The second exercise finds them for
the simplest abelian model and shows that they are not removed by gauge transformations.

::: {#exr-ssg-dterm-flat}
#### D-flat directions of $U(1)$

For two chiral fields of charges $+1$ and $-1$, find the D-flat directions, and show that modulo $U(1)$ gauge
transformations they form a one-complex-parameter family, labelled by the gauge-invariant $\phi_+\phi_-$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$V_D = \tfrac12g^2(|\phi_+|^2 - |\phi_-|^2)^2$ vanishes for $|\phi_+| = |\phi_-|$. Writing $\phi_\pm = re^{i\alpha_\pm}$, the gauge
transformation shifts $\alpha_+ \to \alpha_+ + \theta$, $\alpha_- \to \alpha_- - \theta$, so $\alpha_+ + \alpha_-$ and $r$ are invariant: the
flat directions modulo gauge are labelled by $\phi_+\phi_- = r^2e^{i(\alpha_+ + \alpha_-)}$, one complex number. This is the general
rule that D-flat directions modulo gauge are parametrised by holomorphic gauge invariants.
:::

The third exercise checks the doublet formula on explicit components and the commutator form for an adjoint. It
also finds a family of D-flat directions of the adjoint.

::: {#exr-ssg-dterm-doublet}
#### D-terms in components

With $\phi = (a_1 + ib_1, a_2 + ib_2)$ verify that each $D^a$ is real and $V_D = \tfrac18g^2(\phi^\dagger\phi)^2$, and check the Fierz
identity. For an $SU(2)$ adjoint, relate $\phi^*T^a_{\text{adj}}\phi$ to $\operatorname{tr}(T^a[\phi, \phi^\dagger])$ and show that real directions are
D-flat.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
All four statements hold; the adjoint D-term is, up to a sign fixed by the convention for $T^a_{\text{adj}}$,
$2\operatorname{tr}(T^a[\phi, \phi^\dagger])$, and for a real field $\phi = \phi^\dagger$ the commutator vanishes:

{{< sage exr-ssg-dterm-doublet >}}
:::
::::

#### Spontaneous supersymmetry breaking

No superpartner of a known particle has the same mass, so supersymmetry, if it is a symmetry of nature, must be
broken. The positivity of the energy gives a sharp criterion for spontaneous breaking, and the broken generator
being fermionic, the Goldstone particle is a fermion.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-susy-breaking}
#### Spontaneous supersymmetry breaking

Supersymmetry is **spontaneously broken** if the vacuum is not annihilated by the supercharges, $Q_\alpha|0\rangle \neq
0$; by @exm-superalgebra-energy this holds exactly when the vacuum energy is positive, $\langle V\rangle > 0$, that is
when some $F_i$ or $D^a$ has a non-zero expectation value [@martin1997, Sec. 7.1]. The broken generator is
fermionic, so the Goldstone mode is a massless Weyl fermion, the **goldstino**, with components proportional to
$(\langle D^a\rangle/\sqrt2, \langle F_i\rangle)$ [@martin1997, eq. 7.1.4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The O'Raifeartaigh model is the simplest example of F-term breaking. The first example states its vacuum and its
spectrum, in which the degeneracy of bosons and fermions is lifted.

::: {#exm-breaking-oraifeartaigh}
#### The O'Raifeartaigh model

$W = -k\Phi_1 + m\Phi_2\Phi_3 + \tfrac12y\Phi_1\Phi_3^2$: $F_2 = 0$ forces $\phi_3 = 0$, and then $F_1 = k \neq 0$, so no
supersymmetric vacuum exists and $V \geq k^2 > 0$ (@prp-oraifeartaigh, @fig-oraifeartaigh). At the minimum the
scalar masses squared are $0, 0, m^2, m^2, m^2 \mp yk$ and the fermion masses squared $0, m^2, m^2$: the
degeneracy is lifted, and the massless fermion $\psi_1$ is the goldstino [@martin1997, eqs. 7.3.9-7.3.10]
(@exr-oraifeartaigh).
:::

A D-term can break supersymmetry as well. The second example is the Fayet-Iliopoulos mechanism, in which the gaugino
is the goldstino.

::: {#exm-breaking-fi}
#### Fayet-Iliopoulos breaking

A term $-\kappa D$ for a $U(1)$ modifies the $D$ equation to $D = \kappa - g\sum q_i|\phi_i|^2$, and with massive charged
fields the potential $\sum|m_i|^2|\phi_i|^2 + \tfrac12(\kappa - g\sum q_i|\phi_i|^2)^2$ cannot vanish: the scalars get
masses $|m_i|^2 - gq_i\kappa$, split from their fermions, and the gaugino is the goldstino [@martin1997, Sec. 7.2].
:::

The splittings of tree-level breaking obey a sum rule. The third example states it and explains why it makes
realistic breaking difficult.

::: {#exm-breaking-sum-rule}
#### The supertrace sum rule

At tree level $\operatorname{STr}m^2 = \sum(-1)^{2j}(2j + 1)\operatorname{Tr}m_j^2 = 0$ for theories without $U(1)$
D-terms [@martin1997, eq. 7.1.13]: the splittings go both ways, $m^2 \pm yk$ in the O'Raifeartaigh model, which is
why realistic breaking needs a hidden sector or supergravity (@def-super-higgs).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the masslessness of the goldstino for F-term breaking from the stationarity of the
potential. The argument is two lines and holds at every stationary point.

::: {#exr-ssg-goldstino-proof}
#### Why the goldstino is massless

For $V = \sum_iW^iW^*_i$, show that $\partial V/\partial\phi_j = 0$ implies $W^{ji}F_i = 0$ with $F_i = -W^*_i$. Conclude that the fermion
$\sum_iF_i\psi_i$ is massless at every stationary point, and that it is non-zero exactly when supersymmetry is broken.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W^*_i$ depends only on $\phi^*$, so $\partial V/\partial\phi_j = \sum_iW^{ij}W^*_i = -\sum_iW^{ji}F_i$, using the symmetry of $W^{ij}$. At a stationary
point this vanishes, so the vector $F$ is a null vector of the fermion mass matrix: the combination $\tilde G = F_i\psi_i$
has no mass term in $-\tfrac12W^{ij}\psi_i\psi_j$ (the mass matrix acts on the coefficient vector $F$). It is non-zero exactly
when some $F_i \neq 0$, that is when supersymmetry is broken [@martin1997, eqs. 7.1.4-7.1.8].
:::

The second exercise works out the Fayet-Iliopoulos model with two charged fields and a mass term. It finds the
vacuum energy, the split spectrum and the supertrace, and what happens when the mass is small.

::: {#exr-ssg-fi-spectrum}
#### A Fayet-Iliopoulos model

For a $U(1)$ with FI term $-\kappa D$ ($g, \kappa > 0$) and fields $\Phi_\pm$ of charges $\pm1$ with $W = m\Phi_+\Phi_-$, find $V$, the
vacuum for $m^2 > g\kappa$, the scalar masses, the supertrace, and the vacuum for $m^2 < g\kappa$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$V = m^2(|\phi_+|^2 + |\phi_-|^2) + \tfrac12(\kappa - g(|\phi_+|^2 - |\phi_-|^2))^2$. For $m^2 > g\kappa$ the minimum is the origin with $V =
\tfrac12\kappa^2 > 0$; the scalars have masses squared $m^2 - g\kappa$ and $m^2 + g\kappa$, the fermions form a Dirac pair of mass $m$,
the gaugino is the massless goldstino, and the supertrace $2(m^2 - g\kappa) + 2(m^2 + g\kappa) - 2\cdot2m^2 = 0$. For $m^2 < g\kappa$
the field $\phi_+$ condenses, $|\phi_+|^2 = (\kappa - m^2/g)/g$, with $V = m^2(2g\kappa - m^2)/(2g^2) > 0$: supersymmetry stays broken,
and the gauge symmetry is broken too.

{{< sage exr-ssg-fi-spectrum >}}
:::

The third exercise checks the goldstino theorem on the O'Raifeartaigh model at both kinds of minima. At the shifted
minimum the goldstino is a mixture of two fermions.

::: {#exr-ssg-goldstino}
#### The goldstino of the O'Raifeartaigh model

Compute $W^{ij}F_j$ at the origin and, for $m^2 < yk$, at the shifted minimum $\phi_3^2 = 2(yk - m^2)/y^2$, $\phi_2 = -y\phi_1\phi_3/m$.
Which fermion is the goldstino in each case?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At the origin $F = (k, 0, 0)$ and $W^{ij}F_j = 0$: the goldstino is $\psi_1$. At the shifted minimum $F = (m^2/y, -m\phi_3, 0)$ and again
$W^{ij}F_j = 0$: the goldstino is the combination $(m^2/y)\psi_1 - m\phi_3\psi_2$, for every value of the flat direction $\phi_1$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-goldstino >}}
:::

The phenomenological alternative to spontaneous breaking in the visible sector is to add soft terms that break
supersymmetry explicitly. A compact way to generate them is a spurion, a superfield whose components are constants;
the fourth exercise derives the soft terms it produces [@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 8.18].

::: {#exr-ssg-spurion-soft}
#### Soft terms from a spurion

Multiplying the kinetic and superpotential terms of one chiral superfield by the spurion $S = 1 + \xi_1\theta\theta +
\xi_1^*\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger + \xi_2\theta\theta\,\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger$ adds to the Lagrangian the terms $\xi_1\phi F^* + \xi_1^*\phi^*F + \xi_2|\phi|^2 +
(\xi_1W(\phi) + \text{c.c.})$. Eliminate $F$ and show with Sage that
$V = |W'|^2 + (|\xi_1|^2 - \xi_2)|\phi|^2 + [\xi_1(\phi W' - W) + \text{c.c.}]$. For $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2 + \tfrac16y\phi^3$, read off the soft
mass, the bilinear term $B_0$ and the trilinear term $A_0$, and show that $A_0 = 2B_0$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 8.307
and Problem 8.14].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $F$-dependent terms are $|F|^2 + F(W' + \xi_1^*\phi^*) + \text{c.c.}$, so $F^* = -(W' + \xi_1^*\phi^*)$ and they contribute $-|W' +
\xi_1^*\phi^*|^2 = -|W'|^2 - |\xi_1|^2|\phi|^2 - (\xi_1\phi W' + \text{c.c.})$. Adding $\xi_2|\phi|^2 + \xi_1W + \text{c.c.}$ and changing sign gives
$V$. The soft scalar mass is $m_0^2 = |\xi_1|^2 - \xi_2$, and $\phi W' - W = \tfrac12m\phi^2 + 2 \cdot \tfrac16y\phi^3$: the spurion multiplies each
term of degree $n$ of the superpotential by $(n - 1)\xi_1$, giving $B_0 = \xi_1$ for the mass term and $A_0 = 2\xi_1$ for the
cubic one. These are explicit, universal breaking terms; they keep the cancellation of quadratic divergences, which is
why they are called soft.

{{< sage exr-ssg-spurion-soft >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The absence of a supersymmetric vacuum in the O'Raifeartaigh model is a statement about polynomial equations. It is
stated as a proposition; the spectrum and the sum rule follow in the examples and exercises.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-oraifeartaigh}
#### No supersymmetric vacuum in the O'Raifeartaigh model

For $k \neq 0$ and $m \neq 0$ the equations $k - \tfrac12y\phi_3^2 = 0$, $m\phi_3 = 0$, $m\phi_2 + y\phi_1\phi_3 = 0$ have no
common solution.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Supersymmetry.oraifeartaigh_no_susy_vacuum`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Supersymmetry.oraifeartaigh_no_susy_vacuum >}}

**Sage.** The spectrum $0, 0, m^2, m^2, m^2 \mp yk$ versus $0, m^2, m^2$ and the sum rule are computed in
`figures/oraifeartaigh.sage` and @exr-oraifeartaigh.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example reads off the vacuum energy and the flat direction. The interactive figure shows the potential over
the complex plane of $\phi_3$, with its strictly positive minimum.

::: {#exm-ssg-oraifeartaigh-flat}
#### Vacuum energy and the flat direction

For $m^2 > yk$ the minimum is $\phi_2 = \phi_3 = 0$ with any $\phi_1$, and $V = k^2$ along the whole line: $\phi_1$ is a tree-level flat
direction (a pseudo-modulus), and the vacuum energy $k^2 = |F_1|^2$ sets the scale of breaking, $\sqrt k$ in mass units
(@fig-oraifeartaigh).
:::

When $m^2 < yk$ the origin becomes a saddle and the minimum moves, but the potential stays positive. The second
example states the new minimum, which the figure also shows.

::: {#exm-ssg-oraifeartaigh-shifted}
#### The shifted minimum

For $m^2 < yk$, $V$ restricted to real $\phi_3$ at $F_3 = 0$ is $(k - \tfrac12y\phi_3^2)^2 + m^2\phi_3^2$, minimised at $\phi_3^2 = 2(yk -
m^2)/y^2$ with $V_{\min} = m^2(2yk - m^2)/y^2 = k^2 - (yk - m^2)^2/y^2$: positive and below $k^2$
(@exr-ssg-oraifeartaigh-shifted).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/oraifeartaigh.sage`).
:::

The tree-level spectrum varies along the flat direction. The third example describes how, and what lifts the
degeneracy at one loop.

::: {#exm-ssg-oraifeartaigh-pseudomodulus}
#### Along the flat direction

For $\phi_1 \neq 0$ the fermion mass matrix of $(\psi_2, \psi_3)$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & m \\ m & y\phi_1 \end{pmatrix}$, so the fermion masses
depend on $\phi_1$ while $V$ does not; the one-loop (Coleman-Weinberg) potential, a supertrace of $m^4\log m^2$, then
depends on $\phi_1$ and fixes it, at $\phi_1 = 0$ for this model [@martin1997, Sec. 7.3].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is the computation behind the proposition. It derives the F-terms, the spectrum at the origin
and the supertrace.

::: {#exr-oraifeartaigh}
#### The O'Raifeartaigh spectrum

Compute the F-terms, show they cannot vanish together, and find the tree-level scalar and fermion masses at the
origin and their supertrace.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-oraifeartaigh >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Supersymmetry.oraifeartaigh_no_susy_vacuum >}}

**Sage.** Pending.

The second exercise derives the shifted minimum of the second example by hand. It is single-variable calculus once
the other F-terms are set to zero.

::: {#exr-ssg-oraifeartaigh-shifted}
#### Minimising for $m^2 < yk$

Show that $V \geq |k - \tfrac12y\phi_3^2|^2 + m^2|\phi_3|^2$ with equality when $F_3 = 0$, minimise the right side over real $\phi_3$, and
show that the minimum is positive and smaller than $k^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$V = |F_1|^2 + |F_2|^2 + |F_3|^2$ with $|F_3|^2 \geq 0$, and $F_3 = m\phi_2 + y\phi_1\phi_3$ can be set to zero by choosing $\phi_2$. For real
$x = \phi_3$, $f(x) = (k - \tfrac12yx^2)^2 + m^2x^2$ has $f'(x) = 2x(m^2 - y(k - \tfrac12yx^2))$, vanishing at $x = 0$ and at $x^2 =
2(yk - m^2)/y^2$, which exists for $m^2 < yk$. There $k - \tfrac12yx^2 = m^2/y$ and $f = m^4/y^2 + 2m^2(yk - m^2)/y^2 =
m^2(2yk - m^2)/y^2 = k^2 - (yk - m^2)^2/y^2$, positive since $2yk > m^2$ and smaller than $k^2$; a complex phase of $\phi_3$ only
increases $|k - \tfrac12y\phi_3^2|$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** The figure script `figures/oraifeartaigh.sage` checks the same minimum by exact computation in Sage.
:::

The supertrace of the proposition holds at the origin; the third exercise asks whether it survives along the flat
direction. The answer follows from a general formula for F-term breaking.

::: {#exr-ssg-oraifeartaigh-supertrace}
#### The supertrace along $\phi_1$

For F-terms only, the scalar mass matrix has trace $2\sum_{ij}|W^{ij}|^2$ (counting real fields) and the fermion mass matrix
squared has trace $\sum_{ij}|W^{ij}|^2$. Show that $\operatorname{STr}m^2 = 0$ at every point of the flat direction of the O'Raifeartaigh
model.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The scalar mass matrix in the basis $(\phi, \phi^*)$ has diagonal blocks $W^{*}_{ik}W^{kj}$ and off-diagonal blocks $W^{*}_kW^{kij}$;
only the diagonal blocks contribute to the trace, $2\operatorname{Tr}(W^\dagger W)$. The fermions contribute $\operatorname{Tr}(W^\dagger W)$ per Weyl
fermion with weight $2$ in the supertrace, so $\operatorname{STr}m^2 = 2\operatorname{Tr}(W^\dagger W) - 2\operatorname{Tr}(W^\dagger W) = 0$ at every point,
whatever $\phi_1$ is [@martin1997, eq. 7.1.13]. The individual masses change along the flat direction
(@exm-ssg-oraifeartaigh-pseudomodulus), but the sum rule does not.
:::
::::

#### R-symmetry

The superpotential of @def-superpotential is integrated over half of superspace, and a phase rotation of the
Grassmann coordinates is a symmetry of everything except, possibly, the superpotential. This extra phase symmetry,
which rotates bosons and fermions of one multiplet by different phases, constrains the superpotential and the
gaugino masses, and it is the abelian part of the $U(N)$ of @exr-ssg-r-symmetry for $N = 1$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-ssg-r-symmetry}
#### R-symmetry

An **R-symmetry** is a $U(1)$ transformation $\theta \to e^{i\alpha}\theta$, $\theta^\dagger \to e^{-i\alpha}\theta^\dagger$ under which a chiral superfield of
**R-charge** $r$ transforms as $\Phi(y, \theta) \to e^{ir\alpha}\Phi(y, e^{-i\alpha}\theta)$, so that its components have the charges $r$, $r - 1$
and $r - 2$: $\phi \to e^{ir\alpha}\phi$, $\psi \to e^{i(r - 1)\alpha}\psi$, $F \to e^{i(r - 2)\alpha}F$; the gaugino has R-charge $1$ and the gauge
field and $D$ have $0$. The superpotential terms of @def-superpotential are invariant if and only if every monomial of $W$ has
total R-charge $2$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 8.19, eqs. 8.309-8.318].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The charges of the components follow from those of the superfield and of $\theta$. The first example works them out
for a superpotential with three fields, each appearing in a single monomial.

::: {#exm-ssg-r-nath}
#### Three fields with different powers

For $W = c_1\Phi_1 + c_2\Phi_2^2 + c_3\Phi_3^3$ the monomials have charge $2$ when $r_1 = 2$, $r_2 = 1$ and $r_3 = \tfrac23$. The scalars
then carry $2, 1, \tfrac23$, the fermions $1, 0, -\tfrac13$ and the auxiliary fields $0, -1, -\tfrac43$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs.
8.316-8.317]: R-charges need not be integers, and within one multiplet they always differ by one unit between neighbouring
components.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

R-symmetry is closely tied to supersymmetry breaking. The second example finds it in the O'Raifeartaigh model of
@prp-oraifeartaigh, where the field with the linear term has R-charge $2$.

::: {#exm-ssg-r-oraifeartaigh}
#### The O'Raifeartaigh model is R-symmetric

In $W = -k\Phi_1 + m\Phi_2\Phi_3 + \tfrac12y\Phi_1\Phi_3^2$ the linear term forces $r_1 = 2$, the cubic term then $r_3 = 0$ and the mass
term $r_2 = 2$. The model is R-symmetric, and for a model without supersymmetric vacua this is no accident: Nelson and Seiberg showed
that for a generic superpotential an R-symmetry is necessary for spontaneous supersymmetry breaking, and a spontaneously
broken one sufficient.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The gauginos carry R-charge $1$, so their Majorana masses carry charge $2$. The third example draws the consequence
for the soft gaugino masses that enter @exm-ssg-neutralino.

::: {#exm-ssg-r-gaugino}
#### R-symmetry forbids gaugino masses

A gaugino mass term $\tfrac12M\lambda\lambda + \text{c.c.}$ has R-charge $\pm2$ and is forbidden while the R-symmetry is exact
[@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 8.19]; the gauge interactions and the superpotential do not generate it. Non-zero masses $M_1,
M_2$ of the neutralino matrix require the R-symmetry to be broken, by the hidden sector or, in supergravity, by a constant term in the
superpotential, which has R-charge $0$ instead of $2$ and gives the gravitino its mass $e^{K/2}|W|$ (@prp-ssg-sugra-potential).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Finding R-charges is a linear problem, one equation per monomial of the superpotential. The first exercise solves it
for four models, including one with no solution and one with a family of solutions.

::: {#exr-ssg-r-assign}
#### Assigning R-charges

For each of $W = c_1\Phi_1 + c_2\Phi_2^2 + c_3\Phi_3^3$, the O'Raifeartaigh superpotential, the interacting Wess-Zumino superpotential
$\tfrac12m\Phi^2 + \tfrac16y\Phi^3$ and $W = m\Phi_+\Phi_-$, solve with Sage the linear equations for the R-charges and interpret the
solution space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first two have unique solutions, $(2, 1, \tfrac23)$ and $(2, 2, 0)$. The Wess-Zumino model would need $2r = 2$ and $3r = 2$,
which is impossible: the massive interacting model has no R-symmetry, and it has supersymmetric vacua (@exr-ssg-wz-second-vacuum).
For $m\Phi_+\Phi_-$ the solutions $r_+ + r_- = 2$ form a line: any one of them combined with the ordinary $U(1)$ of charges
$(1, -1)$ gives another, so the R-symmetry is defined only up to mixing with non-R symmetries.

{{< sage exr-ssg-r-assign >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The definition demands total charge $2$ of $W$ because the measure of the $\theta\theta$ component carries charge $-2$. The
second exercise checks the statement in components, where it becomes the invariance of each coupling.

::: {#exr-ssg-r-components}
#### Invariance in components

Let $W$ have R-charge $2$. Show that $W^iF_i$ and $W^{ij}\psi_i\psi_j$ of @def-superpotential are invariant under the R-transformation
of the components, and that the free Lagrangian @eq-wz-free is invariant for any $r$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A monomial $\phi_{i_1}\cdots\phi_{i_k}$ of $W$ has charge $\sum r_{i_l} = 2$, so $W^i$ has charge $2 - r_i$ and $W^iF_i$ has $2 - r_i + r_i - 2
= 0$. Similarly $W^{ij}$ has charge $2 - r_i - r_j$ and $\psi_i\psi_j$ has $r_i - 1 + r_j - 1$, total $0$. In @eq-wz-free each term pairs
a field with its conjugate, $\phi^*\phi$, $\psi^\dagger\psi$, $F^*F$, and is invariant for any charges. If $W$ had a monomial of charge
$q \neq 2$, its contribution would rotate by $e^{i(q - 2)\alpha}$, which is the component form of the statement that $d^2\theta$
carries R-charge $-2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A discrete remnant of R-symmetry, R-parity, is imposed on the supersymmetric Standard Model to forbid terms that would
violate baryon and lepton number. The third exercise computes it for the particles and shows which terms it removes.

::: {#exr-ssg-r-parity}
#### R-parity

With $P_R = (-1)^{3(B - L) + 2s}$, compute $P_R$ for a quark, a squark, a gluon, a gluino, a Higgs boson and a higgsino.
Show that the gauge-invariant terms $LQ\bar d$, $LL\bar e$, $\bar u\bar d\bar d$ and $LH_u$ of @nath2017supersymmetry [eq. 10.16]
violate lepton or baryon number and are odd under the matter parity $(-1)^{3(B - L)}$ of their superfields.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A quark has $B = \tfrac13$, $L = 0$, $s = \tfrac12$: $P_R = (-1)^{1 + 1} = +1$; its squark has $s = 0$ and $P_R = -1$. The gluon has
$P_R = (-1)^2 = +1$ and the gluino $(-1)^1 = -1$; the Higgs boson $+1$ and the higgsino $-1$. Every Standard Model particle is
even and every superpartner odd. The superfields $Q, \bar u, \bar d$ have $B = \pm\tfrac13$ and $L, \bar e$ have $L = \pm1$, so
$LQ\bar d$, $LL\bar e$ and $LH_u$ have $\Delta L = 1$ and $\bar u\bar d\bar d$ has $\Delta B = -1$; for each, $3(B - L)$ is odd and
the term changes sign under matter parity. Imposing R-parity removes them, which also makes the lightest superpartner
stable.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises {#sec-supersymmetry-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the sections of this part: a model with two supersymmetric vacua analysed completely,
the massive chiral multiplet followed from the algebra to the Lagrangian, and supersymmetric QED with a
Fayet-Iliopoulos term, where gauge symmetry and supersymmetry are broken in turn.

The first integrative exercise takes a single superpotential through every step of the part. The vacua, the
spectrum, the supertrace, the Witten index and the domain wall are all computed in Sage.

::: {#exr-ssg-susy-two-vacua}
#### A model with two vacua

For $W = \lambda(\tfrac13\Phi^3 - \mu^2\Phi)$, find the supersymmetric vacua, the scalar and fermion masses in each, the supertrace, the
Witten index (counting the vacua, each a massive multiplet with one bosonic ground state), and the BPS wall between the
vacua with its tension.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W' = \lambda(\phi^2 - \mu^2)$ vanishes at $\phi = \pm\mu$; $W'' = 2\lambda\phi$ gives the mass $2\lambda\mu$ to both real scalars and to the Weyl
fermion in each vacuum, and the supertrace $2(4\lambda^2\mu^2) - 2(4\lambda^2\mu^2) = 0$. Each vacuum contributes $1$ to the Witten index
(@exr-ssg-witten-index), which is $2$, a number that no continuous deformation of the parameters can change. The wall
$\phi(x) = -\mu\tanh(\lambda\mu x)$ solves $\phi' = W'(\phi)$ and has tension $2|W(\mu) - W(-\mu)| = \tfrac83\lambda\mu^3$ (@exm-ssg-fterm-bps):

{{< sage exr-ssg-susy-two-vacua >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise follows the simplest massive multiplet from the algebra to the Lagrangian. It uses
the representation theory of the first section and the field theory of the second and third, and is worked by hand.

::: {#exr-ssg-susy-massive-chiral}
#### The massive chiral multiplet from end to end

For $W = \tfrac12m\phi^2$: (a) count the states of the massive multiplet from the Clifford algebra at rest and compare with the
fields $\phi$, $\psi$; (b) derive the field equations after eliminating $F$ and show that $\phi$ and $\psi$ both satisfy the
Klein-Gordon equation with mass $|m|$; (c) explain why the algebra now closes only on-shell; (d) find the vacuum and
its energy.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) At rest, $\{Q_\alpha, Q^\dagger_{\dot\beta}\} = 2m\delta_{\alpha\dot\beta}$ gives two fermionic oscillators; from a spin-$0$ Clifford vacuum the
multiplet has two spin-$0$ states and one spin-$\tfrac12$ doublet, $2 + 2$ (@exr-ssg-massive-multiplet), matching the complex
scalar and the two helicities of the massive Majorana fermion built from $\psi$. (b) With $F = -m^*\phi^*$, $\mathcal{L} =
\partial^\mu\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi + i\psi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi - |m|^2|\phi|^2 - \tfrac12(m\psi\psi + m^*\psi^\dagger\psi^\dagger)$; the scalar
satisfies $(\Box + |m|^2)\phi = 0$, the fermion $i\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi = m^*\psi^\dagger$, and applying $i\sigma^\nu\partial_\nu$ to the
conjugate equation and using $(p\cdot\sigma)(p\cdot\bar\sigma) = p^2$ (@exm-ssg-sigma-mass-shell) gives $(\Box + |m|^2)\psi = 0$. (c) After
the elimination $\delta F$ is replaced by $\delta(-m^*\phi^*)$, which agrees with the closing rule only on the fermion field
equation (@exr-ssg-closure-eliminated). (d) $V = |m|^2|\phi|^2$ has its unique zero at $\phi = 0$: one supersymmetric vacuum,
with zero energy, and Witten index $1$.
:::

The third integrative exercise combines the D-term potential, the Higgs mechanism and supersymmetry breaking. Without
a superpotential, the Fayet-Iliopoulos term breaks the gauge symmetry and keeps supersymmetry; with one, it breaks
supersymmetry.

::: {#exr-ssg-susy-sqed-fi}
#### Supersymmetric QED with a Fayet-Iliopoulos term

For $U(1)$ with fields $\Phi_\pm$ of charges $\pm1$, coupling $g$ and FI term $-\kappa D$, $\kappa > 0$: (a) without superpotential find the
vacua and show they are supersymmetric but break the gauge symmetry; (b) at $\phi_- = 0$ compute the photon mass and the
mass of the radial scalar, and count the states of the resulting massive multiplet; (c) add $W = m\Phi_+\Phi_-$ and show that
supersymmetry is broken.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $V = \tfrac12(\kappa - g(|\phi_+|^2 - |\phi_-|^2))^2$ vanishes on $|\phi_+|^2 - |\phi_-|^2 = \kappa/g$, where $D = 0$ and all F-terms vanish:
supersymmetric vacua, with charged fields condensed, so the $U(1)$ is broken. (b) With $|\phi_+|^2 = v^2 = \kappa/g$ the photon gets
$m_A^2 = 2g^2v^2 = 2g\kappa$, and the radial scalar the same mass squared $2g\kappa$; the phase is eaten. Vector ($3$) plus scalar
($1$) are $4$ bosonic states, and the gaugino and $\psi_+$ pair into a massive Dirac fermion ($4$): the massive vector
multiplet of @exr-ssg-massive-multiplet. (c) With $W$, $V = m^2(|\phi_+|^2 + |\phi_-|^2) + \tfrac12(\kappa - g(|\phi_+|^2 - |\phi_-|^2))^2$ cannot
vanish, since the first term needs $\phi_\pm = 0$ and the second then equals $\tfrac12\kappa^2$: supersymmetry is broken
(@exr-ssg-fi-spectrum).

{{< sage exr-ssg-susy-sqed-fi >}}
:::
::::

## Supergravity {#sec-supergravity}

Making supersymmetry local forces gravity in: the gravitino is the gauge field of local supersymmetry, and
eleven-dimensional supergravity is the maximal theory of this kind. This part develops it in two sections. Local
supersymmetry and the gravitino introduces Majorana spinors and the charge-conjugation matrix, the dimensions of the
smallest spinors in each spacetime dimension, the gauging of supersymmetry and its gauge field of spin three halves,
the supergravity multiplets of four dimensions up to $N = 8$, and the super-Higgs mechanism by which the gravitino
becomes massive. Eleven-dimensional supergravity defines maximal supergravity, displays the action and the
transformation rules of the unique eleven-dimensional theory, solves its field equations with the Freund-Rubin
ansatz on anti-de Sitter space times a seven-dimensional Einstein space, and counts the supersymmetries that a
background preserves through its Killing spinors. The signature is $(+, -, \dots, -)$ in every dimension, that of
@tanii1998.

### Local supersymmetry and the gravitino {#sec-gravitino}

Making the supersymmetry parameter depend on position forces gravity into the theory: two local supersymmetries
compose to a local translation, which is a coordinate transformation, and the gauge field of local supersymmetry
is a spin-$\tfrac32$ field, the gravitino. This section defines Majorana spinors, local supersymmetry, the
gravitino and the supergravity multiplet, following @tanii1998 [Secs. 1-3], whose signature $(+, -, -, -)$ is ours,
and @martin1997 [Sec. 7.5], with the
charge-conjugation and Rarita-Schwinger identities established on the explicit gamma matrices and the
spinor dimensions, which decide in which dimensions supergravity exists, computed dimension by dimension.

#### Majorana spinors

The supersymmetry parameter and the gravitino are real spinors: a single Weyl spinor together with its conjugate,
written in four-component form. Reality for spinors is defined with a charge-conjugation matrix, and the definition
fixes it for the gamma matrices of this chapter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-majorana-spinor}
#### Majorana spinor

The **charge conjugate** of a Dirac spinor is $\psi^c = C\bar\psi^T$ with the **charge-conjugation matrix** $C$
satisfying $C\gamma^\mu C^{-1} = -(\gamma^\mu)^T$ and $C^T = -C$ [@tanii1998, eq. 2.1]; a **Majorana spinor** is one
with $\psi^c = \psi$, a real spinor in the sense that it has half the components of a Dirac spinor. In the Weyl
basis of @exm-gamma-weyl, $C \propto \gamma^0\gamma^2$ (@prp-charge-conjugation) and a Majorana spinor is a Dirac spinor
$(\xi_\alpha, \xi^{\dagger\dot\alpha})$ built from a single Weyl spinor [@martin1997, eq. 2.29].
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In four-component form a Majorana field has a Lagrangian with factors of one half. The first example translates it
into the two-component language of the first part, where it is the Lagrangian of a single Weyl spinor with a mass.

::: {#exm-majorana-lagrangian}
#### The Majorana Lagrangian

$\mathcal{L} = \tfrac{i}{2}\bar\Psi_M\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\Psi_M - \tfrac12M\bar\Psi_M\Psi_M = i\xi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\xi -
\tfrac12M(\xi\xi + \xi^\dagger\xi^\dagger)$ [@martin1997, eqs. 2.30-2.31]: the factors $\tfrac12$ compensate the
doubling in the four-component form, and the mass term is the $\xi\xi$ of @exm-grassmann-spinor-product.
:::

Whether a reality condition exists depends on the dimension, and so does whether it is compatible with a chirality
condition. The second example states the rules, which decide the size of the smallest spinor in each dimension.

::: {#exm-majorana-dimensions}
#### Which dimensions admit Majorana spinors

A Dirac spinor in $d$ dimensions has $2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$ complex components; a Weyl condition halves this for even
$d$ and a Majorana condition for $d \equiv 2, 3, 4 \pmod 8$ (pseudo-Majorana for $d \equiv 0, 1, 2$), both together
only for $d \equiv 2 \pmod 8$ [@tanii1998, Tables 1-2]. The minimal real spinor has $1, 2, 4, 8, 8, 16, 16, 16, 16,
32$ components for $d = 2, \dots, 11$ (@fig-spinor-dimensions, @prp-spinor-dimensions).
:::

All the fermions of supergravity that are partners of real bosons are Majorana. The third example names them, the
gaugino and the gravitino in four and eleven dimensions.

::: {#exm-majorana-gaugino}
#### Gauginos and gravitini

The gaugino of @def-gauge-multiplet and the gravitino of @def-gravitino are Majorana: a Weyl spinor $\lambda$ and
its conjugate make up a single real spinor, with no independent right-handed partner; in eleven dimensions the
gravitino is a $32$-component Majorana spinor (@sec-sugra11).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the statement of the definition that a Majorana spinor is built from one Weyl spinor. It
needs only the explicit $C$ and the Dirac conjugate.

::: {#exr-ssg-majorana-components}
#### A Majorana spinor in components

With $C = \gamma^0\gamma^2$ and $\Psi = (\xi_\alpha, \chi^{\dagger\dot\alpha})$, compute $\Psi^c = C\bar\Psi^T$ with $\bar\Psi = \Psi^\dagger\gamma^0$, and show
that $\Psi^c = \Psi$ (up to the phase convention of $C$) means $\chi = \xi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\bar\Psi^T = \gamma^{0T}\Psi^* = \gamma^0\Psi^*$, so $\Psi^c = \gamma^0\gamma^2\gamma^0\Psi^* = -\gamma^2\Psi^*$ (since $\gamma^0\gamma^2\gamma^0 = -\gamma^2$). In
blocks $\gamma^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma_2 \\ -\sigma_2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, so $\Psi^c = (-\sigma_2\chi^{\dagger *}, \sigma_2\xi^*)$: the upper
components of $\Psi^c$ are built from $\chi$ and the lower from $\xi$. Since $\sigma_2 = -i\epsilon$ (as matrices, with
$\epsilon^{12} = 1$) and complex conjugation turns an undotted index into a dotted one, $\Psi^c$ is $(\chi_\alpha, \xi^{\dagger\dot\alpha})$ up to a
phase: charge conjugation exchanges the two Weyl spinors, and $\Psi^c = \Psi$ (with the phase of $C$ chosen
accordingly) means $\chi = \xi$ [@martin1997, eqs. 2.29-2.31].
:::

A Majorana mass is not invariant under phase rotations of the Weyl spinor. The second exercise makes the point, which
is why only neutral fermions can have Majorana masses.

::: {#exr-ssg-majorana-phase}
#### Majorana masses break phases

Under $\xi \to e^{i\alpha}\xi$, how do the kinetic term $i\xi^\dagger\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\xi$ and the mass term $\xi\xi + \xi^\dagger\xi^\dagger$
transform? Which fields of the Standard Model can have a Majorana mass?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The kinetic term is invariant ($\xi^\dagger \to e^{-i\alpha}\xi^\dagger$), while $\xi\xi \to e^{2i\alpha}\xi\xi$: the mass term breaks every
$U(1)$ under which $\xi$ is charged. So only a fermion neutral under all unbroken gauge symmetries can have a Majorana
mass: among the Standard Model fields none (a right-handed neutrino would be the candidate), among the
superpartners the gauginos of neutral gauge bosons, as in the bino and wino masses of the supersymmetric Standard
Model, and the gravitino.
:::

The third exercise compares four and ten dimensions. Whether a spinor can be both Majorana and Weyl depends on how
charge conjugation acts on chirality.

::: {#exr-majorana-weyl}
#### Majorana-Weyl spinors

Explain why a Majorana-Weyl spinor exists in $d = 10$ but not in $d = 4$, and give its number of real components.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both conditions are compatible only when the charge conjugation does not exchange the chiralities, which happens
for $d \equiv 2 \pmod 8$ [@tanii1998, p. 11]: in $d = 4$ the conjugate of a left-handed spinor is right-handed
(@def-weyl-spinor), so a Majorana spinor contains both chiralities; in $d = 10$ a single chirality can be real. The
Dirac spinor of $d = 10$ has $32$ complex components, halved twice to $16$ real ones (@fig-spinor-dimensions): the
supercharge of type I and heterotic supergravity.
:::
::::

The charge-conjugation matrix of the definition exists in four dimensions and has the stated symmetry. The
proposition gives it explicitly for our gamma matrices, where both properties are finite matrix identities.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-charge-conjugation}
#### The charge-conjugation matrix

For the Dirac matrices of @exm-gamma-weyl, $C = \gamma^0\gamma^2$ satisfies $C\gamma^\mu = -(\gamma^\mu)^TC$ for all $\mu$ and
$C^T = -C$.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The matrix itself is worth seeing. The first example writes it in two-by-two blocks, where it is built from the
antisymmetric $\epsilon$ symbol of the two-component formalism.

::: {#exm-ssg-c-blocks}
#### $C$ in blocks

$C = \gamma^0\gamma^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma_2 \\ -\sigma_2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -
\sigma_2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_2 \end{pmatrix}$, block diagonal and built from $\sigma_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, which is
$-i$ times the matrix $\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}$: charge conjugation raises and lowers the two-component indices, which is why it
does not mix the chiral blocks (@exr-majorana).
:::

The defining property is what makes charge conjugation a symmetry of the Dirac equation with the sign of the charge
reversed. The second example states it, with the computation left to the third exercise.

::: {#exm-ssg-c-dirac}
#### Charge conjugation of the Dirac equation

If $\psi$ solves $(i\gamma^\mu(\partial_\mu + ieA_\mu) - m)\psi = 0$, then $\psi^c = C\bar\psi^T$ solves the same equation with $e \to -e$
(@exr-ssg-charge-conjugate-dirac): $\psi^c$ describes the antiparticle, and a Majorana spinor, equal to its conjugate,
can only be neutral, as @exr-ssg-majorana-phase found from the mass term.
:::

The symmetry of $C$ and of its products with gamma matrices decides which bilinears of a Majorana spinor vanish. The
third example gives the rule that is used throughout supergravity.

::: {#exm-ssg-c-bilinears}
#### Majorana bilinears

For anticommuting Majorana spinors, $\bar\psi_1\Gamma\psi_2 = +\bar\psi_2\Gamma\psi_1$ for $\Gamma = 1, \gamma^5, \gamma^\mu\gamma^5$ and $-\bar\psi_2\Gamma\psi_1$
for $\Gamma = \gamma^\mu, \gamma^{\mu\nu}$ (@exr-ssg-c-symmetric-products). In particular $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi = 0$ for a single Majorana
spinor, so a Majorana field carries no conserved vector current, and the kinetic term needs the factor $\tfrac12$ of
@exm-majorana-lagrangian.
:::

The symmetry of $C$ is not special to four dimensions: in every even dimension there is a matrix with the same property,
symmetric or antisymmetric according to a simple rule. The fourth example states the rule found by @zhelnorovich2019spinors
for Euclidean signature.

::: {#exm-ssg-c-general}
#### The transposition matrix in any even dimension

In $2\nu$ Euclidean dimensions there is a matrix $E$ with $\gamma_i^T = -E\gamma_iE^{-1}$ for all $i$, unique up to a factor by
Pauli's theorem (@thm-pauli-uniqueness), and $E^T = (-1)^{\nu(\nu + 1)/2}E$ [@zhelnorovich2019spinors, Sec. 1.1, eqs.
1.44-1.53]: antisymmetric for $2\nu = 2, 4, 10$ and symmetric for $2\nu = 6, 8$. For $2\nu = 4$ this is the antisymmetry $C^T = -C$ of
the proposition, and the antisymmetry in ten dimensions is what makes the Majorana bilinears of type II supergravity
behave as in four.
:::

The second exercise classifies the sixteen matrices $C\Gamma$ by symmetry. From this follow the flip rules of the
third example, which are the main tool for manipulating fermion bilinears in supergravity.

::: {#exr-ssg-c-symmetric-products}
#### Symmetric and antisymmetric $C\Gamma$

Determine which of $C$, $C\gamma^5$, $C\gamma^\mu\gamma^5$, $C\gamma^\mu$, $C\gamma^{\mu\nu}$ are symmetric. For Majorana spinors with
$\bar\psi = \psi^TK$, $K = (C^T)^{-1}$, deduce the flip rule $\bar\psi_1\Gamma\psi_2 = \pm\bar\psi_2\Gamma\psi_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$C$, $C\gamma^5$ and $C\gamma^\mu\gamma^5$ are antisymmetric ($6$ matrices), $C\gamma^\mu$ and $C\gamma^{\mu\nu}$ symmetric ($10$). For anticommuting
components, $\psi_1^TM\psi_2 = -\psi_2^TM^T\psi_1$, so the sign is $+$ when $K\Gamma$ is antisymmetric and $-$ when it is symmetric:

{{< sage exr-ssg-c-symmetric-products >}}
:::

The third exercise proves the statement of the second example. It uses the defining property of $C$ and the complex
conjugate of the Dirac equation.

::: {#exr-ssg-charge-conjugate-dirac}
#### $\psi^c$ has the opposite charge

Take the complex conjugate of $(i\gamma^\mu(\partial_\mu + ieA_\mu) - m)\psi = 0$, multiply by suitable matrices, and use $C\gamma^{\mu T}C^{-1} = -
\gamma^\mu$ and $\gamma^0\gamma^{\mu*}\gamma^0 = \gamma^{\mu T}$ to show that $\psi^c = C\gamma^{0T}\psi^*$ satisfies the equation with $e \to -e$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The conjugate equation is $(-i\gamma^{\mu*}(\partial_\mu - ieA_\mu) - m)\psi^* = 0$. Multiply by $C\gamma^0$ on the left (with $\gamma^{0T} = \gamma^0$
in our basis): $C\gamma^0\gamma^{\mu*}\psi^* = C\gamma^{\mu T}\gamma^0\psi^* = -\gamma^\mu C\gamma^0\psi^*$, using $\gamma^0\gamma^{\mu*} = \gamma^{\mu T}\gamma^0$ (the
Hermiticity property $\gamma^0\gamma^\mu\gamma^0 = \gamma^{\mu\dagger}$ transposed) and $C\gamma^{\mu T} = -\gamma^\mu C$. So $(i\gamma^\mu(\partial_\mu - ieA_\mu) -
m)\psi^c = 0$: the charge-conjugate field has charge $-e$.
:::

The rule of @exm-ssg-c-general extends to the products of gamma matrices, whose symmetry under transposition decides
which bilinears of Majorana spinors survive. The fourth exercise checks Zhelnorovich's general formula in all even
dimensions up to ten.

::: {#exr-ssg-zhelnorovich-e}
#### Symmetry of $E\gamma_{i_1\dots i_k}$

With Dirac matrices built from Pauli matrices, $\nu$ of them symmetric and $\nu$ antisymmetric, take $E$ to be the product of the
symmetric ones for even $\nu$ and of the antisymmetric ones for odd $\nu$. Check with Sage, for $2\nu = 2, \dots, 10$, that
$\gamma_i^T = -E\gamma_iE^{-1}$, that $E^T = (-1)^{\nu(\nu + 1)/2}E$, and that $(E\gamma_{i_1\dots i_k})^T = (-1)^{[\nu(\nu + 1) + k(k + 1)]/2}
E\gamma_{i_1\dots i_k}$ for antisymmetrised products [@zhelnorovich2019spinors, eqs. 1.51-1.55].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For even $\nu$, $E = \gamma_1\cdots\gamma_\nu$ (the symmetric ones): transposing $\gamma_i$ through the product gives a sign $(-1)^\nu = 1$ times
$\gamma_i$ for an antisymmetric $\gamma_i$ and $(-1)^{\nu - 1}$ for a symmetric one, which is exactly $-\gamma_i^T$ in both cases; odd $\nu$ is
analogous. Reversing a product of $m$ anticommuting matrices costs $(-1)^{m(m - 1)/2}$, which gives the symmetry of $E$, and
$(\gamma_{i_1\dots i_k})^T = (-1)^{k(k + 1)/2}E\gamma_{i_1\dots i_k}E^{-1}$ gives the second rule [@zhelnorovich2019spinors, eq. 1.54].

{{< sage exr-ssg-zhelnorovich-e >}}
:::

Applying the Weyl and Majorana rules of @exm-majorana-dimensions gives the minimal real spinor dimensions
$1, 2, 4, 8, 8, 16, 16, 16, 16, 32$ for $d = 2, \dots, 11$, in agreement with the standard table, and $32$ for the

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Four dimensions is the familiar case. The first example reads the table there and connects it with the
supercharges of the first part.

::: {#exm-ssg-spinor-four}
#### Four dimensions

$d = 4$: the Dirac spinor has $4$ complex components, a Weyl or a Majorana condition halves it to $4$ real ones (not both).
The $N = 1$ supercharge $(Q_\alpha, Q^\dagger_{\dot\alpha})$ is one Majorana spinor with $4$ real components, and $N = 8$ gives $32$
(@fig-spinor-dimensions).
:::

Ten dimensions is the case where both conditions apply. The second example gives the resulting spinor, which is the
supercharge of the ten-dimensional supergravities.

::: {#exm-ssg-spinor-ten}
#### Ten dimensions

$d = 10$: the Dirac spinor has $2^5 = 32$ complex components; Majorana and Weyl together leave $16$ real ones. Type I and
heterotic supergravity have one such supercharge ($16$), type IIA two of opposite chirality and type IIB two of
the same chirality ($32$ each) [@tanii1998, Sec. 4].
:::

Eleven is the last dimension in which the minimal spinor has at most $32$ components. The third example shows why
twelve fails.

::: {#exm-ssg-spinor-eleven}
#### Eleven and twelve dimensions

$d = 11$: the Dirac spinor has $2^5 = 32$ complex components and a Majorana condition leaves $32$ real ones. In $d = 12$ the
minimal spinor (Weyl, $2^6/2 = 32$ complex, with a Majorana condition not compatible with Weyl in Lorentzian
signature for $d \equiv 4 \pmod 8$) has $64$ real components, beyond the bound of $32$ supercharges.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The number $2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$ is the size of the gamma matrices. The first exercise explains where it comes from, without
constructing the matrices.

::: {#exr-ssg-dirac-dimension}
#### The size of the gamma matrices

Show that in even $d$ the operators $a_k = \tfrac12(\Gamma^{2k} + i\Gamma^{2k+1})$ (suitably normalised to square to zero) form $d/2$
fermionic creation-annihilation pairs, and conclude that the irreducible representation has dimension $2^{d/2}$. What
happens in odd $d$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In Euclidean signature (multiply timelike or spacelike matrices by $i$ to switch) the $d$ matrices satisfy $\{\Gamma^a, \Gamma^b\} =
2\delta^{ab}$, and $a_k = \tfrac12(\Gamma^{2k} + i\Gamma^{2k + 1})$ satisfy $\{a_k, a_l^\dagger\} = \delta_{kl}$, $\{a_k, a_l\} = 0$: $d/2$ fermionic
oscillators, whose Fock space has dimension $2^{d/2}$, as the oscillator $b$ of @prp-susy-oscillator has dimension $2$. In odd
$d$ the extra matrix is the product of the others (up to a factor), so the dimension is $2^{(d - 1)/2} = 2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$
(@exr-ssg-gamma-construction).
:::

The second exercise builds the matrices explicitly as tensor products of Pauli matrices. In eleven dimensions the
product of all eleven is a multiple of the identity, which is why there is no chirality there.

::: {#exr-ssg-gamma-construction}
#### Gamma matrices in $d = 4, 5, 10, 11$

Build $\Gamma^a$ for $d = 4, 5, 10, 11$ as tensor products of Pauli matrices, check the Clifford relations with $\eta =
\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, \dots, -1)$ and the size $2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$, and compute $\Gamma^0\Gamma^1\cdots\Gamma^{10}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Euclidean matrices $\sigma_3 \otimes \dots \otimes \sigma_3 \otimes \sigma_{1,2} \otimes 1 \otimes \dots$ anticommute and square to one;
multiplying the spatial ones by $i$ gives the Lorentzian signature, and for odd $d$ the last matrix is the normalised
product of the others. In $d = 11$ the product of all eleven is $i\cdot1$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-gamma-construction >}}
:::

The table bounds the number of supersymmetries in each dimension. The third exercise derives the maximal $N$ in each
dimension from the bound of $32$ real supercharges.

::: {#exr-ssg-max-supercharges}
#### The maximal $N$ in each dimension

With at most $32$ real supercharges, find the maximal number $N$ of minimal spinor supercharges for $d = 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$N_{\max} = 32/n_{\min}(d)$ with the table of the proposition: $d = 4$: $32/4 = 8$; $d = 5$: $32/8 = 4$ (usually counted as
$N = 8$ in symplectic-Majorana units of half that size); $d = 6$: $32/8 = 4$, realised as $(2, 2)$ chiral pairs; $d = 7$:
$32/16 = 2$; $d = 10$: $32/16 = 2$, types IIA and IIB; $d = 11$: $32/32 = 1$ [@tanii1998, Table 3]. Beyond $d = 11$ even one
supercharge exceeds the bound.
:::

The table of minimal spinors rests on the rule of @exm-majorana-dimensions for which dimensions admit Majorana spinors. The
fourth exercise derives that rule from the reality properties of the Dirac matrices, following the approach of
@zhelnorovich2019spinors [Secs. 1.6.2-1.6.3].

::: {#exr-ssg-majorana-bb}
#### When a Majorana condition is consistent

Let $B$ satisfy $(\Gamma^\mu)^* = sB\Gamma^\mu B^{-1}$ for all $\mu$ with a fixed sign $s = \pm1$. Show that the condition $\psi^* = B\psi$ is
Lorentz covariant and consistent only if $B^*B = 1$, and that the sign of $B^*B$ does not depend on the normalisation of $B$.
Then compute with Sage, for $d = 2, \dots, 11$ and signature $(+, -, \dots, -)$, the signs $s$ for which $B$ exists and the
value of $B^*B$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Applying the condition twice, $\psi = (\psi^*)^* = B^*\psi^* = B^*B\psi$, so $B^*B = 1$ is needed. The Lorentz generators $\Sigma^{\mu\nu} =
\tfrac14[\Gamma^\mu, \Gamma^\nu]$ are real combinations of products of two gamma matrices, so $(\Sigma^{\mu\nu})^* = B\Sigma^{\mu\nu}B^{-1}$ for
either sign $s$ and the condition is preserved by Lorentz transformations. By Pauli's theorem $B$ is unique up to a factor $c$,
which changes $B^*B$ to $|c|^2B^*B$, and $B^*B$ commutes with all $\Gamma^\mu$, hence is a multiple of $1$, real by the same
argument as for Zhelnorovich's eq. (1.141): its sign is invariant. The computation finds $B^*B = +1$ with $s = -1$ for $d \equiv 2, 3, 4
\pmod 8$ (Majorana) and with $s = +1$ for $d \equiv 0, 1, 2 \pmod 8$ (pseudo-Majorana), and $B^*B = -1$ in $d = 5, 6, 7$, in
agreement with @exm-majorana-dimensions.

{{< sage exr-ssg-majorana-bb >}}
:::
