#### Local supersymmetry

When the parameter of a supersymmetry transformation depends on position, the algebra implies that the composition
of two transformations is a translation by a position-dependent vector. That is a general coordinate transformation,
so a theory with local supersymmetry must contain gravity.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-local-supersymmetry}
#### Local supersymmetry

**Local supersymmetry** is the supersymmetry transformation $\delta = \epsilon(x)Q + \epsilon^\dagger(x)Q^\dagger$ with a
position-dependent spinor parameter (@def-global-local-symmetry). Since $\{Q, Q^\dagger\} \propto \gamma^aP_a$, the
commutator of two local supersymmetries is a local translation, $\xi^\mu = i\bar\epsilon_2\gamma^\mu\epsilon_1$, that is a
general coordinate transformation: gauging supersymmetry gauges translations, and the metric must be a dynamical
field [@tanii1998, eq. 1.1 and p. 2]. A theory with local supersymmetry is a **supergravity**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The procedure of gauging is the same as for an internal symmetry. The first example applies it to supersymmetry and
finds the field that must be introduced.

::: {#exm-local-noether}
#### The Noether coupling

Varying a globally supersymmetric action with $\epsilon(x)$ gives $\delta S = \int\partial_\mu\bar\epsilon\,J^\mu$ with the
supercurrent of @def-supercurrent; as for gauge fields (@sec-abelian-gauge), it is cancelled at first order by
coupling a gauge field to the current, $\mathcal{L} \ni -\bar\psi_\mu J^\mu$ with $\delta\psi_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon$: the
gravitino [@martin1997, eq. 7.5.3].
:::

The algebra of local transformations closes on a combination of local symmetries. The second example gives it for
four-dimensional supergravity.

::: {#exm-local-algebra}
#### The local algebra

In $d = 4$, $N = 1$ supergravity, $[\delta_Q(\epsilon_1), \delta_Q(\epsilon_2)] = \delta_G(\xi) + \delta_L(\xi\cdot\hat\omega) +
\delta_Q(\xi\cdot\psi)$ with $\xi^\mu = i\bar\epsilon_2\gamma^\mu\epsilon_1$: a coordinate transformation plus
field-dependent Lorentz and supersymmetry transformations, closing only on-shell [@tanii1998, eq. 2.11].
:::

The converse also holds: supersymmetry and gravity cannot be combined without making supersymmetry local. The third
example spells out both directions.

::: {#exm-local-gravity-needed}
#### Why gravity cannot be avoided

Local translations are diffeomorphisms (@exm-local-coordinate), whose gauge field is the metric with the
Einstein-Hilbert action (@sec-einstein-hilbert): any locally supersymmetric theory contains general relativity, and
conversely any supersymmetric theory coupled to gravity must have local supersymmetry.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the variation of the first example. It is the same computation as for any global symmetry
made local.

::: {#exr-ssg-local-variation}
#### The variation under a local parameter

If $\delta_\epsilon S = 0$ for constant $\epsilon$ and the Noether current is defined by @def-supercurrent, show that for a
position-dependent $\epsilon(x)$, $\delta_\epsilon S = \int d^4x\,(\partial_\mu\epsilon J^\mu + \text{c.c.})$ up to normalisation. Why does the
gravitino coupling cancel it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $\epsilon(x)$ the variation of the Lagrangian differs from the global one only through terms where a derivative acts on
$\epsilon$; these come from $\partial_\mu(\delta X)$ in the kinetic terms and are $\partial_\mu\epsilon$ times the coefficient $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial(\partial_\mu X)$
times the variation per unit parameter, which is the Noether current (the $K^\mu$ term contributes as in the global
case). So $\delta S = \int\partial_\mu\epsilon\,J^\mu + \text{c.c.}$, vanishing for constant $\epsilon$. Adding $-\bar\psi_\mu J^\mu$ with $\delta\psi_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon$
(normalised accordingly) produces $-\int\partial_\mu\epsilon\,J^\mu$, which cancels it at this order; the variation of $J^\mu$ itself
contains the energy-momentum tensor, and cancelling that requires coupling to the metric [@martin1997, Sec. 7.5].
:::

The translation parameter of the definition must be a vector of length dimension one. The second exercise checks
this and identifies where the gravitational coupling must appear.

::: {#exr-ssg-local-dimension}
#### Dimensions in supergravity

With $[\epsilon] = -\tfrac12$, find $[\xi^\mu]$ for $\xi^\mu = i\bar\epsilon_2\gamma^\mu\epsilon_1$. If the gravitino has the canonical dimension $\tfrac32$ of a
fermion, show that $\delta\psi_\mu = \kappa^{-1}\partial_\mu\epsilon$ with a constant $\kappa$ of dimension $-1$, and identify $\kappa$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\xi^\mu] = -\tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = -1$, a length, as a translation must be. $[\partial_\mu\epsilon] = \tfrac12$, so a field of dimension $\tfrac32$ needs a
factor of dimension $1$: $\delta\psi_\mu = \kappa^{-1}\partial_\mu\epsilon$ with $[\kappa] = -1$. The only such constant is the gravitational one,
$\kappa = \sqrt{8\pi G} = 1/M_P$, which @tanii1998 sets to a fixed number ($4\pi G = 1$); the coupling $\kappa\bar\psi_\mu J^\mu$ is then
suppressed by the Planck mass, like every gravitational interaction.
:::

The third exercise looks at the algebra of the second example from the point of view of the gravitino. The
field-dependent supersymmetry in the commutator is a feature without analogue in global supersymmetry.

::: {#exr-ssg-local-algebra}
#### The field-dependent terms

In @exm-local-algebra the commutator contains $\delta_Q(\xi\cdot\psi)$, a supersymmetry with parameter $\xi^\mu\psi_\mu$. Explain why a
term of this kind must appear when $\delta\psi_\mu = D_\mu\epsilon + \dots$, by comparing a coordinate transformation of $\psi_\mu$ with
the transformations generated by $\delta_Q$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A coordinate transformation acts on $\psi_\mu$ by the Lie derivative, $\xi^\nu\partial_\nu\psi_\mu + \partial_\mu\xi^\nu\psi_\nu$. Writing this as $\xi^\nu(\partial_\nu\psi_\mu -
\partial_\mu\psi_\nu) + \partial_\mu(\xi^\nu\psi_\nu)$, the last term has the form of a supersymmetry transformation $D_\mu\epsilon'$ with parameter $\epsilon' =
\xi^\nu\psi_\nu$, and the first is a field strength term that, with the spin connection, gives the Lorentz part. Since the
commutator of two supersymmetries reproduces the full gauge algebra, the general coordinate transformation appears
together with these compensating field-dependent supersymmetry and Lorentz transformations [@tanii1998, eq. 2.11]:
the gauge parameters of supergravity mix.
:::
::::

#### The gravitino

The gauge field of local supersymmetry carries a vector index, because it couples to a current, and a spinor index,
because the parameter is a spinor. Its kinetic term is the Rarita-Schwinger Lagrangian, built with the totally
antisymmetrised product of three gamma matrices.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gravitino}
#### Gravitino

The **gravitino** is the gauge field of local supersymmetry: a Majorana vector-spinor $\psi_\mu$ (a
**Rarita-Schwinger field**) with the inhomogeneous transformation $\delta\psi_\mu = D_\mu\epsilon + \dots$, the
**Rarita-Schwinger Lagrangian** $-\tfrac{i}{2}e\bar\psi_\mu\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}D_\nu\psi_\rho$ with $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}$ the
antisymmetrised product of three gamma matrices, and the field equation $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}D_\nu\psi_\rho = 0$
[@tanii1998, eqs. 2.2-2.4, 2.10, in our signature $(+, -, -, -)$]; it describes a massless particle of spin $\tfrac32$
with two helicity states.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The gravitino's gauge invariance mirrors that of the Maxwell field. The first example states it for flat space, where
the proof is the antisymmetry of $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}$.

::: {#exm-gravitino-gauge}
#### Gauge invariance

On flat space $\delta\psi_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon$ leaves $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\psi_\rho$ invariant because
$\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\partial_\rho\epsilon = 0$, a symmetric tensor contracted with an antisymmetric one
(@prp-rarita-schwinger, @exr-majorana), exactly as $F_{\mu\nu}$ is invariant under $\delta A_\mu = \partial_\mu\alpha$
(@prp-covariant-u1).
:::

Gauge invariance removes components, and the field equation removes more. The second example gives the count in
any dimension, which is needed for the matching of eleven-dimensional supergravity.

::: {#exm-gravitino-dof}
#### Degrees of freedom

In $d$ dimensions a gravitino has $\tfrac12(d - 3)\,2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$ real on-shell components (for a Majorana-type
spinor): the gamma-traceless condition $\gamma^\mu\psi_\mu = 0$ removes one vector component and the first-order
equation halves the rest [@tanii1998, eq. 4.8]. In $d = 4$ this is $2$, matching the graviton; in $d = 11$ it is
$128$ (@exr-gravitino-dof, @fig-sugra11-dof).
:::

In eleven dimensions the gravitino variation contains the four-form flux. The third example displays it, since it
decides which backgrounds preserve supersymmetry.

::: {#exm-gravitino-eleven}
#### The eleven-dimensional gravitino

$\delta\psi_\mu = D_\mu\epsilon + \tfrac{i}{144}(\gamma^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}{}_\mu - 8\gamma^{\beta\gamma\delta}\delta^\alpha_\mu)\epsilon
F_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}$ [@tanii1998, eq. 5.2]: the flux term is what makes the Freund-Rubin background of
@sec-sugra11 supersymmetric for some spinors and not others.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise applies the counting formula of the second example. In four dimensions the gravitino matches the
graviton and in eleven the graviton plus the three-form.

::: {#exr-gravitino-dof}
#### Gravitino degrees of freedom

Using the light-cone formulas, count the on-shell components of a Majorana gravitino in $d = 4$ and $d = 11$ and
compare with the graviton and the three-form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac12(d - 3)2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$ gives $\tfrac12\cdot1\cdot4 = 2$ in four dimensions, equal to the $\tfrac12(d - 2)(d - 1) -
1 = 2$ of the graviton, and $\tfrac12\cdot8\cdot32 = 128$ in eleven, equal to the graviton's $44$ plus the three-form's
$\binom{9}{3} = 84$ [@tanii1998, eq. 4.8] (@exr-dof-11d).
:::

Pure-gauge configurations solve the field equation and carry no physical state. The second exercise checks this on
plane waves, which makes the gauge invariance concrete.

::: {#exr-ssg-rs-plane-wave}
#### Pure-gauge plane waves

Show that $\psi_\mu = p_\mu u\,e^{-ip\cdot x}$, with any constant spinor $u$ and any momentum $p$, solves $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\psi_\rho = 0$, and
that it is a gauge transformation of $\psi_\mu = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\psi_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon$ with $\epsilon = i\,u\,e^{-ip\cdot x}$, since $\partial_\mu\epsilon = p_\mu u\,e^{-ip\cdot x}$. Then $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\psi_\rho =
\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\partial_\rho\epsilon = -\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}p_\nu p_\rho\epsilon = 0$ by antisymmetry (@prp-rarita-schwinger). Every such wave is pure
gauge: physical gravitino states are the solutions modulo these, which is what the counting of @exm-gravitino-dof
does.
:::

The field equation implies constraints that make the counting of the second example work. The third exercise
derives them in flat space.

::: {#exr-ssg-rs-constraints}
#### The constraints of the Rarita-Schwinger equation

In flat four-dimensional space, using $\gamma_\mu\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho} = 2\gamma^{\nu\rho}$ and the gauge freedom, show that the equation
$\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\psi_\rho = 0$ can be reduced to $\gamma^\mu\psi_\mu = 0$, $\partial^\mu\psi_\mu = 0$ and $\gamma^\nu\partial_\nu\psi_\mu = 0$. Count the
remaining components.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Contracting with $\gamma_\mu$ gives $\gamma^{\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\psi_\rho = 0$; with $\gamma^{\nu\rho} = \gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho - \eta^{\nu\rho}$ this is $\partial\!\!\!/(\gamma\cdot\psi) -
\partial\cdot\psi = 0$. A gauge transformation changes $\gamma\cdot\psi$ by $\partial\!\!\!/\epsilon$, so one can impose $\gamma\cdot\psi = 0$; then $\partial\cdot\psi = 0$,
and the original equation, using $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho} = \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho - \eta^{\mu\nu}\gamma^\rho + \eta^{\mu\rho}\gamma^\nu - \eta^{\nu\rho}\gamma^\mu$
(@exr-ssg-gamma3-expansion), reduces to $\partial\!\!\!/\psi^\mu = 0$. Of the $4 \times 4 = 16$ real components of a Majorana
vector-spinor, $\gamma\cdot\psi = 0$ removes $4$, the residual gauge freedom ($\partial\!\!\!/\epsilon = 0$) and $\partial\cdot\psi = 0$ remove $4 + 4$
more on-shell, leaving $4$, halved by the first-order equation to $2$: the helicities $\pm\tfrac32$.
:::
::::

The gauge invariance rests on a property of $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}$ that holds in any representation. The proposition states it
for the explicit matrices, where it can be checked entry by entry.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-rarita-schwinger}
#### Gauge invariance of the Rarita-Schwinger operator

$\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}$ is antisymmetric in $\nu\rho$, and for every symmetric $s_{\nu\rho}$ (the second derivatives
$\partial_\nu\partial_\rho\epsilon$ of a spinor) $\sum_{\nu\rho}\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}s_{\nu\rho} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Supergravity.gamma3_antisymm` and `KaluzaKlein.Supergravity.rarita_schwinger_gauge`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Supergravity.rarita_schwinger_gauge >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The antisymmetrised product is simple to evaluate on distinct indices. The first example records the values, and
the vanishing on repeated ones.

::: {#exm-ssg-gamma3-values}
#### Values of $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}$

For distinct indices the gamma matrices anticommute, so all six orderings agree up to sign and $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho} =
\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho$, for instance $\gamma^{012} = \gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2$; for two equal indices the antisymmetrisation gives $0$.
There are $\binom43 = 4$ independent matrices $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}$ in four dimensions.
:::

In four dimensions the three-index product is dual to a single gamma matrix times $\gamma^5$. The second example gives the
relation, which turns the Rarita-Schwinger Lagrangian into its frequently quoted form with $\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$.

::: {#exm-ssg-gamma3-dual}
#### Duality in four dimensions

With $\epsilon_{0123} = 1$ and $\gamma^5 = i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$, $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho} = -i\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\gamma_\sigma\gamma^5$
(@exr-ssg-gamma3-expansion), so the Rarita-Schwinger Lagrangian is $-\tfrac12\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\bar\psi_\mu\gamma_\sigma\gamma^5\partial_\nu\psi_\rho$
in flat space, and the proposition is the statement $\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\partial_\nu\partial_\rho = 0$.
:::

The third example compares with electromagnetism. The structure is the same, with $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}$ playing the role of the
antisymmetric combination in the field strength.

::: {#exm-ssg-gamma3-maxwell}
#### The analogy with Maxwell

The Maxwell equation $\partial_\nu F^{\nu\mu} = \partial_\nu\partial^\nu A^\mu - \partial^\mu\partial_\nu A^\nu$ is unchanged by $A_\mu \to A_\mu + \partial_\mu\alpha$ because the
symmetric $\partial_\nu\partial_\mu\alpha$ cancels; the Rarita-Schwinger equation is unchanged by $\psi_\mu \to \psi_\mu + \partial_\mu\epsilon$ because the
symmetric $\partial_\nu\partial_\rho\epsilon$ meets the antisymmetric $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}$. In both cases a massless gauge field of spin $s$ keeps only
the helicities $\pm s$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the expansion of a product of three gamma matrices and the duality of the second example.
Both are used repeatedly in supergravity computations.

::: {#exr-ssg-gamma3-expansion}
#### Expanding $\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho$

Verify $\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho = \gamma^{\mu\nu\rho} + \eta^{\mu\nu}\gamma^\rho - \eta^{\mu\rho}\gamma^\nu + \eta^{\nu\rho}\gamma^\mu$ for all indices, and find the
constant $c$ in $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho} = c\,\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\gamma_\sigma\gamma^5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The expansion holds for all $64$ index triples, and $c = -i$ with $\epsilon^{0123} = -1$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-gamma3-expansion >}}
:::

The proposition is about the field equation; the action is invariant too, up to a boundary term. The second
exercise shows this in flat space.

::: {#exr-ssg-rs-action}
#### Invariance of the flat-space action

Show that $S = -\tfrac{i}{2}\int\bar\psi_\mu\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\psi_\rho$ changes by a total derivative under $\delta\psi_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon$,
$\delta\bar\psi_\mu = \partial_\mu\bar\epsilon$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\delta S = -\tfrac{i}{2}\int(\partial_\mu\bar\epsilon\,\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\psi_\rho + \bar\psi_\mu\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\partial_\rho\epsilon)$. The second term vanishes by
the proposition. The first is $\partial_\mu(\bar\epsilon\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\nu\psi_\rho) - \bar\epsilon\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\psi_\rho$, and the last term
vanishes because $\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}$ is antisymmetric in $\mu\nu$ as well. So $\delta S$ is a boundary term. In curved space the
commutator $[D_\mu, D_\nu]$ is the curvature, and the variation no longer vanishes: this is where the metric must
transform too, $\delta e_\mu{}^a = -i\bar\epsilon\gamma^a\psi_\mu$ (@def-supergravity-multiplet).
:::

The third exercise applies the counting formula below four dimensions. In three dimensions the gravitino, like the
graviton, has no propagating states.

::: {#exr-ssg-rs-three}
#### Three dimensions

Evaluate the on-shell counts of the graviton and the gravitino in $d = 3$, and conclude that three-dimensional
supergravity has no propagating degrees of freedom.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The graviton has $\tfrac12(d - 2)(d - 1) - 1 = \tfrac12\cdot1\cdot2 - 1 = 0$ and the gravitino $\tfrac12(d - 3)2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor} = 0$.
Pure supergravity in three dimensions is a topological theory: its field equations make the curvature and the
gravitino field strength vanish, and the only content is global (holonomies), as for three-dimensional gravity.
:::
::::

#### The supergravity multiplet

The vierbein and the gravitino together form the multiplet of local supersymmetry in four dimensions. The definition
gives their action, the supersymmetric extension of the Einstein-Hilbert action, in our signature.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-supergravity-multiplet}
#### Supergravity multiplet

The **supergravity multiplet** of $N = 1$ in four dimensions is the pair $(e_\mu{}^a, \psi_\mu)$ of the vierbein and
the gravitino, the helicity states $(2, \tfrac32)$ and $(-\tfrac32, -2)$ of the massless superalgebra; its action is
$$
\mathcal{L} = -\tfrac14e\hat R - \tfrac{i}{2}e\bar\psi_\mu\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}\hat D_\nu\psi_\rho
$$ {#eq-sugra4}
in our signature $(+, -, -, -)$, which is that of @tanii1998 [eq. 2.2, with $4\pi G = 1$, so that $-\tfrac14e\hat R$ is
the Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian @eq-einstein-hilbert], invariant under
$\delta e_\mu{}^a = -i\bar\epsilon\gamma^a\psi_\mu$, $\delta\psi_\mu = \hat D_\mu\epsilon$ with the torsionful spin connection
$\hat\omega$ of eq. 2.5 there. For $N$-extended supersymmetry there are $N$ gravitini and further fields
[@tanii1998, Table 3].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest supergravity contains only these two fields. The first example records its content and its relation to
general relativity.

::: {#exm-sugra-multiplet-n1}
#### Pure $N = 1$ supergravity

Only $(e, \psi_\mu)$, $2 + 2$ on-shell degrees of freedom: the supersymmetric extension of the Einstein-Hilbert
action of @sec-einstein-hilbert, the vierbein $e_\mu{}^a$ replacing the metric because spinors need the frames of
@sec-coset-vielbeins.
:::

The extended supergravities contain more fields, up to the maximal $N = 8$. The second example gives the content of
the largest, which is the helicity ladder of @exm-ssg-ladders-n8.

::: {#exm-sugra-multiplet-extended}
#### Extended multiplets

$N = 8$ in four dimensions contains the graviton, $8$ gravitini, $28$ vectors, $56$ spin-$\tfrac12$ fields and $70$
scalars, $128 + 128$ states, and $N \geq 9$ would require helicities above $2$, for which no consistent interacting
theory is known [@tanii1998, Table 3 and p. 14]; the $70$ scalars parametrise the coset $E_{7(7)}/SU(8)$, a coset
space of the kind studied in @sec-coset-spaces [@tanii1998, Table 4].
:::

The vectors of an extended supergravity can gauge a group. The third example describes what this adds to the
Lagrangian.

::: {#exm-sugra-multiplet-gauged}
#### Gauged supergravity

When the vectors of an extended theory gauge a non-abelian group, the Lagrangian acquires a cosmological term
$\propto g^2$ and a gravitino mass term $\propto g\,\bar\psi_\mu\gamma^{\mu\nu}\psi_\nu$ [@tanii1998, p. 6]: the four-dimensional
theories obtained by sphere reductions in Part VI are of this type.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Off-shell the supergravity multiplet does not balance without auxiliary fields, as the chiral multiplet did not. The
first exercise counts the components and finds how many auxiliary fields are needed.

::: {#exr-ssg-sugra-offshell}
#### Off-shell counting

Count the off-shell components of $e_\mu{}^a$ modulo diffeomorphisms and local Lorentz transformations, and of the Majorana
$\psi_\mu$ modulo local supersymmetry. How many bosonic auxiliary components are needed?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e_\mu{}^a$ has $16$ components, minus $4$ diffeomorphisms and $6$ Lorentz rotations: $6$. $\psi_\mu$ has $4 \times 4 = 16$ real
components minus $4$ supersymmetry parameters: $12$. So $6$ bosonic auxiliary components are needed for $12 + 12$; the
minimal choice is a complex scalar and a real axial vector ($2 + 4$), the "old minimal" auxiliary fields. Without them
the algebra closes only on-shell (@exm-local-algebra), as in @exm-closure-counting.
:::

The content of all the extended supergravities follows from the helicity ladders of the first part. The second
exercise reads it off for each $N$ and compares with the table of @tanii1998.

::: {#exr-ssg-extended-content}
#### The extended multiplets

From the CPT-completed gravity ladders, list the numbers of gravitons, gravitini, vectors, spin-$\tfrac12$ fields and real
scalars for $N = 1, \dots, 6, 8$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A field of spin $s > 0$ accounts for helicities $\pm s$, a real scalar for one helicity-$0$ state:

{{< sage exr-ssg-extended-content >}}
:::

The scalars of the extended theories live on coset spaces. The third exercise checks the dimension of the coset of
$N = 8$ and its five-dimensional counterpart with Sage's Lie algebra data.

::: {#exr-ssg-e7-coset}
#### The scalar coset of $N = 8$

Check that $\dim E_7 - \dim SU(8) = 70$ and $\dim E_6 - \dim USp(8) = 42$, and find the smallest representation of $E_7$. Why is it
the right size for the vectors?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$133 - 63 = 70$ and $78 - 36 = 42$, the scalars of $N = 8$ supergravity in four and five dimensions. The smallest
representation of $E_7$ is the $56$, which under $SU(8)$ is $28 \oplus \overline{28}$: the $28$ vectors with their magnetic duals,
which $E_{7(7)}$ rotates into each other (an electric-magnetic duality symmetry of the field equations):

{{< sage exr-ssg-e7-coset >}}
:::
::::

When supersymmetry is spontaneously broken in a supergravity, the massless goldstino does not survive: it becomes
part of the gravitino, as a Goldstone boson becomes part of a massive vector. The definition names this mechanism.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-super-higgs}
#### Super-Higgs mechanism

When supersymmetry is spontaneously broken in a supergravity, the gravitino acquires a mass by absorbing the
goldstino of @def-susy-breaking as its helicity-$\pm\tfrac12$ states, the **super-Higgs mechanism**; the massive
gravitino has four helicity states and a mass $m_{3/2} \sim \langle F\rangle/M_P$ for F-term breaking [@martin1997, Sec.
7.5], the fermionic analogue of @def-higgs-mechanism.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The number of states must be the same before and after. The first example checks this, as for the ordinary Higgs
mechanism.

::: {#exm-super-higgs-counting}
#### Counting states

Massless: gravitino $2$ plus goldstino $2$; massive: gravitino $4$. The count matches as in the Higgs mechanism
($2 + 1 = 3$ for the vector), with the goldstino becoming the longitudinal helicities.
:::

The gravitino mass depends on two scales. The second example examines its limits and the resulting orders of
magnitude in the usual scenarios.

::: {#exm-super-higgs-scale}
#### The gravitino mass scale

$m_{3/2}$ vanishes both as $\langle F\rangle \to 0$ (supersymmetry restored) and as $M_P \to \infty$ (gravity off); in
gravity-mediated models it is comparable to the superpartner masses, in gauge-mediated ones much smaller
[@martin1997, eq. 7.5.4].
:::

Supersymmetry can also be broken by the geometry of extra dimensions. The third example notes this possibility,
which is the subject of later parts.

::: {#exm-super-higgs-reduction}
#### Breaking by reduction

Compactifications that preserve no Killing spinor (@def-supercharge-counting) break supersymmetry spontaneously
and give the gravitino a mass of order the inverse internal radius: the Scherk-Schwarz mechanism and the
supersymmetry breaking by coset reduction of @manousselis2000 in Part V.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise counts the states of a massive particle of spin three halves. It confirms that two helicities are
missing in the massless gravitino, which the goldstino provides.

::: {#exr-ssg-super-higgs-states}
#### A massive spin-$\tfrac32$ particle

How many states does a massive particle of spin $\tfrac32$ have? Which helicities does the massless gravitino lack, and which
massless field provides them? Compare with the massive vector.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A massive particle of spin $j$ has $2j + 1$ states: $4$ for $j = \tfrac32$, with $J_z = \pm\tfrac32, \pm\tfrac12$. The massless gravitino has only the
helicities $\pm\tfrac32$; the goldstino, a massless Weyl fermion, provides $\pm\tfrac12$. Likewise a massive vector has $3$ states, two
from the massless vector and one from the Goldstone scalar.
:::

The gravitino mass sets the scale at which gravitational effects of supersymmetry breaking appear. The second
exercise evaluates it for typical breaking scales with the reduced Planck mass.

::: {#exr-ssg-gravitino-mass-scale}
#### Numbers

With $m_{3/2} = \langle F\rangle/(\sqrt3M_P)$ and $M_P = 2.4 \times 10^{18}$ GeV, compute $m_{3/2}$ for $\sqrt{\langle F\rangle} = 10^5$ GeV and $10^{11}$ GeV.
In the O'Raifeartaigh model, express the vacuum energy $k^2$ in terms of $m_{3/2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sqrt F = 10^5$ GeV gives $m_{3/2} \approx 2.4$ eV (gauge mediation, a very light gravitino); $\sqrt F = 10^{11}$ GeV gives $\approx 2.4$ TeV
(gravity mediation). With $F = k$, $V = k^2 = 3m_{3/2}^2M_P^2$, the term that the supergravity potential $V = |F|^2 -
3|W|^2/M_P^2$ can cancel by a constant in $W$ [@martin1997, eqs. 7.5.4-7.5.6]:

{{< sage exr-ssg-gravitino-mass-scale >}}
:::

In supergravity the vacuum energy is not the order parameter of supersymmetry breaking any more. The third exercise
explains why, from the form of the supergravity potential.

::: {#exr-ssg-super-higgs-cosmological}
#### Breaking with zero vacuum energy

The F-term potential of supergravity is $V = |F|^2 - 3|W|^2/M_P^2$ (in the simplest case). Explain why supersymmetry can be
broken with $V = 0$, contrary to the global criterion of @def-susy-breaking, and what the constant term of $W$ does.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In global supersymmetry $H = \tfrac14\sum\{Q, Q^\dagger\} \geq 0$ makes $V > 0$ the signal of breaking. In supergravity the
algebra is local and the energy includes gravity; the potential acquires the negative term $-3|W|^2/M_P^2$, so a
vacuum with $F \neq 0$ (broken) can have $V = 0$ if $|W| = |F|M_P/\sqrt3$. A constant added to $W$, irrelevant in global
supersymmetry (@exr-ssg-fterm-nonneg), now matters: it sets the gravitino mass $m_{3/2} = |W|/M_P^2$ and can cancel the
positive vacuum energy, giving flat space with broken supersymmetry; the breaking is then signalled by $m_{3/2} \neq 0$
[@martin1997, Sec. 7.5].
:::

The gravitino couples to the other fields with the gravitational strength $1/M_P$, so it decays slowly. The fourth
exercise estimates its lifetime and the bound that the history of the early universe places on its mass
[@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 18.4].

::: {#exr-ssg-gravitino-lifetime}
#### The gravitino lifetime

The decay rate of a gravitino into a photon and a light photino is $\Gamma = m_{3/2}^3/(4M_P^2)$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq.
18.91, neglecting the photino mass]. With $M_P = 2.4 \times 10^{18}$ GeV and $\hbar = 6.58 \times 10^{-25}$ GeV s, find the lifetime for
$m_{3/2} = 1$ TeV, and the mass above which the gravitino decays before $0.1$ s, so that it does not disturb the
nucleosynthesis of light elements.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Gamma = 10^9/(4 \times 5.76 \times 10^{36})$ GeV $= 4.3 \times 10^{-29}$ GeV, so $\tau = \hbar/\Gamma = 1.5 \times 10^4$ s, deep in the epoch of
nucleosynthesis (about $1$ to $10^3$ s). Since $\tau \propto m_{3/2}^{-3}$, $\tau < 0.1$ s requires $m_{3/2} > 1\text{ TeV} \times (1.5 \times
10^5)^{1/3} \approx 53$ TeV. With the non-reduced Planck mass the lifetime is larger by $(1.22/0.24)^2 \approx 26$, and the bound
rises to about $150$ TeV, the order of magnitude, $100$ TeV, quoted by Nath: an unstable gravitino must be much heavier
than the electroweak scale.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

#### The supergravity scalar potential

When chiral multiplets are coupled to supergravity, their kinetic terms are no longer fixed to the canonical form
and their potential is no longer the sum of squares of @prp-f-term. The couplings are encoded in two functions, the
superpotential and a real function of the scalars that plays the role of a potential for the metric of field space;
this subsection defines that function and states the resulting potential [@nath2017supersymmetry, Ch. 12].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-ssg-kahler-potential}
#### Kähler potential

A **Kähler potential** is a real function $K(\phi, \phi^*)$ of the complex scalars $\phi^i$ whose matrix of mixed second derivatives
$K_{i\bar\jmath} = \partial^2K/\partial\phi^i\partial\phi^{*j}$ is positive definite; it fixes the scalar kinetic term $K_{i\bar\jmath}\,
\partial_\mu\phi^i\partial^\mu\phi^{*j}$, so that $K_{i\bar\jmath}$ is the metric of the space of scalar fields. A **Kähler transformation**
$K \to K + f(\phi) + f^*(\phi^*)$ with $f$ holomorphic leaves $K_{i\bar\jmath}$ unchanged; in supergravity, in units $M_P = 1$, it is
accompanied by $W \to e^{-f}W$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 12.5-12.9 and 12.15-12.16, where $K$ is normalised with
additional factors of $\kappa$].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The globally supersymmetric theories of the first part of the chapter have the simplest Kähler potential. The first
example identifies it and shows that it reproduces the kinetic terms used so far.

::: {#exm-ssg-kahler-canonical}
#### The canonical Kähler potential

$K = \sum_i\phi^{*i}\phi^i$ has $K_{i\bar\jmath} = \delta_{ij}$ and gives the kinetic term $\partial_\mu\phi^i\partial^\mu\phi^{*i}$ of @eq-wz-free: field space is
flat $\mathbb{C}^n$. It is the $\theta\theta\,\theta^\dagger\theta^\dagger$ component of $\sum\Phi^{\dagger i}\Phi^i$ (@exm-ssg-kahler-term), and a general $K$ is
the top component of a general real function of the superfields.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

String and higher-dimensional theories produce Kähler potentials with logarithms, whose field spaces are curved. The
second example gives the one that governs the volume of a compact space and recognises its field space as a coset.

::: {#exm-ssg-kahler-no-scale}
#### The no-scale Kähler potential

For one field $T$, $K = -3\log(T + T^*)$ has $K_{T\bar T} = 3/(T + T^*)^2$. With $T = x + iy$, $x > 0$, the field-space metric is
$\tfrac{3}{4x^2}(dx^2 + dy^2)$, the upper half-plane with constant negative curvature (@exr-ssg-kahler-curvature), which is the coset
$SL(2, \mathbb{R})/SO(2)$, a small relative of the scalar manifold $E_{7(7)}/SU(8)$ of @exr-ssg-e7-coset. In reductions $x$ measures
the volume of the compact space and $y$ comes from a form field [@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 18.4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A Kähler transformation changes $K$ without changing the metric. The third example shows that in global supersymmetry
it is invisible, while in supergravity it must act on the superpotential as well.

::: {#exm-ssg-kahler-shift}
#### A Kähler transformation

$K = |\phi|^2 + a\phi + a^*\phi^*$ differs from the canonical potential by the Kähler transformation with $f = a\phi$, and gives the same
kinetic term. In supergravity $K$ also enters $D_iW = W_i + K_iW$ and the factor $e^K$ of @prp-ssg-sugra-potential, and the change
$e^{K} \to e^{K}|e^{a\phi}|^2$ is compensated by $W \to e^{-a\phi}W$: only the combination $G = K + \log|W|^2$ is physical.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The curvature of the no-scale field space is computed from the metric with Sage's differential geometry. The first
exercise finds it and its dependence on the coefficient of the logarithm.

::: {#exr-ssg-kahler-curvature}
#### The curvature of the no-scale field space

Compute the Gaussian curvature (@def-gauss-curvature) of the metric $K_{T\bar T}(dx^2 + dy^2)$ for $K = -n\log(T + T^*)$, $n = 1, 2, 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The metric is $\tfrac{n}{4x^2}(dx^2 + dy^2)$, the Poincaré half-plane metric $\tfrac{1}{x^2}(dx^2 + dy^2)$ of curvature $-1$ scaled by
$\tfrac n4$, so the curvature is $-4/n$; for the no-scale value $n = 3$ it is $-\tfrac43$. The coefficient of the logarithm is therefore a
geometric invariant of field space.

{{< sage exr-ssg-kahler-curvature >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The physical content of supergravity couplings depends only on the combination $G$. The second exercise proves its
invariance and that of the metric.

::: {#exr-ssg-kahler-g-invariance}
#### The invariant function $G$

Show that $K_{i\bar\jmath}$, $G = K + \log|W|^2$ and the gravitino mass $m_{3/2} = e^{K/2}|W|$ are invariant under $K \to K + f + f^*$,
$W \to e^{-f}W$, and that $D_iW = W_i + K_iW$ transforms as $D_iW \to e^{-f}D_iW$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_i\partial_{\bar\jmath}(f + f^*) = 0$ since $f$ is holomorphic and $f^*$ antiholomorphic. $\log|e^{-f}W|^2 = \log|W|^2 - f - f^*$
cancels the shift of $K$, so $G$ and $e^{G/2} = e^{K/2}|W| = m_{3/2}$ are invariant. Finally $\partial_i(e^{-f}W) + (K_i + f_i)e^{-f}W =
e^{-f}(W_i - f_iW + K_iW + f_iW) = e^{-f}D_iW$: $D_iW$ is covariant, and $e^K|D_iW|^2$ is invariant
[@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 12.15-12.16].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

String compactifications typically produce a Kähler potential with one logarithm for the dilaton and one for the
volume. The third exercise computes its field space.

::: {#exr-ssg-kahler-two-moduli}
#### The dilaton and the volume

For $K = -\log(S + S^*) - 3\log(T + T^*)$ find $K_{i\bar\jmath}$ and the curvatures of the two factors of field space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$K$ is a sum of a function of $S$ and a function of $T$, so $K_{S\bar T} = 0$, $K_{S\bar S} = 1/(S + S^*)^2$ and $K_{T\bar T} = 3/(T + T^*)^2$:
field space is the product of two half-planes, $SL(2, \mathbb{R})/SO(2) \times SL(2, \mathbb{R})/SO(2)$, with curvatures $-4$ and $-\tfrac43$
by @exr-ssg-kahler-curvature.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

With the Kähler potential and the superpotential in hand, the potential of supergravity coupled to chiral multiplets
can be stated. It is no longer a sum of squares: a negative term proportional to $|W|^2$ appears, the gravitational
counterpart of the positive energy of global supersymmetry.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-ssg-sugra-potential}
#### The supergravity scalar potential

In units $M_P = 1$, the F-term potential of chiral multiplets coupled to supergravity is
$$
V = e^K\left(K^{i\bar\jmath}D_iW\,\overline{D_jW} - 3|W|^2\right), \qquad D_iW = \partial_iW + K_iW,
$$ {#eq-ssg-sugra-potential}
with $K^{i\bar\jmath}$ the inverse of $K_{i\bar\jmath}$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 12.12-12.14]. It equals $e^G(G^{i\bar\jmath}G_iG_{\bar\jmath} -
3)$ with $G = K + \log|W|^2$, and it is invariant under Kähler transformations. Supersymmetry is unbroken exactly where all
$D_iW = 0$, and there $V = -3e^K|W|^2 \leq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest supersymmetric vacuum of supergravity has negative energy. The first example finds it for a constant
superpotential and relates it to the anti-de Sitter space of @exm-freund-rubin-s7.

::: {#exm-ssg-sugra-ads}
#### A constant superpotential

For $K = |\phi|^2$ and $W = W_0$, $D_\phi W = \phi^*W_0$ vanishes at $\phi = 0$, where $V = -3|W_0|^2$: an unbroken supersymmetric vacuum with a
negative cosmological constant, anti-de Sitter space, and a gravitino mass $m_{3/2} = |W_0|$ that does not break supersymmetry. In
global supersymmetry a supersymmetric vacuum has $V = 0$ (@exm-superalgebra-energy); with gravity the bound becomes $V \geq
-3m_{3/2}^2$, and anti-de Sitter supersymmetry is compatible with negative energy.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Supersymmetry can also be broken with zero vacuum energy, as the super-Higgs mechanism requires. The second example
is the classic model of this kind, with one field and a linear superpotential.

::: {#exm-ssg-polonyi}
#### The Polonyi model

$K = |\phi|^2$, $W = \mu(\phi + \beta)$ with $\beta = 2 - \sqrt3$ has a minimum at $\phi = \sqrt3 - 1$ with $V = 0$, where $D_\phi W = \sqrt3\mu \neq 0$
(@exr-ssg-polonyi): supersymmetry is broken, $|D_\phi W|^2 = 3|W|^2$ cancels the negative term, and the gravitino eats the
fermion of the multiplet (@def-super-higgs) to acquire $m_{3/2} = e^{2 - \sqrt3}\mu$. The constant $\beta$ is tuned to make the
cosmological constant vanish, the price of this mechanism.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The supergravity potential must reduce to the global one when gravity decouples. The third example restores the
Planck mass and takes the limit.

::: {#exm-ssg-sugra-global-limit}
#### The limit $M_P \to \infty$

With $M_P$ restored, $V = e^{K/M_P^2}(K^{i\bar\jmath}D_iW\overline{D_jW} - 3|W|^2/M_P^2)$ and $D_iW = W_i + K_iW/M_P^2$. For fixed fields and
couplings, as $M_P \to \infty$ the exponential tends to $1$, $D_iW \to W_i$ and the negative term disappears, leaving
$K^{i\bar\jmath}W_i\overline{W_j}$, which for the canonical $K$ is the F-term potential $\sum|W_i|^2$ of @def-f-term-potential.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A potential that vanishes identically, whatever the values of the fields, is the defining property of no-scale
supergravity. The first exercise establishes it for the no-scale Kähler potential and a constant superpotential,
@nath2017supersymmetry [Problem 12.1] in our normalisation.

::: {#exr-ssg-no-scale}
#### No-scale supergravity

For $K = -n\log(T + T^*)$ and $W = W_0$ compute $D_TW$ and $V$ with Sage, and show that $V \equiv 0$ for $n = 3$ although supersymmetry is
broken.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$K_T = -n/(T + T^*)$, $K_{T\bar T} = n/(T + T^*)^2$, $D_TW = -nW_0/(T + T^*)$, so $K^{T\bar T}|D_TW|^2 = n|W_0|^2$ and $V = e^K(n - 3)|W_0|^2 =
(n - 3)|W_0|^2/(T + T^*)^n$. For $n = 3$ the potential vanishes for every $T$, while $D_TW \neq 0$ breaks supersymmetry with
$m_{3/2} = |W_0|/(T + T^*)^{3/2}$: the scale of breaking is set by the undetermined value of $T$, hence the name.

{{< sage exr-ssg-no-scale >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Polonyi example asserts a minimum with vanishing energy. The second exercise checks it, including the positivity
of the second derivatives that makes it a minimum.

::: {#exr-ssg-polonyi}
#### The Polonyi minimum

For $K = |\phi|^2$, $W = \mu(\phi + \beta)$, $\beta = 2 - \sqrt3$, write $V$ along real $\phi = x$, check with Sage that $x = \sqrt3 - 1$ is a critical point
of $V(x + iy)$ with $V = 0$ and positive Hessian, and compute $D_\phi W$ and $m_{3/2}$ there.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$D_\phi W = \mu + \phi^*\mu(\phi + \beta)$, so along real $\phi$, $V = \mu^2e^{x^2}[(1 + x(x + \beta))^2 - 3(x + \beta)^2]$. At $x = \sqrt3 - 1$,
$x + \beta = 1$ and $1 + x = \sqrt3$, so the bracket is $3 - 3 = 0$. The gradient vanishes and the Hessian eigenvalues are $1.83\mu^2$
and $11.84\mu^2$, so it is a minimum; $D_\phi W = \sqrt3\mu$ and $m_{3/2} = e^{x^2/2}\mu = e^{2 - \sqrt3}\mu \approx 1.31\mu$.

{{< sage exr-ssg-polonyi >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The two forms of the potential in the proposition and its value at supersymmetric points are short computations. The
third exercise carries them out.

::: {#exr-ssg-sugra-g-form}
#### The potential in terms of $G$

Show that $V$ of @eq-ssg-sugra-potential equals $e^G(G^{i\bar\jmath}G_iG_{\bar\jmath} - 3)$, deduce its Kähler invariance from
@exr-ssg-kahler-g-invariance, and show that $V \leq 0$ at a supersymmetric point.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$G_i = K_i + W_i/W$ and $G_{i\bar\jmath} = K_{i\bar\jmath}$, since $\log W$ is holomorphic. Then $WG_i = D_iW$, so $e^G G^{i\bar\jmath}G_iG_{\bar\jmath} =
e^K|W|^2K^{i\bar\jmath}\frac{D_iW\,\overline{D_jW}}{|W|^2} = e^KK^{i\bar\jmath}D_iW\overline{D_jW}$ and $3e^G = 3e^K|W|^2$. Since $G$ is
invariant, so is $V$. Where all $D_iW = 0$ the first term vanishes and $V = -3e^K|W|^2 \leq 0$, zero only if $W = 0$ there; in
supergravity, unlike @exm-superalgebra-energy, positive energy is not the criterion of supersymmetry breaking, $D_iW \neq 0$ is.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Eleven-dimensional supergravity {#sec-sugra11}

The largest dimension in which a supergravity exists is eleven, and the theory there is unique: a graviton, a
gravitino and a three-form potential. It is the starting point of the supergravity compactifications surveyed in
Part VI, and its simplest compactification, on a round seven-sphere with flux, is the Freund-Rubin solution.
This section displays the action and transformation rules from @tanii1998 [Sec. 5], defines the Freund-Rubin
ansatz following @duff2025, and proves the Levi-Civita identities from which the curvatures of the
solution follow.

#### Maximal supergravity

The bound on the number of supercharges comes from the helicity ladders: with more than $32$ real supercharges every
massless multiplet contains helicities above $2$. Combined with the size of the smallest spinor in each dimension,
this singles out eleven dimensions.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-maximal-supergravity}
#### Maximal supergravity

A supergravity is **maximal** if it has $32$ real supercharges, the largest number for which all massless
multiplets have helicities at most $2$; since a Majorana spinor in $d$ dimensions has at least $2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$
real components (@prp-spinor-dimensions), $32$ supercharges fit in a single spinor only for $d \leq 11$, and the
**eleven-dimensional supergravity** of Cremmer, Julia and Scherk is the unique $d = 11$, $N = 1$ theory
[@tanii1998, pp. 14-16].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The field content of the eleven-dimensional theory is fixed by the multiplet. The first example lists it with the
number of on-shell states of each field.

::: {#exm-maximal-eleven}
#### The eleven-dimensional multiplet

The vielbein $e_\mu{}^a$ ($44$ on-shell degrees of freedom), the Majorana gravitino $\psi_\mu$ ($128$) and the three-form
$B_{\mu\nu\rho}$ ($84$): $44 + 84 = 128$ bosons and $128$ fermions (@fig-sugra11-dof, @prp-sugra11-dof).
:::

Reducing on a torus does not change the number of supercharges. The second example names the four-dimensional theory
that results from seven circles.

::: {#exm-maximal-four}
#### $N = 8$ in four dimensions

Reducing on a seven-torus gives the $N = 8$ multiplet of @exm-sugra-multiplet-extended with $128 + 128$ states, the
same count in every dimension from eleven down to four [@tanii1998, Table 3] (@exr-dof-11d).
:::

Reducing on a single circle gives a ten-dimensional theory. The third example identifies it with one of the two
maximal supergravities in ten dimensions.

::: {#exm-maximal-ten}
#### Type IIA

Reducing on a circle gives the $(1, 1)$ supergravity of ten dimensions, with two Majorana-Weyl gravitini of
opposite chirality, the massless sector of the type IIA superstring; the chiral $(2, 0)$ theory of type IIB is
not a reduction of the eleven-dimensional theory [@tanii1998, p. 17].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise combines the two bounds that define maximal supergravity. It is a short argument, but it is the
reason why eleven dimensions appear at all.

::: {#exr-ssg-max-dimension}
#### Why eleven

Using @prp-ssg-massless-multiplets and @prp-spinor-dimensions, explain why there is no supergravity with helicities at most
$2$ in $d \geq 12$ (in signature with one time).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Reduced to four dimensions on a torus, a theory with $\mathcal{N}$ real supercharges becomes an $N = \mathcal{N}/4$ theory, whose
massless ladders span $N/2 = \mathcal{N}/8$ units of helicity; helicities at most $2$ require a span of at most $4$, so
$\mathcal{N} \leq 32$. In $d = 12$ the smallest spinor has $64$ real components (@exm-ssg-spinor-eleven), so even one supercharge
exceeds the bound; eleven is the largest dimension where a single spinor has $32$ components.
:::

The light-cone count uses the little group of a massless particle. The second exercise identifies the eleven-dimensional
fields as representations of $SO(9)$ and checks their dimensions.

::: {#exr-ssg-so9-little-group}
#### The little group $SO(9)$

Identify the graviton, the three-form and the gravitino as representations of $SO(9)$, compute their dimensions with the
Weyl character ring of $B_4$, and show that the vector-spinor decomposes as gravitino plus spinor.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The graviton is the symmetric traceless tensor ($44$), the three-form the third exterior power of the vector ($84$), the
gravitino the gamma-traceless vector-spinor ($9 \times 16 - 16 = 128$); $\mathbf 9 \otimes \mathbf{16} = \mathbf{128} \oplus \mathbf{16}$, the
$\mathbf{16}$ being the gamma trace:

{{< sage exr-ssg-so9-little-group >}}
:::

The reduction to four dimensions preserves the counting at every step. The third exercise follows it through all the
intermediate dimensions.

::: {#exr-ssg-dof-reduction-chain}
#### Reduction on $T^n$, step by step

Reduce the bosonic fields on $T^n$ for $n = 0, \dots, 7$, list the fields in $d = 11 - n$ dimensions, and count their on-shell
states.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The metric gives a $d$-metric, $n$ vectors and $\tfrac12n(n + 1)$ scalars; the three-form gives a three-form, $n$ two-forms,
$\binom n2$ vectors and $\binom n3$ scalars. The total is $128$ in every dimension; in $d = 4$ the seven two-forms are dual to
scalars and the three-form carries no state, giving $28$ vectors and $70$ scalars:

{{< sage exr-ssg-dof-reduction-chain >}}
:::
::::

The boson-fermion balance of the eleven-dimensional multiplet, and of its four-dimensional reduction, is the content
of the proposition. It follows from the light-cone counting of the transverse components of each field.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sugra11-dof}
#### Degrees of freedom

$44 + 84 = 128$ bosonic and $128$ fermionic on-shell degrees of freedom in eleven dimensions, and $2 + 56 + 70 = 128$,
$16 + 112 = 128$ for $N = 8$ in four (@exr-dof-11d).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![Physical degrees of freedom of eleven-dimensional supergravity and of its $N = 8$ reduction to four dimensions,
counted with the light-cone formulas: the graviton $\tfrac12(d - 2)(d - 1) - 1$, a $p$-form $\binom{d - 2}{p}$, a
Majorana gravitino $\tfrac12(d - 3)2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$, a Majorana spin-$\tfrac12$ field $\tfrac12 2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$. In
both dimensions $128 + 128$. Generated by `figures/sugra11_dof.sage`.](figures/sugra11_dof.svg){#fig-sugra11-dof width=75%}

The first example evaluates the light-cone formulas in eleven dimensions. Each count is the dimension of a
representation of the little group.

::: {#exm-ssg-dof-eleven}
#### Eleven dimensions

Graviton: $\tfrac12\cdot9\cdot10 - 1 = 44$; three-form: $\binom93 = 84$; gravitino: $\tfrac12\cdot8\cdot32 = 128$. Bosons $44 + 84 = 128$
equal the fermions, as @def-supermultiplet requires and @exr-ssg-so9-little-group confirms representation-theoretically.
:::

In four dimensions the count is that of the $N = 8$ ladder. The second example reads it in terms of fields.

::: {#exm-ssg-dof-four}
#### Four dimensions

Bosons: graviton $2$, $28$ vectors $\times 2 = 56$, $70$ scalars: $128$. Fermions: $8$ gravitini $\times 2 = 16$, $56$ Majorana spinors
$\times 2 = 112$: $128$ (@exm-ssg-ladders-n8, @fig-sugra11-dof).
:::

Ten dimensions has two maximal theories, both with $32$ supercharges. The third example counts the one obtained from
eleven dimensions on a circle.

::: {#exm-ssg-dof-iia}
#### Type IIA in ten dimensions

Bosons: graviton $35$, three-form $\binom83 = 56$, two-form $28$, vector $8$, scalar $1$: $128$. Fermions: two Majorana-Weyl
gravitini of $\tfrac12\cdot7\cdot32/2 = 56$ each and two Majorana-Weyl spin-$\tfrac12$ fields of $8$ each: $128$ (@exr-dof-11d).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise performs the counting in several dimensions with the light-cone formulas. It is the computation
behind the proposition and the figure.

::: {#exr-dof-11d}
#### Degrees of freedom in $d = 11, 10, 5, 4$

Count the physical degrees of freedom of the maximal supergravity multiplets with the light-cone formulas and
check the boson-fermion matching.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-dof-11d >}}
:::

The other maximal theory in ten dimensions is chiral. The second exercise counts its fields, including a four-form with
a self-dual field strength.

::: {#exr-ssg-dof-iib}
#### Type IIB

The type IIB multiplet contains the graviton, two scalars, two two-forms, a four-form with self-dual field strength,
two Majorana-Weyl gravitini of the same chirality and two Majorana-Weyl spin-$\tfrac12$ fields of the other. Count the
states.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Graviton $35$, scalars $2$, two-forms $2 \times 28 = 56$, four-form $\tfrac12\binom84 = 35$ (self-duality halves the $70$): $128$.
Gravitini $2 \times 56 = 112$, spin-$\tfrac12$ $2 \times 8 = 16$: $128$. The same totals as IIA, with a different, chiral field content
that cannot come from eleven dimensions on a circle [@tanii1998, Sec. 4].
:::

The fermions of the four-dimensional theory come from the eleven-dimensional gravitino. The third exercise traces
them, splitting the vector index and the spinor index.

::: {#exr-ssg-fermions-from-eleven}
#### The four-dimensional fermions

Split the eleven-dimensional gravitino $\psi_M$ into $\psi_\mu$ and $\psi_m$ on $M_4 \times T^7$, and its $32$-component spinor index into
four-dimensional spinors. How many four-dimensional gravitini and spin-$\tfrac12$ fields result?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $32$ real components of the eleven-dimensional Majorana spinor form $8$ four-dimensional Majorana spinors of $4$
components ($32 = 4 \times 8$, the $8$ being a spinor of the internal $SO(7)$). So $\psi_\mu$ gives $8$ gravitini and the seven $\psi_m$
give $7 \times 8 = 56$ spin-$\tfrac12$ fields (after a field redefinition removing the gamma trace from $\psi_\mu$), as in
@exm-ssg-dof-four. The eight gravitini are the $N = 8$ of the reduced theory (@exr-ssg-sugra-11-to-4).
:::

Ten-dimensional supergravity also exists with half the maximal supersymmetry, and then it can be coupled to gauge fields,
as in the low-energy limit of the heterotic string. The fourth exercise counts its states and those of its gauge sector
[@nath2017supersymmetry, Secs. 18.2.3-18.2.5].

::: {#exr-ssg-heterotic-count}
#### Ten-dimensional supergravity with gauge fields

The $N = 1$ supergravity multiplet in ten dimensions contains the graviton, a two-form $B_{\mu\nu}$, a scalar, a Majorana-Weyl
gravitino and a Majorana-Weyl spinor; a gauge multiplet contains a vector and a Majorana-Weyl gaugino. Count the states of
each with the little group $SO(8)$, and the states of the gauge sector when the gauge group is $SO(32)$ or $E_8 \times E_8$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Graviton $35$, two-form $\binom82 = 28$, scalar $1$: $64$ bosonic states; gravitino $56$ and spinor $8$: $64$ fermionic, half of the
$128 + 128$ of @prp-sugra11-dof. A gauge multiplet has $8 + 8$ states. $\dim SO(32) = \tfrac{32 \cdot 31}{2} = 496$ and $\dim E_8 = 248$, so
both groups have dimension $496$ and the gauge sector has $496 \times 8$ bosonic and as many fermionic states
[@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 18.2.3]. The equality of dimensions is not a coincidence: the cancellation of the gauge and
gravitational anomalies by the Green-Schwarz mechanism requires $\dim G = 496$ together with conditions on the traces, and
$SO(32)$ and $E_8 \times E_8$ satisfy them [@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 18.2.5].
:::

#### The action

The eleven-dimensional theory has a remarkably short action. Besides the kinetic terms of the three fields it
contains a Pauli coupling of the gravitino to the flux and a Chern-Simons term cubic in the three-form; the
definition displays it in our signature.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sugra11-action}
#### Eleven-dimensional supergravity action

In our signature $(+, -, \dots, -)$, which is that of @tanii1998 [eq. 5.1, with $4\pi G = 1$], and with $F_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} =
4\partial_{[\mu}B_{\nu\rho\sigma]}$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L} = {} & -\tfrac14eR - \tfrac{i}{2}e\bar\psi_\mu\gamma^{\mu\nu\rho}D_\nu\psi_\rho - \tfrac{1}{48}eF_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} \\
& + \tfrac{1}{96}e\left(\bar\psi_\mu\gamma^{\mu\nu\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\psi_\nu + 12\bar\psi^\alpha\gamma^{\beta\gamma}\psi^\delta\right)F_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}
+ \tfrac{2}{144^2}\epsilon^{\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_4\beta_1\cdots\beta_4\mu\nu\rho}F_{\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_4}F_{\beta_1\cdots\beta_4}B_{\mu\nu\rho}
+ (\text{4-fermi terms}),
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-sugra11}
the Einstein-Hilbert, Rarita-Schwinger and Maxwell-type terms, the Pauli coupling of the gravitino to the flux,
and the **Chern-Simons term** $F \wedge F \wedge B$. It is *displayed and cited*, not derived (@prp-sugra11-text).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The bosonic part of the action is what the Freund-Rubin solution solves. The first example gives it with its field
equations, and records the sign change from the mostly-plus metric.

::: {#exm-sugra11-bosonic}
#### The bosonic action

Dropping the fermions, $\mathcal{L} = -\tfrac14eR - \tfrac{1}{48}eF^2 + \tfrac{2}{144^2}\epsilon FFB$: gravity coupled to a
three-form, the Lagrangian whose field equations $R_{MN} - \tfrac12g_{MN}R = -\tfrac13(F_{MPQR}F_N{}^{PQR} -
\tfrac18g_{MN}F^2)$ are solved by the Freund-Rubin ansatz. @duff2025 [eq. 7] writes the right side with the opposite
sign in the mostly-plus metric: under $g_{MN} \to -g_{MN}$ the left side is unchanged while $F_{MPQR}F_N{}^{PQR}$ (three
inverse metrics) and $g_{MN}F^2$ both change sign (@sec-conventions-indices).
:::

The three-form has a gauge symmetry, as the Maxwell field does. The second example states it and checks that the
Chern-Simons term respects it.

::: {#exm-sugra11-gauge}
#### The gauge symmetry of the three-form

$\delta B_{\mu\nu\rho} = 3\partial_{[\mu}\Lambda_{\nu\rho]}$ leaves $F$ invariant [@tanii1998, eq. 5.3], the three-form analogue
of @def-gauge-field-u1; the Chern-Simons term changes by a total derivative, as $F \wedge F$ is closed
(@def-exterior-derivative).
:::

The fields of the action reduce to the fields of four-dimensional $N = 8$ supergravity. The third example lists the
bosons that come from each.

::: {#exm-sugra11-reduction}
#### Reduction of the fields

On $M_4 \times T^7$ the metric gives $7$ vectors and $28$ scalars, the three-form $7$ two-forms (dual to scalars),
$21$ vectors and $35$ scalars: $28$ vectors and $70$ scalars in all, the $N = 8$ content (@exr-dof-11d), each
counted by the branching rules of @sec-branching.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Chern-Simons term is special to eleven dimensions in this form. The first exercise checks that the index count
works and that the term needs no metric.

::: {#exr-ssg-cs-term}
#### The Chern-Simons term

Count the indices of $\epsilon^{\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_4\beta_1\cdots\beta_4\mu\nu\rho}F_{\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_4}F_{\beta_1\cdots\beta_4}B_{\mu\nu\rho}$, show that it is the component form of $F
\wedge F \wedge B$ (with $\epsilon$ the Levi-Civita symbol, a density), and explain why it is independent of the metric and of the
signature convention.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$4 + 4 + 3 = 11$ indices, all contracted with the eleven-index symbol, which is what $F \wedge F \wedge B$ is in components, an
eleven-form integrated over the eleven-dimensional manifold. The symbol $\epsilon^{\alpha_1\cdots}$ with entries $0, \pm1$ is a density and
needs no $e$ in front; no metric appears, so the term is topological in the sense of @def-exterior-derivative and does
not change under $g \to -g$, which is why it has the same form in both signatures.
:::

Every term of the bosonic action scales in the same way under a rescaling of the metric and the three-form. The
second exercise checks this, which is a useful test of the relative powers of fields in the action.

::: {#exr-ssg-sugra11-scaling}
#### A scaling symmetry

Under $g_{MN} \to \ell^2g_{MN}$, $B \to \ell^3B$, find the power of $\ell$ by which each term of the bosonic Lagrangian scales. Why
does this make the field equations invariant?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e \to \ell^{11}e$, $R \to \ell^{-2}R$, so $eR \to \ell^9eR$; $F^2$ has four inverse metrics, $F^2 \to \ell^{6 - 8}F^2$, and $eF^2 \to \ell^9eF^2$; the
Chern-Simons term has no metric and three $B$'s, $\ell^9$. The action scales homogeneously, $S \to \ell^9S$, so its stationary
points are mapped to stationary points: a symmetry of the field equations, though not of the action (the
"trombone" symmetry). The relative coefficient of the Chern-Simons term is not affected by such rescalings and is
fixed by supersymmetry:

{{< sage exr-ssg-sugra11-scaling >}}
:::

The field equation of the three-form contains the Chern-Simons term, which makes it non-linear. The third exercise
derives its structure schematically and checks its consistency.

::: {#exr-ssg-sugra11-b-equation}
#### The field equation of the three-form

Vary the bosonic action with respect to $B$ and show that the result has the form $d{\star}F = c\,F \wedge F$ for a constant $c$.
Why is $F \wedge F$ a closed form, as it must be for consistency?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Maxwell-type term gives $d{\star}F$ (the divergence $\partial_M(eF^{MNPQ})$), and the Chern-Simons term, cubic in $B$ with two
derivatives, gives a term $F \wedge F$ after integrating by parts (each of the three $B$'s contributes equally, which is
where the factor $3$ in front comes from) [@tanii1998, eq. 5.1]. Applying $d$ to the equation gives $0 = c\,d(F \wedge F)$,
which holds since $dF = 0$ and $d(F \wedge F) = dF \wedge F + F \wedge dF = 0$ for an even form: the equation is consistent.
:::

Reducing the eleven-dimensional theory on a circle gives type IIA supergravity in ten dimensions. The fourth exercise
carries out the first step, the metric ansatz and the choice of frame, with the reduction formula of Kaluza-Klein theory
taken as given [@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 18.1.1].

::: {#exr-ssg-iia-reduction}
#### The metric of the reduction to type IIA

Take the eleven-dimensional vielbein $\tilde e^{\hat a}{}_{\hat\mu} = \begin{pmatrix} e^{c\phi}e^a{}_\mu & 0 \\ e^\phi A_\mu & e^\phi\end{pmatrix}$
[@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 18.23], with the tangent metric $\operatorname{diag}(\eta_{ab}, -1)$ of our signature. Compute the metric
$\tilde g_{\hat\mu\hat\nu}$ and $\sqrt{|\tilde g|}$. Using that, for constant $\phi$, $\sqrt{|\tilde g|}\tilde R = e^{(8c + 1)\phi}\sqrt{|g|}(R -
\tfrac14e^{2\phi - 2c\phi}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})$, find $c$ so that the ten-dimensional Einstein term has no factor of $e^\phi$, and the
resulting factor of $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tilde g_{\hat\mu\hat\nu} = \tilde e^{\hat a}{}_{\hat\mu}\tilde e^{\hat b}{}_{\hat\nu}\eta_{\hat a\hat b}$ gives $\tilde g_{\mu\nu} = e^{2c\phi}g_{\mu\nu} - e^{2\phi}A_\mu A_\nu$,
$\tilde g_{\mu 10} = -e^{2\phi}A_\mu$, $\tilde g_{10\,10} = -e^{2\phi}$, the form of @nath2017supersymmetry [eq. 18.24] with the sign of the
circle direction of our signature. The vielbein is block triangular, so $\det\tilde e = e^{10c\phi}e^\phi\det e$ and $\sqrt{|\tilde g|} =
e^{(10c + 1)\phi}\sqrt{|g|}$; the curvature of $e^{2c\phi}g$ is $e^{-2c\phi}R$ for constant $\phi$, hence the factor $e^{(8c + 1)\phi}$. It is $1$ for $c =
-\tfrac18$, the Einstein frame, and then the vector term carries $e^{(2 - 2c)\phi} = e^{\frac94\phi}$, the exponent of
@nath2017supersymmetry [eq. 18.29]. In the factor $e^{(2 - 2c)\phi}$, the $e^{2\phi}$ is the size of the circle and the $e^{-2c\phi}$ comes
from raising the indices of $F$ with $e^{-2c\phi}g^{\mu\nu}$ and taking out the common factor $e^{-2c\phi}$ of the Einstein term.
:::

The theory is invariant under local supersymmetry with a single $32$-component parameter. The definition displays the
transformations and defines the Killing spinors of a background, which count its supersymmetries.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sugra11-transformation}
#### Local supersymmetry of the eleven-dimensional theory

The action @eq-sugra11 is invariant under
$$
\delta e_\mu{}^a = -i\bar\epsilon\gamma^a\psi_\mu, \qquad \delta B_{\mu\nu\rho} = \tfrac32\bar\epsilon\gamma_{[\mu\nu}\psi_{\rho]}, \qquad
\delta\psi_\mu = D_\mu\epsilon + \tfrac{i}{144}\left(\gamma^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}{}_\mu - 8\gamma^{\beta\gamma\delta}\delta^\alpha_\mu\right)\epsilon\,F_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}
+ (\text{3-fermi terms})
$$ {#eq-sugra11-susy}
with a $32$-component Majorana parameter $\epsilon$ [@tanii1998, eq. 5.2]. A bosonic background is
**supersymmetric** for the spinors $\epsilon$ with $\delta\psi_\mu = 0$, the **Killing spinors** of the background.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Flat space without flux is the simplest background, and every constant spinor solves the equation there. The first
example counts its Killing spinors.

::: {#exm-killing-spinor-flat}
#### Flat space

With $F = 0$ and $D_\mu = \partial_\mu$, every constant $\epsilon$ is a Killing spinor: Minkowski space preserves all $32$
supercharges, and so does its reduction on any torus, where the Killing spinors are constant (@exm-maximal-four).
:::

With flux the Killing spinor equation acquires extra terms proportional to the flux. The second example states its
form on the Freund-Rubin background.

::: {#exm-killing-spinor-flux}
#### With flux

On the Freund-Rubin background the operator $\tilde D_\mu = D_\mu + m\gamma_\mu\gamma_5$ on $AdS_4$ and $\tilde D_m = D_m -
\tfrac12m\Gamma_m$ on the internal space [@duff2025, eqs. 12-13] replaces $D$, and the Killing spinors are the
solutions of $\tilde D_m\eta = 0$ on the internal space: $8$ of them on the round $S^7$, giving $N = 8$, and $1$ on
the squashed sphere [@duff2025, Sec. 2].
:::

Without flux the Killing spinors are parallel spinors. The third example relates their existence to the holonomy of
the internal space.

::: {#exm-killing-spinor-holonomy}
#### Holonomy

Killing spinors of $D_m$ alone are parallel spinors, which exist when the holonomy group (@exm-gauss-holonomy) of the
internal manifold is reduced: $SU(3)$ on a Calabi-Yau threefold, $G_2$ on a seven-manifold, the cases of Part VI.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise counts the Killing spinors of flat space with a periodic identification. Whether the spinors
survive depends on how they are continued around the circle.

::: {#exr-ssg-killing-torus}
#### Killing spinors on a circle

On $M_{10} \times S^1$ with flat metric, the constant spinors are Killing spinors if spinors are periodic around the circle.
How many supersymmetries survive if instead the spinors are antiperiodic?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With periodic spinors every constant $\epsilon$ is globally defined and all $32$ supersymmetries survive. With antiperiodic
spinors a constant non-zero $\epsilon$ is not allowed (it would have to change sign around the circle) and the Killing
spinor equation $\partial_\mu\epsilon = 0$ has no other solutions: no supersymmetry survives, although the metric is flat. This is
the simplest Scherk-Schwarz breaking of @exm-super-higgs-reduction, the gravitino acquiring a mass $1/(2R)$.
:::

The Killing spinor equation with a mass term can be solved explicitly on a sphere. The second exercise does this on
the two-sphere, the simplest analogue of the seven-sphere of the Freund-Rubin solution.

::: {#exr-ssg-killing-s2}
#### Killing spinors on $S^2$

On the unit two-sphere with $e^1 = d\theta$, $e^2 = \sin\theta\,d\phi$, $\omega^{12} = -\cos\theta\,d\phi$ and $\gamma_a = \sigma_a$, solve $D_m\eta =
\tfrac{is}{2}\gamma_m\eta$ for $s = \pm1$, and count the solutions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $\theta$ equation $\partial_\theta\eta = \tfrac{is}{2}\sigma_1\eta$ gives $\eta = e^{is\theta\sigma_1/2}\chi(\phi)$; conjugating the $\phi$ equation by
$e^{is\theta\sigma_1/2}$ rotates $\cos\theta\,\sigma_3 + s\sin\theta\,\sigma_2$ into $\sigma_3$, leaving $\partial_\phi\chi = \tfrac12\gamma_{12}\chi$, so $\eta =
e^{is\theta\sigma_1/2}e^{\phi\gamma_{12}/2}\eta_0$ for any constant $\eta_0$: two independent solutions for each sign, the maximal number. They
are antiperiodic in $\phi$ in this frame, as spinors must be in a frame that rotates once around the pole:

{{< sage exr-ssg-killing-s2 >}}
:::

The integrability condition of the Killing spinor equation restricts the geometry. The third exercise derives it for
the equation $D_m\eta = \tfrac12m\Gamma_m\eta$ of the Freund-Rubin background.

::: {#exr-ssg-killing-integrability}
#### Integrability

In our signature the internal gamma matrices satisfy $\{\Gamma_m, \Gamma_n\} = 2g_{mn} = -2\gamma_{mn}$, so $\Gamma_m = i\hat\gamma_m$ with Hermitian
$\hat\gamma_m$, $\{\hat\gamma_m, \hat\gamma_n\} = 2\gamma_{mn}$. From $D_m\eta = \tfrac12m\Gamma_m\eta$ derive $[D_m, D_n]\eta = \tfrac12m^2\hat\gamma_{mn}\eta$, with
$\hat\gamma_{mn} = \tfrac12[\hat\gamma_m, \hat\gamma_n]$. Using $[D_m, D_n] = \tfrac14R_{mnab}\hat\gamma^{ab}$ and the curvature $R_{mnab} =
a^{-2}(\gamma_{ma}\gamma_{nb} - \gamma_{mb}\gamma_{na})$ of the round sphere of radius $a$, show that the condition holds for every $\eta$
exactly when $a = 1/m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$D_mD_n\eta = \tfrac12m\Gamma_nD_m\eta = \tfrac14m^2\Gamma_n\Gamma_m\eta$ (the gamma matrices are covariantly constant, and the Christoffel
terms cancel in the commutator because the connection has no torsion), so $[D_m, D_n]\eta = \tfrac14m^2[\Gamma_n, \Gamma_m]\eta = -
\tfrac14m^2[\hat\gamma_n, \hat\gamma_m]\eta = \tfrac12m^2\hat\gamma_{mn}\eta$. On the round sphere $\tfrac14R_{mnab}\hat\gamma^{ab} = \tfrac14a^{-2}(\hat\gamma_{mn} -
\hat\gamma_{nm}) = \tfrac12a^{-2}\hat\gamma_{mn}$, so the integrability condition $(\tfrac12a^{-2} - \tfrac12m^2)\hat\gamma_{mn}\eta = 0$ holds for every
$\eta$ exactly when $a = 1/m$, the radius of @exm-freund-rubin-s7. With Hermitian gamma matrices the same equation reads
$D_m\eta = \tfrac{i}{2}m\hat\gamma_m\eta$, the form solved on $S^2$ in @exr-ssg-killing-s2 (with $m = 1$); a real constant with Hermitian
matrices would require negative curvature instead. An internal space with fewer Killing spinors only needs the
condition on a subspace of spinors, which allows other Einstein spaces.
:::
::::

The action and the transformation rules are quoted, not derived, and so are their invariance and the closure of the
algebra. The proposition records this status explicitly, so that no later statement presents a quoted formula as
one derived here.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sugra11-text}
#### The eleven-dimensional action and transformation rules

@eq-sugra11 and @eq-sugra11-susy are *displayed and cited* from @tanii1998 [eqs. 5.1-5.2], as are the
invariance of the action and the on-shell closure of the algebra; they are not re-derived here.
:::
