:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Some consequences of the quoted formulas can nevertheless be read off directly. The first example notes that the
fermions can be set to zero consistently, which is how bosonic backgrounds are found.

::: {#exm-ssg-sugra11-truncation}
#### Setting the fermions to zero

Every term of @eq-sugra11 contains an even number of fermions, so the fermionic field equations are at least linear in
the fermions and are solved by $\psi_\mu = 0$; the bosonic equations at $\psi = 0$ are those of @exm-sugra11-bosonic. Every bosonic
solution is therefore a solution of the full theory, the starting point of the Freund-Rubin ansatz.
:::

The supersymmetry variations of the bosons are proportional to the gravitino. The second example draws the
consequence for bosonic backgrounds.

::: {#exm-ssg-sugra11-boson-variations}
#### Variations at $\psi = 0$

At $\psi_\mu = 0$, $\delta e_\mu{}^a = 0$ and $\delta B = 0$ identically by @eq-sugra11-susy, so a bosonic background is supersymmetric
exactly when $\delta\psi_\mu = 0$: the definition of Killing spinors in @def-sugra11-transformation is the whole condition.
:::

In flat space with no flux the gravitino equation reduces to that of the previous section. The third example states
this limit.

::: {#exm-ssg-sugra11-linear}
#### The linearised gravitino

Linearising @eq-sugra11 around flat space with $F = 0$, the gravitino term is the Rarita-Schwinger Lagrangian of
@def-gravitino with $D_\nu = \partial_\nu$, the eleven-dimensional gamma matrices of @exr-ssg-gamma-construction, and $128$ on-shell
states (@exm-gravitino-dof).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise makes the argument of the first example precise. It is the reason why the search for solutions of
supergravity can start with bosonic fields only.

::: {#exr-ssg-sugra11-consistency}
#### Consistency of the bosonic truncation

Show that if every term of a Lagrangian contains an even number of fermion fields, then $\psi = 0$ solves the fermion field
equations for any bosonic configuration. Does the same argument apply to setting the three-form to zero?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The fermion field equation is $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\bar\psi = 0$ (with derivatives), and differentiating a term with an even number $\geq 2$ of
fermions leaves an odd number $\geq 1$, which vanishes at $\psi = 0$. For $B$ the answer is no in general: the $B$ equation
$d{\star}F = cF \wedge F$ is solved by $F = 0$, but the Einstein equation then has no flux source, so $B = 0$ is a consistent
truncation to pure gravity; with $F \neq 0$ (Freund-Rubin) the flux must satisfy its own equation, which the ansatz does
since $F \wedge F = 0$ when $F$ lives on four directions only.
:::

The transformation of the gravitino involves products of four and three gamma matrices. The second exercise counts the
independent antisymmetrised products in eleven dimensions, the basis in which such expressions are written.

::: {#exr-ssg-clifford-count}
#### The Clifford basis in eleven dimensions

How many independent antisymmetrised products $\Gamma^{a_1\cdots a_k}$ are there in eleven dimensions, and why do the products with
$k \leq 5$ already span all $32 \times 32$ matrices?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
There are $\binom{11}{k}$ products for each $k$, $2^{11} = 2048$ in all. Since $\Gamma^0\cdots\Gamma^{10} \propto 1$ (@exr-ssg-gamma-construction),
$\Gamma^{a_1\cdots a_k}$ is proportional to $\epsilon^{a_1\cdots a_k b_1\cdots b_{11-k}}\Gamma_{b_1\cdots b_{11 - k}}$, so $k$ and $11 - k$ are dependent; $k = 0, \dots,
5$ give $1 + 11 + 55 + 165 + 330 + 462 = 1024 = 32^2$, exactly the dimension of the $32 \times 32$ matrices. The gravitino variation uses
$\Gamma^{(4)}$ and $\Gamma^{(3)}$, and the Pauli term of @eq-sugra11 uses $\Gamma^{(6)} \propto \Gamma^{(5)}$.
:::

The quoted transformations can be tested on dimensions. The third exercise checks that the flux term in $\delta\psi_\mu$ has the
same dimension as $D_\mu\epsilon$.

::: {#exr-ssg-sugra11-dimensions}
#### Dimensions of the transformation rules

In units where the eleven-dimensional gravitational constant is set to a number, give the length dimensions of $e_\mu{}^a$,
$B$, $F$ and $\epsilon$ for which the terms of $\delta\psi_\mu$ in @eq-sugra11-susy are consistent, with $\psi_\mu$ of the same dimension as $D_\mu\epsilon$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With the gravitational constant set to a number, the only scale is a length. Take coordinates with the dimension of
length, so that the metric and the vielbein are dimensionless, and so are $\Gamma^a$ and $\gamma^\mu = e_a{}^\mu\Gamma^a$; take $\epsilon$
dimensionless too. Then $D_\mu\epsilon$ has dimension $[\text{length}]^{-1}$, and since the flux term contains $F_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}$ contracted
with dimensionless gamma matrices and inverse metrics, $F$ must have dimension $[\text{length}]^{-1}$, like a connection. With
$F = 4\partial_{[\mu}B_{\nu\rho\sigma]}$, $B$ is dimensionless, like the metric. The action is then consistent: $eR$ and $eF^2$ both have
dimension $[\text{length}]^{-2}$, and the Chern-Simons term $\epsilon FFB$ the same, the overall factor $1/(16\pi G_{11})$ supplying
the remaining $[\text{length}]^{-9}$.
:::
::::

#### The Freund-Rubin solution

The simplest way to curl up seven dimensions in eleven-dimensional supergravity is to let the four-form flux fill
spacetime. The field equations then force spacetime to be anti-de Sitter and the internal space to be an Einstein
space of positive curvature; the definition states the ansatz and the resulting curvatures in our signature.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-freund-rubin-ansatz}
#### Freund-Rubin ansatz

On a product $M_4 \times X_7$ the **Freund-Rubin ansatz** fills the four-form flux along spacetime,
$$
F_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = 3m\,\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}, \qquad F_{mnpq} = 0, \qquad F_{\mu\nu\rho m} = \dots = 0,
$$ {#eq-freund-rubin}
with a constant $m$ [@duff2025, eq. 9]; the Levi-Civita contractions $\epsilon_{\mu\alpha\beta\gamma}\epsilon_\nu{}^{\alpha\beta\gamma}
= -6g_{\mu\nu}$ and $\epsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\epsilon^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} = -24$ (@prp-levi-contraction), which hold in
either signature since they depend only on $\det\eta = -1$, turn the field equations into $R_{\mu\nu} = 12m^2g_{\mu\nu}$
and $R_{mn} = -6m^2g_{mn}$ in our signature: spacetime is anti-de Sitter (in $(+, -, -, -)$ a positive multiple of
$g_{\mu\nu}$ is negative curvature, the opposite of the de Sitter sign $R_{\mu\nu} = -3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ of
@exm-vacuum-de-sitter) and the internal space, with $g_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$, an Einstein manifold of positive curvature,
$R_{mn} = 6m^2\gamma_{mn}$. @duff2025 [eqs. 10-11] write $R_{\mu\nu} = -12m^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $R_{mn} = 6m^2g_{mn}$ in the
mostly-plus metric, the same geometry (@prp-freund-rubin).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The round seven-sphere is the first example. Its radius and the anti-de Sitter radius follow from the curvatures of
the definition.

::: {#exm-freund-rubin-s7}
#### $AdS_4 \times S^7$

The round seven-sphere of radius $a$ has $R_{mn} = 6a^{-2}\gamma_{mn}$ for its positive-definite metric
(@exm-einstein-spheres), so $a = 1/m$, and $AdS_4$ of radius $L$, with $R_{\mu\nu} = 3L^{-2}g_{\mu\nu}$ in our signature, has
$L = 1/2m$: the sphere is twice as large as the anti-de Sitter radius, and the
four-dimensional cosmological constant is $\Lambda = -12m^2$, huge and negative (@exr-freund-rubin).
:::

Nothing in the field equations requires the round sphere, only an Einstein metric with the right constant. The second
example lists other internal spaces, all of them coset spaces.

::: {#exm-freund-rubin-einstein}
#### Any Einstein seven-manifold

The internal equations ask only for $R_{mn} = 6m^2\gamma_{mn}$, so every compact Einstein seven-manifold with positive
curvature gives a Freund-Rubin solution: the squashed $S^7$, the spaces $M^{pqr}$, $N^{pqr}$ and $Q^{pqr}$, all coset
spaces $G/H$ of the kind studied in Part I [@duff2025, Sec. 8]; how much supersymmetry survives depends on their
Killing spinors.
:::

The sign of the flux is a further choice that the field equations do not fix. The third example describes the
solution obtained by reversing it.

::: {#exm-freund-rubin-dual}
#### Orientation reversal

Reversing the sign of $m$ (equivalently the orientation of $X_7$) gives another solution with the same curvatures,
the **skew-whiffed** background, which in general preserves no supersymmetry although it is classically stable
[@duff2025, p. 5].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise extracts the four-dimensional cosmological constant from the curvature of the definition. Its size
is set by the internal radius.

::: {#exr-fr-cosmological}
#### The cosmological constant of the Freund-Rubin vacuum

From $R_{\mu\nu} = 12m^2g_{\mu\nu}$ find $\Lambda$ in the four-dimensional Einstein equations and compare its scale with
the internal radius.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A vacuum solution with cosmological constant has $R_{\mu\nu} = -\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ in four dimensions
(@def-vacuum-solution), so $\Lambda = -12m^2 = -12/a^2$ with $a$ the sphere radius: a negative cosmological constant of
the order of the inverse square of the internal size, far too large in magnitude for any realistic internal radius.
Removing it requires additional ingredients, the central difficulty of flux compactifications in Part VI.
:::

The ratio of the two radii is fixed. The second exercise derives it and the scalar curvatures of the two factors.

::: {#exr-ssg-fr-radii}
#### The two radii

From the curvatures of the definition compute $L/a$ for $AdS_4 \times S^7$ and the scalar curvatures of the two factors, and check
that they add up to the eleven-dimensional $R = 6m^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$12m^2 = 3/L^2$ gives $L = 1/(2m)$ and $6m^2 = 6/a^2$ gives $a = 1/m$, so $L/a = \tfrac12$. The traces are $g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu} = 4 \cdot 12m^2
= 48m^2$ and $g^{mn}R_{mn} = 7\cdot(-6m^2) = -42m^2$, adding up to $6m^2$, the eleven-dimensional scalar curvature of
@prp-freund-rubin. In terms of the positive-definite $\gamma_{mn}$ the sphere has scalar curvature $+42m^2 = 42/a^2$, the value
$n(n - 1)/a^2$ for $n = 7$.
:::

The Freund-Rubin construction works with the flux on the internal space as well, when the internal space has four
dimensions. The third exercise finds the resulting $AdS_7 \times S^4$ with a brute-force computation of the contractions.

::: {#exr-ssg-fr-ads7}
#### $AdS_7 \times S^4$

With $F_{mnpq} = c\,\epsilon_{mnpq}$ on the four internal directions, compute $F_{MPQR}F_N{}^{PQR}$ and $F^2$ at a point in an orthonormal frame,
use $R_{MN} = -\tfrac13(F_{MPQR}F_N{}^{PQR} - \tfrac{1}{12}g_{MN}F^2)$ (@exr-ssg-fr-trace-reversed), and find the two radii. Check the same code on $AdS_4
\times S^7$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F^2 = 24c^2$, $R_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac23c^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $R_{mn} = -\tfrac43c^2g_{mn}$, so $L_{AdS_7}^2 = 9/c^2$ and $a_{S^4}^2 = 9/(4c^2)$: here the anti-de Sitter
radius is twice the sphere radius, the opposite of $AdS_4 \times S^7$, which the same code reproduces with $c = 3m$:

{{< sage exr-ssg-fr-ads7 >}}
:::
::::

The curvatures of the definition rest on two contractions of the Levi-Civita symbol in Lorentzian signature. The
proposition states them; both are finite sums that can be evaluated over all index values.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-levi-contraction}
#### Levi-Civita contractions

In Lorentzian signature, $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$, with $\epsilon_{0123} = 1$ and indices raised by $\eta$,
$\sum_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\epsilon_{\mu\alpha\beta\gamma}
\epsilon_{\nu\alpha\beta\gamma}\eta^{\alpha\alpha}\eta^{\beta\beta}\eta^{\gamma\gamma} = -6\eta_{\mu\nu}$ and the full contraction is $-24$ (both
values depend only on $\det\eta = -1$).
:::

exhaustive evaluation.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Supergravity.levi_contraction >}}

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example evaluates the contraction on the time-time component. Only the three spatial indices can be
contracted, and each raised spatial index contributes a minus sign.

::: {#exm-ssg-levi-time}
#### The time component

For $\mu = \nu = 0$ the indices $\alpha\beta\gamma$ run over the $3! = 6$ orderings of $1, 2, 3$, each with $\epsilon_{0\alpha\beta\gamma}^2 = 1$ and
$\eta^{\alpha\alpha}\eta^{\beta\beta}\eta^{\gamma\gamma} = (-1)^3$: the sum is $-6 = -6\eta_{00}$.
:::

A spatial component contains the time index among the contracted ones. The second example shows that the sign then
comes out opposite, as the formula requires.

::: {#exm-ssg-levi-space}
#### A spatial component

For $\mu = \nu = 1$ the contracted indices are orderings of $0, 2, 3$, and $\eta^{00}\eta^{22}\eta^{33} = (+1)(-1)(-1) = +1$: the sum is
$+6 = -6\eta_{11}$. Off-diagonal components vanish because $\epsilon_{\mu\alpha\beta\gamma}\epsilon_{\nu\alpha\beta\gamma}$ needs $\{\mu\} = \{\nu\}$ as the missing index.
:::

The general rule is that the contractions carry the sign of the determinant. The third example compares Euclidean
and Lorentzian signature and the seven-dimensional internal metric of our convention.

::: {#exm-ssg-levi-sign}
#### The sign of the determinant

In $n$ dimensions $\epsilon_{m a_1\cdots a_{n - 1}}\epsilon_n{}^{a_1\cdots a_{n - 1}} = (n - 1)!\,\operatorname{sign}(\det g)\,g_{mn}$ and the full contraction is
$n!\operatorname{sign}(\det g)$: $+6\delta_{\mu\nu}$ and $+24$ in Euclidean four dimensions, $-6\eta_{\mu\nu}$ and $-24$ in Lorentzian, and for the internal
metric $g_{mn} = -\delta_{mn}$ of seven dimensions $720\cdot(-1)g_{mn} = 720\delta_{mn}$ and $-5040$ (@exr-ssg-levi-signatures).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the general rule of the third example by brute force. It covers all three cases needed for
the Freund-Rubin solution.

::: {#exr-ssg-levi-signatures}
#### Contractions in three signatures

Compute $\epsilon_{m\cdots}\epsilon_n{}^{\cdots}$ and the full contraction for $g = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1, 1, 1)$, $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$ and $-1_7$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The results are $(n - 1)!\operatorname{sign}(\det g)g_{mn}$ and $n!\operatorname{sign}(\det g)$ in all three cases:

{{< sage exr-ssg-levi-signatures >}}

:::

Contractions over fewer indices give antisymmetrised Kronecker deltas. The second exercise derives the two-index case,
which appears when the flux is contracted with two free indices.

::: {#exr-ssg-levi-two}
#### Two free indices

Show that in four Lorentzian dimensions $\epsilon_{\mu\nu\alpha\beta}\epsilon^{\rho\sigma\alpha\beta} = -2(\delta_\mu^\rho\delta_\nu^\sigma - \delta_\mu^\sigma\delta_\nu^\rho)$, and recover the
proposition by contracting $\nu$ with $\sigma$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both sides are antisymmetric in $\mu\nu$ and in $\rho\sigma$ and invariant under rotations and boosts, so the left side is a multiple
$k(\delta_\mu^\rho\delta_\nu^\sigma - \delta_\mu^\sigma\delta_\nu^\rho)$. For $\mu\nu = 01$ and $\rho\sigma = 01$ the left side is $\epsilon_{0123}\epsilon^{0123} + \epsilon_{0132}\epsilon^{0132} =
2\epsilon_{0123}\epsilon^{0123} = 2\cdot(-1)$, since raising four indices gives $\det\eta^{-1} = -1$; so $k = -2$. Contracting $\nu = \sigma$:
$\epsilon_{\mu\nu\alpha\beta}\epsilon^{\rho\nu\alpha\beta} = -2(4\delta_\mu^\rho - \delta_\mu^\rho) = -6\delta_\mu^\rho$, which is the proposition with one index lowered.
:::

The Lorentzian sign is easy to lose when converting between conventions. The third exercise asks what happens to
the Freund-Rubin curvatures if the contraction is taken with the wrong sign.

::: {#exr-ssg-levi-wrong-sign}
#### A sign check

If one used the Euclidean values $+6g_{\mu\nu}$ and $+24$ in the Freund-Rubin computation, what would come out for $R_{\mu\nu}$ and $R_{mn}$?
Why is this geometrically impossible for a compact internal space with the flux along spacetime?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With the trace-reversed equation $R_{MN} = -\tfrac13(FF_{MN} - \tfrac1{12}g_{MN}F^2)$, the Euclidean values $FF_{\mu\nu} = +54m^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $F^2 = +216m^2$
give $R_{\mu\nu} = -\tfrac13(54 - 18)m^2g_{\mu\nu} = -12m^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $R_{mn} = +6m^2g_{mn} = -6m^2\gamma_{mn}$: a negatively curved internal space. A
compact Einstein space of negative curvature has no continuous isometries (by Bochner's theorem), so no gauge fields
would arise from it, and the spacetime would be de Sitter; the actual result, with the Lorentzian sign, is $AdS_4$ times a positively
curved sphere, as in @duff2025. The sign of $\det\eta$ is what makes the internal space a sphere.
:::
::::

With the contractions in hand, the field equations on the ansatz become algebraic. The proposition states the result,
and the examples that follow carry out the computation step by step.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-freund-rubin}
#### The Freund-Rubin curvatures

On the ansatz @eq-freund-rubin, $F_{\mu PQR}F_\nu{}^{PQR} = -54m^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $F^2 = -216m^2$; with the field equations
$R_{MN} - \tfrac12g_{MN}R = -\tfrac13(F_{MPQR}F_N{}^{PQR} - \tfrac18g_{MN}F^2)$ of @exm-sugra11-bosonic this gives $R = 6m^2$,
$R_{\mu\nu} = 12m^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $R_{mn} = -6m^2g_{mn}$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example evaluates the two flux contractions on the ansatz. They are $9m^2$ times the Levi-Civita contractions
of the previous proposition.

::: {#exm-ssg-fr-contractions}
#### The flux contractions

$F_{\mu PQR}F_\nu{}^{PQR} = 9m^2\epsilon_{\mu\alpha\beta\gamma}\epsilon_\nu{}^{\alpha\beta\gamma} = 9m^2(-6g_{\mu\nu}) = -54m^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $F_{mPQR}F_n{}^{PQR} = 0$ since $F$ has no
internal index, and $F^2 = 9m^2(-24) = -216m^2$.
:::

The trace of the field equation determines the scalar curvature first, before the individual Ricci components. The
second example carries out this step.

::: {#exm-ssg-fr-trace}
#### The scalar curvature

Tracing the eleven-dimensional equation, $R - \tfrac{11}{2}R = -\tfrac13(F^2 - \tfrac{11}{8}F^2) = \tfrac18F^2$, so $R = -\tfrac{1}{36}F^2 = 6m^2$;
substituting back gives the trace-reversed form $R_{MN} = -\tfrac13(F_{MPQR}F_N{}^{PQR} - \tfrac{1}{12}g_{MN}F^2)$ (@exr-ssg-fr-trace-reversed).
:::

The Ricci tensors then follow by substitution. The third example gives them and the check that their traces add up.

::: {#exm-ssg-fr-ricci}
#### The two Ricci tensors

$R_{\mu\nu} = -\tfrac13(-54m^2 + 18m^2)g_{\mu\nu} = 12m^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $R_{mn} = -\tfrac13(0 + 18m^2)g_{mn} = -6m^2g_{mn}$; the traces $4\cdot12m^2 + 7\cdot(-6m^2) =
6m^2$ reproduce $R$ (@exr-ssg-fr-radii).
:::

::: {#exr-ssg-fr-trace-reversed}
#### The trace-reversed field equation

Show that $R_{MN} - \tfrac12g_{MN}R = -\tfrac13(FF_{MN} - \tfrac18g_{MN}F^2)$ in eleven dimensions is equivalent to $R = -\tfrac1{36}F^2$ and
$R_{MN} = -\tfrac13(FF_{MN} - \tfrac1{12}g_{MN}F^2)$, and evaluate on the Freund-Rubin ansatz.

The third exercise asks how the solution depends on the one free parameter. The answer shows that the flux quantum
fixes all scales.

::: {#exr-ssg-fr-scaling}
#### The flux sets the scale

How do the radii $L$ and $a$, the cosmological constant and the volume of $S^7$ depend on $m$? Using the scaling symmetry of
@exr-ssg-sugra11-scaling, explain why a one-parameter family of solutions was to be expected.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$L = 1/(2m)$, $a = 1/m$, $\Lambda = -12m^2$ and $\operatorname{Vol}(S^7) = \tfrac{\pi^4}{3}a^7 \propto m^{-7}$. The scaling $g \to \ell^2g$, $B \to \ell^3B$
maps solutions to solutions and multiplies all lengths by $\ell$. On the ansatz, $F_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} \to \ell^3F_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ while the tensor
$\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$, which contains $\sqrt{|g|}$, goes to $\ell^4\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$, so $F = 3m\epsilon$ is mapped to the ansatz with $m \to m/\ell$.
The scaling therefore generates the whole family from one solution, and the dimensionless ratio $L/a = \tfrac12$ cannot
depend on $m$. In the quantum theory the flux through $S^7$ is quantised, which fixes $m$ in Planck units.
:::
::::

Not every Freund-Rubin solution is equally supersymmetric. The definition counts the four-dimensional
supersymmetries of a compactification by the Killing spinors of its internal space.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-supercharge-counting}
#### Counting preserved supercharges

The number of four-dimensional supersymmetries of a compactification is the number of Killing spinors of the
internal background (@def-sugra11-transformation): $N$ counts the independent solutions of $\delta\psi_m = 0$, and the
four-dimensional theory has $4N$ real supercharges. A torus preserves all $32$; a Freund-Rubin sphere preserves
$N = 8$; manifolds of special holonomy preserve fractions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The torus is the simplest case, since it is flat and has no flux. The first example counts its Killing spinors.

::: {#exm-counting-torus}
#### The torus

$T^7$ is flat, every constant spinor is parallel, and all $32$ supercharges survive as the $N = 8$ of
@exm-maximal-four: dimensional reduction on a torus never breaks supersymmetry.
:::

The same manifold can preserve different amounts of supersymmetry with different metrics. The second example
compares the round and the squashed seven-sphere.

::: {#exm-counting-sphere}
#### Round and squashed spheres

The round $S^7$ has $8$ Killing spinors ($N = 8$ in four dimensions, the gauged $SO(8)$ supergravity), the squashed
$S^7$ has $1$ ($N = 1$), and its skew-whiffed version none [@duff2025, Sec. 2]: the same manifold with different
metrics or orientations gives different amounts of supersymmetry.
:::

Without flux, a reduced holonomy group leaves some spinors invariant. The third example lists the fractions that
result for the special holonomy groups.

::: {#exm-counting-special-holonomy}
#### Special holonomy

Reducing on a Calabi-Yau threefold preserves $\tfrac14$ of the supercharges ($N = 2$ from eleven or ten dimensions)
and a $G_2$-manifold $\tfrac18$ ($N = 1$), the fractions dictated by the invariant spinors of @exm-killing-spinor-holonomy;
these are the compactifications of Part VI, and CSDR with supersymmetry breaking by the coset
(@manousselis2000) is their field-theory counterpart.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise converts fractions of preserved supersymmetry into four-dimensional $N$. It is arithmetic, but it
makes the dictionary explicit.

::: {#exr-ssg-count-fractions}
#### From fractions to $N$

A compactification of eleven-dimensional supergravity to four dimensions preserves a fraction $f$ of the $32$
supercharges. Give $N$ for $f = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18$ and name an internal space realising each.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$N = 32f/4 = 8f$: $f = 1$, $N = 8$ ($T^7$, or the round $S^7$ with flux); $f = \tfrac12$, $N = 4$ ($K3 \times T^3$, holonomy $SU(2)$); $f = \tfrac14$,
$N = 2$ ($CY_3 \times S^1$, holonomy $SU(3)$); $f = \tfrac18$, $N = 1$ (a $G_2$-manifold, or the squashed $S^7$ with flux). Each halving
corresponds to a further reduction of the holonomy group, which leaves fewer of the eight internal spinor components
invariant.
:::

The holonomy argument can be made concrete in the simplest case. The second exercise counts the invariant spinors of
$SU(2) \subset SO(4)$ acting on the spinors of four Euclidean dimensions.

::: {#exr-ssg-holonomy-su2}
#### Invariant spinors of $SU(2)$ holonomy

The spinor of $SO(4) = SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R$ is $(\mathbf 2, \mathbf 1) \oplus (\mathbf 1, \mathbf 2)$. If the holonomy is $SU(2)_L$, how many spinor components
are invariant? What fraction of supersymmetry does a four-dimensional internal space with this holonomy (a K3
surface) preserve?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$SU(2)_L$ acts on $(\mathbf 2, \mathbf 1)$ as a doublet, which has no invariant vector, and trivially on $(\mathbf 1, \mathbf 2)$, which gives $2$ invariant
components out of $4$: half of the spinor is parallel, and a K3 surface preserves half of the supersymmetry. This
is the mechanism behind the $f = \tfrac12$ case of @exr-ssg-count-fractions and the analogue, with $SU(3) \subset SO(6)$ and $G_2 \subset
SO(7)$, of @exm-counting-special-holonomy.
:::

The third exercise returns to the explicit Killing spinors of @exr-ssg-killing-s2. It compares the count on the
two-sphere with that on the seven-sphere.

::: {#exr-ssg-count-spheres}
#### Killing spinors on spheres

On $S^n$ of radius $1/m$ the equation $D_m\eta = \pm\tfrac12m\Gamma_m\eta$ (with the factor $i$ of @exr-ssg-killing-s2 in even dimensions) has, for
each sign, as many solutions as the dimension of the spinor. Give the numbers for $S^2$ and $S^7$, and explain the $N = 8$ of
$AdS_4 \times S^7$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $S^2$ the spinor has $2$ complex components and there are $2$ solutions for each sign (@exr-ssg-killing-s2). On $S^7$ the
spinor of $SO(7)$ has $8$ components, and the round sphere has $8$ Killing spinors for each sign of the constant. The flux
selects the sign that enters $\delta\psi_m = 0$, and each of the $8$ solutions, tensored with the four-component Killing spinors of
$AdS_4$, gives a four-dimensional supersymmetry: $N = 8$, all $32$ supercharges preserved (@exm-counting-sphere). Because the
round sphere has Killing spinors of both signs, both orientations of the flux preserve $N = 8$; skew-whiffing breaks
supersymmetry only for internal spaces, such as the squashed sphere, whose Killing spinors all have one sign
[@duff2025, Sec. 2].
:::
::::

### Exercises {#sec-supergravity-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the sections of this part: eleven-dimensional supergravity reduced on a torus and
compared with the helicity ladder of $N = 8$, the Freund-Rubin vacuum $AdS_4 \times S^7$ from the flux to the supersymmetry it
preserves, and the super-Higgs mechanism in the O'Raifeartaigh model coupled to supergravity.

The first integrative exercise checks the reduction on $T^7$ against the representation theory of the first part. The
fields, the fermions and the supercharges are all counted in Sage.

::: {#exr-ssg-sugra-11-to-4}
#### From eleven to four dimensions

Reduce eleven-dimensional supergravity on $T^7$: list the four-dimensional bosons from the metric and the three-form and
the fermions from the gravitino, compare with the CPT-completed $N = 8$ ladder of @prp-ssg-massless-multiplets, count the
states, and count the four-dimensional supercharges.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Bosons: $1$ graviton, $7 + 21 = 28$ vectors, $28 + 35 + 7 = 70$ scalars (the seven two-forms dualised). Fermions: $32 = 8 \times 4$
gives $8$ gravitini and $7 \times 8 = 56$ spin-$\tfrac12$ fields. These are the multiplicities $1, 8, 28, 56, 70$ of the ladder, with
$128 + 128$ states, and the $32$ real supercharges become $N = 8$ four-component ones (@exm-counting-torus):

{{< sage exr-ssg-sugra-11-to-4 >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise follows the Freund-Rubin vacuum from the flux to the four-dimensional theory. It
uses the curvature computation, the Killing spinors and the supergravity multiplets.

::: {#exr-ssg-sugra-ads4-s7}
#### The $AdS_4 \times S^7$ vacuum

For the Freund-Rubin ansatz with parameter $m$ on the round $S^7$: (a) give the radii, the cosmological constant and the
eleven-dimensional scalar curvature; (b) the number of preserved supersymmetries; (c) the isometry group of $S^7$ and the
number of four-dimensional gauge fields it provides; (d) compare with the field content of the $N = 8$ multiplet, and
say which coupling distinguishes the resulting theory from the $T^7$ reduction.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $a = 1/m$, $L = 1/(2m)$, $\Lambda = -12m^2$, $R = 6m^2$ (@prp-freund-rubin, @exr-ssg-fr-radii). (b) Eight Killing spinors, $N = 8$, all
$32$ supercharges (@exr-ssg-count-spheres). (c) The isometry group is $SO(8)$, of dimension $28$; each Killing vector gives a
gauge field in the reduction (@sec-flows-killing). (d) The $N = 8$ multiplet has exactly $28$ vectors
(@exm-ssg-ladders-n8), which on $S^7$ gauge $SO(8)$: the four-dimensional theory is the gauged $SO(8)$ supergravity of
@exm-sugra-multiplet-gauged, with the gauge coupling $g \propto m$ setting the cosmological constant $\propto -g^2$ and the gravitino
mass-like terms, absent in the ungauged $T^7$ reduction where the vectors are abelian.
:::

The third integrative exercise couples supersymmetry breaking to gravity. It combines the O'Raifeartaigh model, the
goldstino and the super-Higgs mechanism.

::: {#exr-ssg-sugra-super-higgs}
#### The O'Raifeartaigh model in supergravity

Couple the O'Raifeartaigh model (with $m^2 > yk$) to $N = 1$ supergravity. (a) Which fermion is eaten, and how many states
does the gravitino have afterwards? (b) Give $m_{3/2}$ in terms of $k$ and $M_P$, and its value for $\sqrt k = 10^{11}$ GeV. (c) What
must be added to $W$ to have zero vacuum energy, and how does this change the count of fermions? (d) Count all
on-shell states before and after the breaking.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) The goldstino is $\psi_1$ (@exr-ssg-goldstino); it supplies the helicities $\pm\tfrac12$ of the massive gravitino, which has $4$ states
(@exr-ssg-super-higgs-states). (b) $F = k$, so $m_{3/2} = k/(\sqrt3M_P) \approx 2.4$ TeV for $\sqrt k = 10^{11}$ GeV (@exr-ssg-gravitino-mass-scale).
(c) A constant $W_0$ with $|W_0| = kM_P/\sqrt3$ cancels the vacuum energy $k^2$ in $V = |F|^2 - 3|W|^2/M_P^2$
(@exr-ssg-super-higgs-cosmological); the fermion content is unchanged except that $\psi_1$ is now part of the gravitino. (d)
Before: graviton $2$ + three complex scalars $6$ = $8$ bosonic; gravitino $2$ + three Weyl fermions $6$ = $8$ fermionic. After:
the same $8$ bosonic states (the scalars split in mass, @exm-breaking-oraifeartaigh), and a massive gravitino $4$ plus two
Weyl fermions $\psi_2, \psi_3$ forming a Dirac fermion of mass $m$, $4$: still $8$. The super-Higgs mechanism reshuffles states
between fields without changing their number.
:::
::::
